The interval fixes that by reporting x̄ ± margin of error : “we are 95% confident the true cost increase lies between 0.9% and 2.1%.” The probability is set first, the range follows — the mirror image of ordinary probability problems. 02 The margin of error machine E = z(α/2) · σ/√n — three z-values worth memorising α = .10 · α/2 = .05 90% z = 1.645 α = .05 · α/2 = .025 95% z = 1.960 α = .01 · α/2 = .005 99% z = 2.576 03 Worked — the new-store decision 260 outlets, n = 36, x̄ = $41,100, σ = $4,500, 95% confidence The full computation — income in the marketing area α = 1 − 0.95 = 0.05 α/2 = 0.025 z(α/2) = 1.960 σx̄ = σ/√n = 4,500/√36 = 750 ← standard error E = 1.960 × 750 = 1,470 ← margin of error 95% CI = x̄ ± E = 41,100 ± 1,470 = [39,630 , 42,570] Compare: 90% → 41,100 ± 1,234 → [39,866 , 42,334] 99% → 41,100 ± 1,932 → [39,168 , 43,032] The confidence dial — buy certainty with width pick a confidence level 90% confidence · z = 1.645 95% confidence · z = 1.96 99% confidence · z = 2.576 x̄ = 41,100 39,630 42,570 Margin of error ±1,470 Interval width 2,940 The trade-off more confidence → wider interval Like planning a journey: a bigger time margin (99%) almost guarantees arrival — but the statement gets vaguer. A tight margin (90%) is sharper yet more likely to miss. Same data, same σ — confidence is purchased with width . 04 Read the interval like a statistician What 95% confidence does — and does not — mean The correct reading “95% confident” is a statement about the procedure , not one interval: if we built intervals from many samples this way, 95% of them would capture μ . Alpha is split evenly between the two tails because the normal curve is symmetric — that is why z(α/2) carries the “half”. How big should n be? n > 30 rides the Central Limit Theorem. Roughly normal or symmetric populations tolerate n ≈ 15; highly skewed populations (income is the classic) want 50+ . Bigger samples narrow the interval — the precision budget vs cost trade-off is a management decision, not a formula output. 05 Check yourself Two quick taps All else equal, moving from 95% to 99% confidence makes the interval… Lecture 22 · check A wider B narrower C unchanged D first narrower, then wider Increasing the sample size from 50 to 200 stores (Sahadri) makes the margin of error… Lecture 22 · check A 1/4 of the original B 1/2 of the original C 4× the original D unchanged — n does not affect E Key takeaways Interval estimation fixes probability first and computes the range second: x̄ ± z(α/2)·σ/√n . The three z-values: 1.645 (90%), 1.960 (95%), 2.576 (99%) — alpha is split across both tails. Income decision: 41,100 ± 1,470 → [39,630, 42,570] at 95%; the dial shows the 90/99 versions. Confidence is a procedure guarantee — 95% of intervals built this way capture μ — and width is the price of confidence. Only n buys both.

chapters.label: The sampling lab
chapters.text: Lecture 23 — sampling distributions, by hand in Excel The sampling laboratory Theory, verified with a spreadsheet. This lecture builds a population of 2,500 employees, draws dozens of random samples of 50, and watches the sample means cluster around μ = 71,800 — the sampling distribution made visible, plus the assessment update everyone was waiting for. 01 Assessment update Announced in this lecture — in writing by week's end The quiz pattern, revised Count two quizzes total (not three) — best of the two scores counts Quiz 2 syllabus everything through Chapter 8 — interval estimation included Logistics dates and details communicated in writing by the end of the week (Lecture 13's original plan — two 20-mark quizzes plus a combined syllabus quiz, best two of three — is superseded by this.) 02 The RANDBETWEEN recipe Draw a random sample of 50 salaries from 2,500 01 · draw =RANDBETWEEN(1, 2500) in a helper column — one random ID per draw slot 02 · fill copy the formula across all 50 rows of the sample 03 · freeze Copy → Paste Special → Values Only — THE step everyone skips 04 · sort sort the IDs ascending (filter → sort) to fetch matching salaries 05 · measure =AVERAGE(B2:B51) — the sample mean of your 50 draws 06 · repeat draw again: every independent sample yields a different x̄ — that IS the sampling distribution The trap — why step 03 exists RANDBETWEEN is volatile : every edit, sort or recalculation redraws every number, so an unfrozen sample mutates while you analyse it. Paste-Special-Values converts the formulas to static IDs — the sample exists, the way a photograph stops the wind. Sort after freezing, never before. 03 What the draws showed The empirical sampling distribution The population and the draws population: 2,500 employee salaries μ = 71,800 · σ = 4,000 sample: n = 50, drawn repeatedly observed sample means across draws: ≈ 71,000 · 71,400 · 71,900 72,100 · 72,500 … all hovering near μ = 71,800 — none wandering far: σx̄ = 4000/√50 ≈ 566 Why random sampling is non-negotiable · every element must carry an EQUAL chance of selection — otherwise the mean aims somewhere other than μ · sampling is cheaper and faster than the census — sometimes the census is impossible outright · each INDEPENDENT random sample gives a different mean: the wobble is not error in your work, it is the object of study 04 The SE shrink machine Buy precision with √n — live The SE shrink machine — σ = 4,000 salaries, choose your n n = 25 n = 50 n = 100 n = 200 n = 400 σx̄ = 4000/√n 565.69 ±1.96·σx̄ (95% band) ±1109 Band width 2217 μ = 71,800 · the violet band is where 95% of sample means land Fourfold n buys a halved standard error: 25 → 800, 100 → 400, 400 → 200. Precision is sold at √n per unit — the lecture's empirical means (71,000–72,500 at n = 50) sit comfortably inside the ±784 band this machine shows. 05 Check yourself Two lab questions Your RANDBETWEEN sample keeps changing every time you sort the sheet. The fix is… Sampling lab · check A Copy → Paste Special → Values Only — convert formulas to static numbers B sort descending instead C widen the columns D replace RANDBETWEEN with AVERAGE Population salaries: μ = 71,800, σ = 4,000. At n = 50 the standard error is ≈ 566. At n = 200 it is… Sampling lab · check A ≈ 283 — quadrupling n halves σx̄ B ≈ 1,132 — it doubles C ≈ 566 — n does not affect σx̄ D ≈ 142 Key takeaways Assessment : two quizzes, best-of-2, Quiz 2 through Chapter 8 — details in writing by week's end. The recipe : RANDBETWEEN → fill → paste values → sort → AVERAGE → repeat; the paste-values step is what makes the sample real. The sight : n = 50 means hovering at 71,000–72,500 around μ = 71,800 — the sampling distribution, seen not imagined; σx̄ = 566 → 283 when n quadruples.

chapters.label: The t-distribution
chapters.text: Lecture 24 · Interval Estimation — population σ unknown Student's t — honesty about σ Real populations rarely hand you σ. When it is unknown, the sample must estimate both the mean and the spread — and that extra estimation costs width. The t-distribution is the price list, and degrees of freedom is the currency. 01 Guinness, small samples, and a pseudonym 1908 — 'Student' publishes while brewing in Dublin Why a new distribution at all? Replace σ with s in the margin of error and the ratio (x̄ − μ)/(s/√n) no longer follows the normal curve — the sample standard deviation wobbles too. William Gosset, working quality control at Guinness, mapped the true curve and published under the name “Student” . Symmetric around zero like the normal — but a family of curves indexed by df, each with slightly heavier tails. Degrees of freedom = n − 1 df counts the independent pieces of information going into s. Estimating the mean from the same n values spends one piece — fixing one value determines the last — so df = n − 1 . More df → less dispersion → closer to normal; beyond df ≈ 100 treat t as z. 02 The decision rule Known σ → z · unknown σ → t with s in its place One shelf, two intervals σ KNOWN σ UNKNOWN ——————————————— ——————————————— x̄ ± z(α/2) · σ/√n x̄ ± t(α/2) · s/√n ↑ n − 1 df from the t-table Both shrink at the same √n speed. The t merely charges a honesty premium for the estimated standard deviation. The df morph — heavy tails at small n drag the degrees of freedom normal (z) t (df = 15) heavier tails → wider intervals Degrees of freedom df = n − 1 = 15 t(0.025, df) — the 95% multiplier 2.131 vs the z it is standing in for 1.960 paying 0.171 extra width for estimating σ Slide df down toward 1 and the violet curve grows heavy tails — extra uncertainty from estimating σ with s. Past df ≈ 100 the t is indistinguishable from the dashed normal. The curve is not one distribution but a family , one member per df. 03 Worked — off-campus housing n = 16 one-bedroom apartments · x̄ = $750 · s = $55 · 95% confidence The full computation — mean monthly rent near campus α = 0.05 α/2 = 0.025 df = n − 1 = 15 t(0.025, 15) = 2.131 ← from the t-table σx̄ → s/√n = 55/√16 = 13.75 E = 2.131 × 13.75 = 29.3 95% CI = 750 ± 29.3 = [720.7 , 779.3] "We are 95% confident the mean monthly rent within half a mile of campus is between $720.70 and $779.30." 04 Planning in reverse — how big a sample? n = (z·σ/E)² — and always round UP Discount Sounds — margin of $500 Goal: estimate mean annual income within ±$500 at 95% confidence; planning value σ = 4,500 (from a previous study). n = (z(α/2) · σ / E)² = (1.96 × 4,500 / 500)² = (17.64)² = 311.17 → round UP → n = 312 Rounding down would silently break the $500 promise — the margin would exceed E. Where the planning σ comes from Before sampling you need a σ guess: a pilot study , a previous study of a similar population, or a professional educated guess from known ranges. For σ unknown at planning time, the same formula runs with t and s — iterate once if needed. Sample-size math is the cheapest insurance in statistics. 05 Check yourself t-table instincts For a 95% interval with n = 16 and σ unknown, the correct multiplier is… Lecture 24 · check A t(0.025, 15) = 2.131 B z = 1.960 C t(0.05, 16) = 1.753 D z = 2.576 As degrees of freedom increase, the t-distribution… Lecture 24 · check A becomes more dispersed with heavier tails B converges to the standard normal distribution C becomes bimodal D shifts its mean above zero Key takeaways σ unknown → estimate it with s and switch to the t-distribution : x̄ ± t(α/2)·s/√n with df = n − 1 . The t is a family of symmetric curves — heavier tails at low df, visually identical to the normal past df ≈ 100. Housing: 750 ± 2.131 × 13.75 = [720.7, 779.3] — the df-morph shows exactly what the 2.131 (vs 1.960) is buying. Planning sample size: n = (z·σ/E)² , Discount Sounds → 312 . Always round up — the margin promise is a floor.

chapters.label: Proportion estimation
chapters.text: Lecture 25 · Interval Estimation — population proportion Proportions get their interval Means are not the only thing managers estimate. What share of voters backs the candidate? What fraction of boxes ships defective? The machinery is identical — swap x̄ for p̂ and σ/√n for √[p̂(1−p̂)/n]. 01 The proportion interval p̂ ± z(α/2) · √[p̂(1−p̂)/n] — with the normality gate checked first The gate — check before you compute Normal approximation holds when BOTH hold: np ≥ 5 n(1−p) ≥ 5 Exit poll: n = 500, p̂ = 0.44 500 × 0.44 = 220 ≥ 5 ✓ 500 × 0.56 = 280 ≥ 5 ✓ → the sampling distribution of p̄ is approximately normal — proceed. Same skeleton as the mean Point estimate → standard error → multiplier: x̄ ↔ p̂ , σ/√n ↔ √[p̂(1−p̂)/n] , z(α/2) unchanged. Learn one skeleton and both estimates come free — that parallel is the exam's favourite question. 02 Worked — the exit poll PSI surveys 500 registered voters · 220 favour candidate C · 95% confidence The full computation — support for candidate C p̂ = 220 / 500 = 0.44 α = 0.05 → α/2 = 0.025 → z(α/2) = 1.96 σ(p̂) = √[0.44 × 0.56 / 500] = √0.0004928 = 0.0222 E = 1.96 × 0.0222 = 0.0435 95% CI = 0.44 ± 0.0435 = [0.3965 , 0.4835] "PSI is 95% confident the true share of voters favouring C lies between 39.65% and 48.35%." 03 Planning the poll — how many voters? n = z²·p*(1−p*)/E² — the planning-value lab The planning-value curve — p* = 0.5 is the safe maximum drag the planning p* peak at p* = 0.50 p* = 0.05 p* = 0.95 Planning value p* = 0.50 (p*(1−p*) = 0.2500) Required n (99%, E = 0.03) 1,844 If you guessed p* = 0.5 instead 1,844 the conservative ceiling — never undersampled n is driven by p*(1−p*) , and that product peaks at 0.25 when p* = 0.5 — the Excel sweep 0.1, 0.2, … 0.9 in the lecture confirms it. No clue about p? Spend on p* = 0.5 and the promised margin cannot be exceeded. PSI upgrades the poll — 99% confidence, ±0.03 z(0.005) = 2.576 E = 0.03 planning value p* = 0.44 (from this survey): n = (2.576)² × 0.44 × 0.56 / (0.03)² = 1,817 planning value p* = 0.50 (no information): n = (2.576)² × 0.25 / (0.03)² = 1,843 ← the conservative ceiling From 500 voters to ~1,817: confidence up 95% → 99% AND margin down ±0.0435 → ±0.03. 04 Check yourself Proportion instincts With no prior information about p, the safest planning value for sample-size computation is… Lecture 25 · check A p* = 0.5, because p(1−p) is maximised there B p* = 0.1, to minimise cost C p* = 1.0, the worst case D any p* — n does not depend on p Other things equal, demanding a smaller margin of error for a proportion… Lecture 25 · check A increases the required sample size B decreases the required sample size C leaves n unchanged — only confidence matters D makes the interval wider Key takeaways Proportion interval: p̂ ± z(α/2)·√[p̂(1−p̂)/n] — same skeleton as the mean, different standard error. Check the gate first: np ≥ 5 and n(1−p) ≥ 5 before using the normal approximation. Exit poll: 0.44 ± 0.0435 → [0.3965, 0.4835] at 95%. Sample sizing uses a planning value p* ; unknown p → p* = 0.5 gives the maximum n (PSI: 1,843) and can never undersample.

chapters.label: Metropolitan Research
chapters.text: Lecture 26 — the transmission file Metropolitan Research — the warranty audit The course's last full case: a consumer research firm, fifty repair records, and a mean that looks acceptable until you meet the interval's lower bound. Descriptive statistics opens the file, a t-interval prices the uncertainty, and the early-failure tail closes the argument. 01 Case — Metropolitan Research An interval estimate — and the early-failure red flag Case · Lecture 26 — a warranty question, computed Metropolitan Research — how early do transmissions really fail? Consumer complaints about early transmission failures reached Metropolitan Research, which pulled 50 repair records from a Detroit transmission firm: kilometres driven before failure for each vehicle. The automaker's design standard says transmissions should hold without early failure — the data says otherwise. The descriptive read — n = 50 mean x̄ = 73,340 miles median = 72,700 miles (25 fail before, 25 after) s = 24,849 miles ← huge spread mode = none — failures scattered, not clustered skewness ≈ 0+ — nearly symmetric 95% CI (σ unknown → t): x̄ ± E = 73,340 ± 7,076 = [66,264 , 80,416] miles Planning the follow-up study Target: ±5,000 miles at 95% confidence, planning σ = 24,849 (from this sample): n = (z·σ/E)² = (1.96 × 24,849 / 5,000)² = 95.26 → round up → ≈ 100 vehicles Cost per mile of precision: the mean cost of the s = 24,849 spread is width — the only cure is more data. The red-flag arithmetic 19 vehicles failed below 66,264 — earlier than the lower confidence bound — and 18 failed above 80,416 . The mean of ~73,000 hides a heavy tail of early failures , and those are the warranty-killer: averages comfort, distributions decide. Where the analysis goes next Supply side: production batches, material quality, plants, suppliers . Demand side: driver behaviour, terrain, climate, maintenance . Layer those variables on with regression or ML models and correlate against failure mileage — the univariate answer here is exactly where the next statistics course begins. 02 Check yourself One case, two instincts Metropolitan's interval is [66,264, 80,416] and 19 of 50 cars failed below 66,264. The managerial lesson is… Case file II · check A averages hide the early-failure tail — distributions drive warranty risk B the sample mean should be replaced by the mode C the confidence interval proves no quality problem exists D the sample size of 50 is already sufficient — no follow-up needed To promise ±5,000 miles at 95% confidence with planning σ = 24,849, Metropolitan needs… Case file II · check A n = (1.96 × 24,849 / 5,000)² ≈ 95.3 → 100 vehicles B n = 24,849 / 5,000 ≈ 5 vehicles C n = 1.96 × 24,849 ≈ 48,700 vehicles D n = 50 — the current sample suffices Key takeaways The descriptive read : x̄ = 73,340, median = 72,700, s = 24,849, no mode, skew ≈ 0 — spread is the headline, not the mean. The interval : x̄ ± 7,076 → [66,264, 80,416] ; 19 early failures below the bound are the warranty story. The follow-up : n = (1.96 × 24,849/5,000)² ≈ 95.3 → 100 vehicles for a ±5,000 promise — then supply- and demand-side variables explain the tail.

chapters.label: Hypothesis testing framework
chapters.text: Lecture 27 · Hypothesis Testing — the framework Two claims, one verdict Interval estimates describe; hypothesis testing decides. Put a claim about μ on trial: the null hypothesis holds the status quo with its equality, the alternate carries what you hope to show — and the sample data delivers the only two verdicts statistics allows. 01 The two competing statements H₀ always carries the equality — =, ≥, or ≤ Null hypothesis — H₀ · A tentative assumption about a population parameter · The status quo, the current belief, the “nothing changed” · Always contains =, ≥, or ≤ · The statement we attempt to reject with sample evidence Alternate hypothesis — Hₐ · The opposite of the null — what the researcher hopes to prove · Carries the inequality: <, >, or ≠ · Becomes the conclusion only if H₀ is rejected · Sets the tail — and therefore where the evidence must land 02 Two ways to set the stage Research objective focus — or challenge an assumption Approach 1 — prove something new Put what you want to demonstrate in Hₐ . A new battery claims more life? Hₐ: μ > the old life , so the burden of proof sits on the new product — the data must actively contradict the status quo before the claim wins. Approach 2 — challenge a belief Put the existing belief in H₀ and let the sample try to knock it down. Quality control lives here: H₀: the process meets spec , and only strong evidence shuts the line. Common in verification and audit scenarios. 03 The three forms — and where the region lives Left · right · two-tailed — set by Hₐ's inequality The three forms — where does the rejection region live? tap a form Left-tailed test Right-tailed test Two-tailed test μ₀ — the claimed value rejection region · α H₀ μ ≥ μ₀ Hₐ μ < μ₀ Lecture example Emergency response: H₀: μ ≥ 12 min vs Hₐ: μ < 12 — meet the 12-minute goal? 04 The courtroom of errors Type I is priced (α) · Type II is the silent one The decision courtroom — tap a verdict presumption: H₀ is “innocent until proven guilty” Reject H₀ — but H₀ is true Type I error · P = α Reject H₀ — and H₀ is false Correct · power Fail to reject — H₀ is true Correct decision Fail to reject — but H₀ is false Type II error Type I error — the false positive You rejected H₀ when it was actually true: the innocent person goes to jail, a good batch is scrapped. Its probability is exactly α — the level of significance, and the error statisticians control directly. The court can only convict or acquit — never declare innocence. Same in statistics: we reject or fail to reject H₀; “accepting” the null is how Type II errors sneak into reports. A hypothesis is a testable statement, never a conclusion. 05 Check yourself Read the claim, name the test An online platform claims average test scores of 70; a researcher suspects the true average is lower. The hypotheses are… Lecture 27 · check A H₀: μ ≥ 70 vs Hₐ: μ < 70 B H₀: μ < 70 vs Hₐ: μ ≥ 70 C H₀: μ = 70 vs Hₐ: μ ≠ 70 D H₀: x̄ ≥ 70 vs Hₐ: x̄ < 70 A quality inspector concludes a process is out of control when it was actually meeting spec. This is… Lecture 27 · check A a Type I error — probability α B a Type II error — probability α C a correct decision D a Type I error with probability β Key takeaways H₀ holds the equality (=, ≥, ≤) and the status quo; Hₐ carries the inequality and the research hope. The tail follows Hₐ. Three forms: μ ≥ μ₀ vs μ < μ₀ (left) · μ ≤ μ₀ vs μ > μ₀ (right) · μ = μ₀ vs μ ≠ μ₀ (two-tailed). Type I = rejecting a true H₀ (probability α, controlled). Type II = failing to reject a false H₀ — the silent error. The only verdicts are reject and fail to reject — “accept” is not a statistical word.

Computing is what a computer does — you can’t define one without the other Computing is the abstract problem-solving process through defined step-by-step procedures — the computer is just the fast executor Computing is the physical electronic tool that executes processes with speed and precision Computing is another word for programming Computing existed for thousands of years before electronic computers — pen and paper, an abacus. The intelligence comes from the humans who design the algorithms; the computer is the physical tool that executes them fast. In the exam, define computing WITHOUT mentioning computers — focus on process and methodology. mt-8 <SectionHead eyebrow= title={ What exactly is computing? } lead= /> Working definition Computing is the process of using{ } well-defined steps to solve problems by{ } collecting information , processing it , and producing a useful result . Notice: no mention of screens, keyboards or silicon. Computing is a{ } process — the machine is just its fastest executor. The formal definition “Computing is any goal-oriented activity requiring, benefiting from, or creating computers.” — ACM (Association for Computing Machinery) Every example you’ll meet in this course obeys one deep pattern: a defined set of instructions → acting on data → to produce a result Computing did not start with computers {TIMELINE.map((t, i) => ( {t.icon} {t.era} {t.text} ))} The IPO model — foundation of all computing Input → Process → Output The fundamental principle underlying every computing process. chapters.text: Lecture 02 · Data & DIKW. Data → information → knowledge → wisdom. data Pillar 1 · The raw material grad-text Without data there is nothing to process, nothing to store, nothing to output. Understanding what data is — and how a raw number climbs the ladder into meaning — is the first step in understanding computing. grid gap-5 lg:grid-cols-2 card-warm h-full p-7 flex items-center gap-3 h-6 w-6 #c2410c text-xl font-bold mt-4 text-[.95rem] leading-relaxed text-[#2b2014] mt-3 rounded-xl bg-[#fdf1e0] p-4 text-center text-[.95rem] font-bold text-[#7c4a12] card-warm h-full p-7 text-xl font-bold mt-3 raw Any unprocessed fact or observation that can be recorded and stored meaning By itself, data has no meaning — 42 is just a number, ‘Mumbai’ is just a word context Only when we give data context — process and interpret it — does it become information mt-12 card-warm p-6 md:p-8 eyebrow mt-2 text-2xl font-bold grad-text mt-2 max-w-3xl text-[.92rem] text-muted-warm mt-6 mt-8 card-warm p-6 md:p-8 eyebrow mt-2 text-2xl font-bold mt-2 max-w-3xl text-[.92rem] text-muted-warm mt-5 grid gap-3 md:grid-cols-2 xl:grid-cols-4 rounded-xl bg-[#fffdf9] p-4 1px dashed #e5c79d inline-flex items-center rounded-full px-3 py-1 text-[.7rem] font-black text-white mt-2 text-[.86rem] leading-relaxed text-[#2b2014] mt-4 text-center text-[.8rem] text-muted-warm mt-8 card-warm p-6 md:p-8 flex items-center gap-3 h-6 w-6 #c2410c text-2xl font-bold grad-text mt-3 max-w-3xl text-[.92rem] leading-relaxed text-[#2b2014] mt-4 grid gap-3 md:grid-cols-2 rounded-xl bg-[#fffdf9] p-4 1px dashed #e5c79d font-bold text-[#7c4a12] mt-1 text-[.88rem] leading-relaxed text-[#2b2014] rounded-xl p-4 #fbe9e4 1px solid #e6a08c font-bold #9c3a3a mt-1 text-[.88rem] leading-relaxed text-[#2b2014] mt-10 grid gap-5 md:grid-cols-2 Course quiz A nurse writes 38.5 on a chart. The ward screen later shows “Temperature: 38.5 °C — above the fever threshold”. At what exact moment did the data become information? When the nurse wrote the number down When the number was given context — a reading, a scale and a fever threshold When the doctor prescribed treatment Never — 38.5 is always information 38.5 alone is raw data. It becomes information the moment context and structure give it meaning — a temperature reading, on a scale, compared against a threshold. The prescription comes later, at the wisdom rung. Course quiz Which sequence shows the correct DIKW ladder? Data → Knowledge → Information → Wisdom Data → Information → Knowledge → Wisdom Information → Data → Knowledge → Wisdom Data → Wisdom → Knowledge → Information Data gains context to become information; information is synthesized into knowledge; knowledge plus judgement becomes wisdom. Each rung adds what the one below lacks. Course quiz “The doctor prescribes a specific treatment based on patterns recognized from thousands of similar cases.” Which DIKW level is this? Data Information Knowledge Wisdom Acting on patterns with judgement — applying what was learned to make the right call — is the top of the pyramid: wisdom. The recognized pattern itself was knowledge; the number was data. mt-10 <SectionHead eyebrow= title={ Data — the raw material of computing } lead= /> “38.5” — is that data? 38.5 is data. But{ } “The patient’s temperature is 38.5 °C, which means the patient has a mild fever” is information . Computing transforms data into information. What data actually is The ladder of meaning Data → Information → Knowledge → Wisdom Each rung adds something the rung below lacks — structure, then synthesis, then judgement. Case study · a clinic ward One temperature reading, four rungs of the ladder The same 38.5 climbs the whole pyramid — watch what each rung adds. {CLINICAL_STEPS.map((s) => ( {s.k} · {s.name} {s.body} ))} Raw number → trend → diagnosis → prescription. That is the whole ladder — and computing builds every rung below wisdom. Data in modern AI systems Data is the lifeblood of AI . Advanced models require significantly larger datasets than traditional machine learning — the principles never change: {AI_PRINCIPLES.map((p) => ( {p.k} {p.v} ))} The hard limit Without data, even the most sophisticated algorithms are completely useless — no model outlearns what it was fed. <Takeaways items={[ Data is raw and meaningless alone — computing transforms data into information . 38.5 is data; “the patient has a fever” is information. , Context is everything: the same number becomes information only once a scale, a threshold and a purpose surround it. , The DIKW ladder — Data → Information → Knowledge → Wisdom — adds structure, then synthesis, then judgement, one rung at a time, from a fever chart to a prescription. , Data is the lifeblood of AI : more advanced models need more training data, and better quality plus quantity means better predictions — without data, even the most sophisticated algorithms are completely useless. , ]} />

grid gap-5 md:grid-cols-2 Concept check Amazon star ratings (1–5) are qualitative data. Which subtype — and why can't you take a strict mean of 'experiences'? Nominal — no order exists Ordinal — order is meaningful but the gaps between stars are unequal Discrete quantitative Continuous quantitative Stars rank (order is meaningful) but the distance between 3★ and 4★ isn't a fixed quantity — that's ordinal. It's still qualitative: no true measurement scale. Concept check Monthly marks of the SAME 500 students tracked over six months is… Cross-sectional data Time-series data Panel (longitudinal) data Unstructured data Panel data tracks multiple subjects over multiple time periods — combining cross-sectional breadth with trend analysis. Time series would follow ONE subject only. mt-6 <SectionHead eyebrow= title={ Data, classified — the taxonomy that decides everything } lead= /> You cannot compute a mean of blood groups, and averaging a "city of birth" yields nothing meaningful. Type of data determines which operations are meaningful and valid — proper classification ensures appropriate analysis methods and reliable conclusions. The 80% problem text images audio video sensor streams ≈80% of all data generated globally is UNSTRUCTURED Quantitative — quant Numerical and measurable. You can count it or measure it. Discrete Countable whole numbers — 30 students, 3 goals, 47 apps Continuous Any value in a range, decimals allowed — height 172.4 cm, temperature 36.8°C, time 9.5 s Operations: mean, median, standard deviation, correlation. Collected via surveys; answers{ } what · how often · how many · how much . Quick to analyze, generalizable with representative samples. Qualitative — qual Categorical and non-numerical — labels, qualities, opinions. Nominal — no natural order Blood group A/B/AB/O, city of birth, phone brand. Operations: mode, frequency count, chi-square Ordinal — meaningful order, unequal gaps Amazon stars 1–5, education level, satisfaction: poor/fair/good/excellent Deep contextual insight, collected via interviews; answers how · why . Costs: prone to researcher bias, needs thematic/content analysis, interpretation is subjective. The taxonomy, in runnable Python <Takeaways items={[ By format : structured (rows/columns), semi-structured (JSON/XML), unstructured — ≈80% of global data . , By time : cross-sectional (one moment), panel (many subjects × many periods), time series (one subject over time). , By nature : quantitative (discrete/continuous — means and medians are legal) vs qualitative (nominal/ordinal — mode only). , The type of data determines the valid operations — classify first, analyze second. , ]} />

Primary · secondary · metadata. data-origin Lecture 05 · where data comes from grad-text The fourth and final classification of data, completing the taxonomy: format, time, nature — and now origin. Where data comes from decides how much you can trust it, what it costs, and whether it actually fits the question you are asking. 1 Primary data — collected firsthand Original, not previously published — gathered by the researchers who will use it grid gap-5 lg:grid-cols-[1.4fr_1fr] grid content-start gap-4 insight When to go primary 2 Secondary data — collected by someone else Collected for a different purpose, reused for new analysis grid gap-5 lg:grid-cols-[1.4fr_1fr] story When to go secondary 3 Metadata — data about data Describes the characteristics and context of data without being the actual data itself card-warm p-6 md:p-8 flex items-center gap-3 h-6 w-6 #c2410c text-2xl font-bold grad-text mt-3 max-w-3xl text-[.92rem] leading-relaxed text-[#2b2014] mt-5 grid gap-4 sm:grid-cols-2 lg:grid-cols-4 h-full rounded-xl bg-[#fffdf9] p-4 1px dashed #e5c79d flex h-9 w-9 items-center justify-center rounded-xl linear-gradient(135deg,#fde8cf,#fbcf9f) #8a3d10 mt-2 font-bold text-[#7c4a12] mt-2 flex flex-wrap gap-1.5 inline-block rounded-md bg-[#fbf3e3] px-2 py-0.5 text-[.72rem] font-semibold text-[#7c4a12] mt-5 rounded-xl bg-[#fdf1e0] p-4 text-[.78rem] font-extrabold uppercase tracking-[.16em] text-[#8a5a10] mt-2 grid gap-1.5 text-[.88rem] leading-relaxed text-[#2b2014] md:grid-cols-3 mt-10 grid gap-5 md:grid-cols-2 Concept check A researcher downloads SEBI market records and WHO Global Health Statistics instead of running her own survey. The downloaded material is: Primary data Secondary data Metadata Quantitative data Collected by someone else for a different purpose and reused for new analysis — that is secondary data. SEBI, IRDAI, NSSO, WHO statistics, census tables and Wikipedia structured data are all classic secondary sources. Concept check Which of the following is metadata — data about data — rather than the data itself? The pixels of a photo — what you actually see The photo's file size, creation date and GPS location The patients a hospital treated last year A WHO health-statistics spreadsheet Metadata describes the characteristics and context of data without being the data: file name, size, creation date, GPS location, camera model and resolution all describe the photo — the pixels themselves are the data. mt-6 <SectionHead eyebrow= title={ Data classification: origin —{ } primary, secondary & metadata } lead= /> When the question is yours — a screen-time survey of your school, an experiment you designed, sensors you deployed. You pay with time, money and human resources, but you get data that fits exactly and methods you can defend. When the question is big — national income, insurance trends, global health. NSSO surveys, SEBI filings and WHO statistics were built by organizations with resources no individual can match. The catch: someone else decided{ } what to measure, and sometimes a subscription stands between you and the data. Metadata: data about data A photo file holds the actual data — the image pixels, what we see — plus metadata that describes it: file name, file size, creation date, GPS location, camera model, resolution. The pixels are the data; everything that describes them is metadata. Four everyday examples: {META_EXAMPLES.map((m, i) => ( {m.icon} {m.name} {m.fields.map((f) => ( {f} ))} ))} Why metadata matters • Critical for organizing, finding and governing large datasets • Reveals information without exposing the actual content • Essential for data management and system organization <Takeaways items={[ Primary data is collected firsthand for your exact question — tailored, reliable and controlled, but slow, expensive and often limited to small samples. , Secondary data is someone else's collection, reused — large-scale, often free and authoritative; but it may not match your question, and quality depends on the original collector. , Metadata is data about data — photo EXIF, database schemas, library catalogs, WhatsApp message logs — revealing information without exposing content. , Metadata is what makes large datasets organizable, findable and governable — the index-card system of the digital world. , ]} />

The recipe is ordered and repeatable; now make the idea precise. Formal definition An algorithm is a finite, unambiguous, step-by-step procedure { } for solving a well-defined problem. It takes an input , processes it through a series of defined steps , and produces a correct output every time it is executed. • Algorithms exist independent of computers — a recipe, a dance routine, a long-division method. • A computer just executes them fast — billions of steps per second. • The quality of computing depends on the quality of the algorithm . • A bad algorithm gives a wrong or slow result no matter how powerful the hardware . A 9th-century Persian word on your Instagram feed The word algorithm derives from{ } Muhammad ibn Musa Al-Qarizmi , a 9th-century Persian mathematician whose work on arithmetic and algebra introduced systematic problem-solving methods to the world. The word algebra also originates from the title of his book. His methods are the reason your feed is sorted at all. Algorithms existed long before modern computers — during World War II, women “computers” calculated artillery trajectories by hand. And quality has always mattered more than muscle: a well-optimized algorithm works even with less computing power — exactly how 1990s AI researchers made progress on limited hardware. ROM is read-only RAM is volatile — contents vanish without power SSDs are too slow The CPU lacks cores RAM is volatile: it holds your program, variables and open files only while powered. Save to secondary storage and the data persists in non-volatile memory. Concept check Why do modern AI systems depend so heavily on GPUs? GPUs have better marketing Training neural networks means doing the same math on billions of numbers simultaneously — GPU parallelism fits perfectly CPUs cannot do multiplication GPUs use less electricity overall A GPU’s thousands of small cores apply one operation to many data points at once — exactly the shape of neural-network training. CPUs have few powerful cores better suited to complex sequential logic. <SectionHead eyebrow= title={ Hardware — silicon that makes ideas run } lead= /> Why hardware decided the AI revolution The explosion of AI over the last decade wasn’t just a breakthrough in software — it was a triumph of hardware . At the absolute center sits the Graphics Processing Unit (GPU) : designed for mass parallel processing , it breaks a complex task into thousands of smaller, simpler tasks and solves them all{ } simultaneously . That raw parallel horsepower is what built the foundations of modern AI. The turnaround: AI research had been crawling along since the 1990s , starved of compute — researchers compensated by optimizing algorithms, not hardware. Then in 2012 , scientists built AlexNet , a computer-vision model trained on GPUs, and demonstrated to the world what parallel hardware could do. Today every frontier model trains the same way: large language models like ChatGPT , image generators like DALL-E ,{ } Midjourney and Stable Diffusion , and video AI — all of them

What kind of communication is email? Real-time messaging Asynchronous communication Live video streaming Peer-to-peer file sharing Email clients like Gmail and Outlook enable asynchronous communication — the message waits for the recipient — using SMTP to send and IMAP to receive. Concept check Which of the following is a job of a web browser? Compiling source code to machine code Parsing and rendering HTML, CSS and JavaScript Defragmenting the disk Allocating RAM to other programs A browser parses and renders HTML, CSS and JavaScript, manages multiple simultaneous network connections, and provides developer tools — Chrome, Firefox and Safari all do this. Concept check A C program contains a syntax error. What happens when you compile and run it? It runs and shows partial output The error is found at compile time — no output is produced It runs, just slower than usual The error appears line by line as the program executes Compilers translate the entire source code before execution — errors surface at compile time and nothing runs until they are fixed. That all-or-nothing model is why compiled programs produce no output when errors exist. Concept check An IDE combines four tools in one. Which set is correct? Browser, firewall, antivirus, VPN Editor, code runner, debugger, version control Spreadsheet, presentation, database, word processor Disk cleanup, partitioning, encryption, compression An IDE is the all-in-one: a code editor for writing, a runner for executing, a debugger that pinpoints errors, and version control — PyCharm, VS Code and Google Colab all qualify. mt-8 <SectionHead dark eyebrow= title={ Application software — the programs you actually touch } lead= /> {APP_GROUPS.map((a) => ( {a.icon} {a.k} {a.points.map((p) => ( • {p} ))} ))} Specialized / professional software Where domains meet algorithms meet Python Domain Software examples Key algorithms used Python connection {PRO_TABLE.map((r) => ( {r.domain} {r.sw} {r.alg} {r.py} ))} Notice the last column: whatever field you enter, Python follows you in . Naming rules — break these and Python errors • Variable names can contain only letters, numbers and underscores • Must start with a letter or underscore — never a number ( message_1 ✓, 1_message ✗) • Spaces are not allowed — use underscores ( greeting_message ✓, greeting message ✗) • Avoid Python keywords and built-in function names — print , if , else , try , while , return Naming guidelines — style, not law • Short but descriptive : student_name , not s_n ; name_length , not length_of_persons_name • Be cautious with lowercase l and uppercase O — they resemble the numbers 1 and 0 • Use lowercase variable names as best practice — uppercase w

Arithmetic · BODMAS · floats · str() · lists intro. # The arithmetic five print(2 + 3) # addition → 5 print(3 - 2) # subtraction → 1 print(2 * 3) # multiplication → 6 (asterisk) print(3 / 2) # division → 1.5 print(3 ** 2) # exponentiation → 9 (double asterisk) # Order of operations — Python follows PEMDAS/BODMAS; # parentheses override the default order print(2 + 3 * 4) # 14 print((2 + 3) * 4) # 20 # Integers vs floats — whole numbers vs a decimal point print(16 / 2) # 8.0 — division always returns a float print(1_000_000) # underscores make big numbers readable print(0.2 + 0.1) # expect 0.3? print(0.2 + 0.1 == 0.3) # False! # Every language has this quirk: computers store # decimals in BINARY, and 0.1 has no exact binary # form. Harmless for most apps — and fixable for # display: result = 0.2 + 0.1 print(f"{result:.2f}") # two decimal places age = 23 # message = "happy " + age + "rd birthday" # TypeError! # Python refuses: + joins strings OR adds numbers, # never both. message = "happy " + str(age) + "rd birthday" print(message) # The number stays a number for maths elsewhere: print(age + 1, "next year") favorite_number = 7 message = f"My favorite number is {favorite_number}." print(message) # Say hello to everyone. print("Hello Python people!") # The hash (#) starts a comment — Python ignores the rest of the line. # Write comments for the WHY, not the what: the code already says what it does. bicycles = ['trek', 'cannondale', 'redline', 'specialized'] print(bicycles) # a whole set of information, one variable print(bicycles[0]) # one item out of the set numbers Lecture 10 · numbers, strings & comments grad-text This lecture builds progressively from basic string manipulation to working with numbers and handling mixed data types — the arithmetic five, order of operations, the float precision surprise, str() conversion and comments, before lists enter the story. 1 String operations — the recap Everything strings can do so far, in one compact card card-warm p-6 md:p-8 grid gap-2.5 Series of characters Strings are series of characters written between single or double quotes — anything inside quotes is a string. Concatenation Combine multiple strings with the + operator. Special characters \ adds a tab; \ starts a new line. Whitespace management strip() removes unwanted spaces from both sides; lstrip() from the left; rstrip() from the right. Parentheses override the PEMDAS/BODMAS order whenever you need them to. 3 Float precision — the 0.30000000000000004 surprise Why 0.2 + 0.1 refuses to equal 0.3 — and why nobody worries float_precision.py 0.30000000000000004 False 0.30 A float is any number with a decimal point — a floating-point number. Python may display unexpected decimal places because of how computers internally represent numbers; this minor precision issue occurs in ALL programming languages and is generally of little concern for most applications. Lecture 11 · Lists. Ordered collections, indexing, add & remove. bicycles = ['trek', 'cannondale', 'redline', 'specialized'] print(bicycles) # the whole list print(bicycles[0]) # first element print(bicycles[0].title()) # Index positions START AT 0, not 1! print(bicycles[1]) # 2nd item print(bicycles[3]) # 4th item print(bicycles[-1]) # last item — negative indexes count backwards motorcycles = ['honda', 'yamaha', 'suzuki'] # MODIFY — assign by index motorcycles[0] = 'ducati' # ADD motorcycles.append('honda') # to the end motorcycles.insert(0, 'ducati') # at any index # REMOVE — three ways del motorcycles[0] # by index popped = motorcycles.pop() # removes & RETURNS last first = motorcycles.pop(0) # pops any index too_expensive = 'yamaha' motorcycles.remove(too_expensive) # by VALUE (first match only) guests = ['ida', 'leo', 'asma'] for g in guests: print(f"{g.title()}, please come to dinner.") print("
Sadly, asma can't make it.") guests[guests.index('asma')] = 'amir' # replace by index for g in guests: print(f"{g.title()}, please come to dinner.") print("
Bigger table found!") guests.insert(1, 'kabir') # middle guests.append('tara') # end for g in guests: print(f"{g.title()}, please come to dinner.") print("
Only two seats now.") while len(guests) > 2: sorry = guests.pop() print(f"Sorry, {sorry.title()} — no room this time.") for g in guests: print(f"{g.title()}, you're still invited.") lists Lecture 11 · lists grad-text A list is a collection of items arranged in a particular order — letters, numbers or names, related or not — stored in one variable between square brackets. 'trek' 'cannondale' 'redline' IndexError Index positions start at 0, so index 1 is the SECOND element: 'cannondale'. Index -1 would give the last item. Concept check Which removal method returns the removed value so you can keep using it? del motorcycles[0] motorcycles.remove('ducati') popped = motorcycles.pop() None of them pop() removes AND returns — perfect when the removed value still matters (a popped player, a printed design). del is gone forever; remove() drops by value with nothing returned. mt-6 Try It Yourself — the guest list (Lecture 11) one list, one loop, one f-string per invitation index assignment replaces a name in place insert(index, guest) shifts everything after it one seat right pop() returns the name you just removed — use it in the apology mt-6 Using individual values: f <SectionHead dark eyebrow= title={ Lists — and working with them like a pro } lead= /> Choosing the right deletion method Three ways out — pick by intent {DELETION_GUIDE.map((d) => ( {d.m} {d.when} ))} del needs an index; pop() hands the value back; remove() hunts by value — three different questions, three different tools. The deck's dinner-party drill guest_list.py — invitations, edits and apologies The classic exercise that touches every operation: invite three guests, one declines — replace them, find a bigger table — insert a guest mid-list, append one to the end, then cut the list down with pop. <Practice title= items={[ { q: Make a guest list with at least three people you would invite — living or deceased — and use it to print a personalized invitation to each person. , hint: }, { q: Add a statement announcing which guest cannot make it; replace that guest’s name with a new invitee and print a new set of invitation messages. , hint: }, { q: Announce a bigger table: use insert() to add one guest to the middle of the list, append() to add one to the end, and print updated invitations for all guests. , hint: }, { q: Only two guests can come: announce it, pop() guests one by one, then del the remaining two — print messages confirming who is still invited. , hint: }, ]} /> <Takeaways dark items={[ Lists are ordered and mutable ; indexes start at 0 ; -1 is the last item. , Grow with append()/insert() ; shrink with del/pop()/remove() — pop returns the value. , remove() deletes only the first occurrence ; loop it to purge them all (Lecture 26 does exactly that). , Ordering, slicing and tuples live in their own lectures — ordering in Lecture 12 , numeric lists and slices in Lecture 15 , tuples in Lecture 16 . , ]} />

chapters.label: Organize
chapters.text: Lecture 12 · Organize. sort · sorted · reverse · len · index errors. cars = ['bmw', 'audi', 'toyota', 'subaru'] # sorted() — a temporary look, the list survives print("sorted copy :", sorted(cars)) print("original :", cars) print("reverse copy:", sorted(cars, reverse=True)) # sort() — permanent, the original order is GONE cars.sort() print("after sort :", cars) cars.sort(reverse=True) print("after sort R:", cars) # reverse() — flips the CURRENT order, not alphabetical cars.reverse() print("after flip :", cars) motorcycles = ['honda', 'yamaha', 'suzuki'] print("len() =", len(motorcycles)) # 3 items print("valid indices: 0 …", len(motorcycles) - 1) print("last item, safely:", motorcycles[len(motorcycles) - 1]) print("shortcut to last :", motorcycles[-1]) # THE CLASSIC CRASH — uncomment to meet it: # print(motorcycles[3]) # IndexError: list index out of range list-organize Lecture 12 · organizing a list grad-text Data rarely arrives sorted. Python gives you four tools — two that rearrange forever, two that only look. The difference between them is the difference between a tidy program and a mysterious bug. 1 The four calls, side by side sort() · sorted() · reverse() · len() — two rearrange forever, two only look card-warm p-6 md:p-8 eyebrow mt-2 text-2xl font-bold mt-5 overflow-x-auto warm-table min-w-[640px] font-mono-warm font-bold text-[#8a4508] mt-8 grid gap-5 lg:grid-cols-2 cars.py — permanent vs temporary sorted copy : ['audi', 'bmw', 'subaru', 'toyota'] original : ['bmw', 'audi', 'toyota', 'subaru'] reverse copy: ['toyota', 'subaru', 'bmw', 'audi'] after sort : ['audi', 'bmw', 'subaru', 'toyota'] after sort R: ['toyota', 'subaru', 'bmw', 'audi'] after flip : ['audi', 'bmw', 'subaru', 'toyota'] Run it and watch: sorted() always prints the same answer from the same list — until sort() permanently rewrites the original. Editing the code to add your own cars is encouraged. grid content-start gap-4 insight Which one do I want? warn reverse() is not sort(reverse=True) 2 len() — and the off-by-one trap A list of length 4 has indices 0, 1, 2, 3 — never 4 grid gap-5 lg:grid-cols-2 index_bounds.py — the length/index handshake len() = 3 valid indices: 0 … 2 last item, safely: suzuki shortcut to last : suzuki The error message 'list index out of range' is Python telling you the index you asked for doesn't exist. An EMPTY list errors on any index at all. grid content-start gap-4 story Why 'off-by-one' is a rite of passage mt-8 grid gap-5 md:grid-cols-2 Concept check What is the key difference between cars.sort() and sorted(cars)? No difference sort() sorts permanently; sorted() returns a sorted copy sorted() is only for numbers sort() is faster but wrong sort() mutates the list permanently; sorted(cars) leaves the original untouched and hands you a new sorted list. Same for reverse=True on both. Concept check A list holds 4 items. Which index crashes? cars[0] cars[3] cars[-1] cars[4] Valid indices run 0–3 (length − 1). cars[4] is one past the end → IndexError: list index out of range. cars[-1] is always safe for the last item. mt-6 Try It Yourself — organizing drills mt-6 <SectionHead eyebrow= title={ Putting lists in order } lead= /> The four calls, side by side sort() · sorted() · reverse() · len() Call Effect Variation {SORTED_TABLE.map((r) => ( {r.call} {r.effect} {r.alt} ))} Need a one-off view of the data in order — for display, for a report — while the program keeps its own order? Use sorted() . Want every later line of the program to see the new order? Use sort() . Choose deliberately, never accidentally. reverse() simply flips whatever order the list is currently in — no alphabetical arrangement at all. Flip it again and you are back where you started. Humans count from 1; Python counts from 0. The third item lives at index 2 . Every programmer has asked a list for the item one past its end — the error is harmless, and now you can read it like a native. <Practice title= items={[ { q: Store at least five travel destinations in a list, deliberately unsorted. Print the original order. }, { q: Show the list in alphabetical order with sorted() — then print the original to prove it survived. }, { q: Show reverse-alphabetical order with sorted(reverse=True) — original still untouched? }, { q: Use reverse() to flip the real list, print it, then reverse() again to restore the original order. }, { q: Now commit: sort() the list alphabetically and print. There is no going back — that is the point. }, { q: Apply all four tools (sort, sorted, reverse, len) to a list of mountains, rivers, countries or languages. }, { q: Intentionally cause an index error (motorcycles[5] on a three-item list). Read the error, fix it with len()-1 or a negative index. }, ]} /> <Takeaways items={[ sort() changes the list forever; sorted() hands back a sorted copy — reverse=True works on both. , reverse() flips the current order permanently (call twice to undo) — it is not alphabetical sorting. , len() counts items; valid indices run 0 … len−1 , and −1 is always the last. , Requesting an index that does not exist raises IndexError: list index out of range — empty lists error on everything. , ]} />

chapters.label: For loops
chapters.text: Lecture 13 · For loops. Loop a list · the indentation law. magicians = ['alice', 'david', 'carolina'] for magician in magicians: print(magician) # Doing more work inside the loop for magician in magicians: print(f"{magician.title()}, that was a great trick!") print(f"I can't wait to see your next trick, {magician.title()}.\\n") print("Thank you, everyone. That was a great magic show!") # runs once, after the loop {mode} for-loops Lecture 13 · working with lists grad-text Printing 250 values means 250 print statements — until the for loop. One line walks the whole list for you, and whitespace stops being a style choice: in Python, indentation IS the grammar. 1 Looping through an entire list The for loop walks every item — one line replaces 250 print statements card-warm p-6 md:p-8 mb-5 text-[.92rem] leading-relaxed text-[#e9d7bf] mt-5 grid gap-5 lg:grid-cols-2 magicians.py alice david carolina Alice, that was a great trick! ... text-[.8rem] font-extrabold uppercase tracking-[.16em] text-[#d9b88c] mt-2 grid gap-1.5 text-[.88rem] text-[#e9d7bf] font-mono-warm font-mono-warm font-mono-warm font-mono-warm insight Why this beats copy-paste 2 The indentation law Four classic errors — click through each one and learn to read the traceback mt-6 why The key principle font-mono-warm mt-8 grid gap-5 md:grid-cols-2 Concept check for magician in magicians\ print(magician) — what happens? It prints all three names IndentationError: expected an indented block It prints only the last name NameError: magician is not defined The body after the colon MUST be indented. With no indentation Python cannot even start — SyntaxError: expected an indented block. Concept check In a for loop, the LAST print line is accidentally NOT indented. What happens? SyntaxError — program won't run It runs once, after the loop, using the final loop value It runs once per item, like the rest The loop is skipped entirely The nastiest of the four: no syntax error is raised, the program runs — but the unindented line executes only once, after the loop, holding the last value. A logical error in disguise. mt-6 Try It Yourself — loop drills mt-6 <SectionHead dark eyebrow= title={ Loops & the indentation law } lead= /> The for loop takes the first value from the list, stores it in your loop variable, runs every indented line, then moves to the next value — and stops automatically when the list is exhausted. Code adapts to the list's length with zero changes: Reading the syntax, piece by piece • for — keyword that opens the loop • magician — a fresh variable that holds one item per pass • in magicians — the list to walk through • : — the colon that opens the body • the indented block — runs once PER item • unindented lines after — run ONCE, after the loop finishes Loop code adapts automatically if the list length changes — add a fourth magician and every line still works. That is the difference between code and paperwork. The scope of a for loop is determined entirely by indentation levels . Any indented line after the for statement is part of the loop; non-indented lines that follow are outside it. Before running: verify colons, verify indentation. <Practice title= items={[ { q: Store three friends' names; print a personalized message to each with a for loop. }, { q: Loop a list of transport modes (motorcycle, car, bicycle…) printing "I would like to own a { }!" }, { q: Write a loop with the body deliberately unindented — meet the error, then fix it. }, { q: Write a loop whose second statement escapes the body by accident — predict the output BEFORE running, then verify. }, { q: Break a loop with a missing colon, read the SyntaxError, repair it. }, ]} /> <Takeaways dark items={[ for item in list: runs the indented body once per item — the loop ends automatically. , Indentation (4 spaces) is syntax, not style : it decides what is inside the loop and what is not. , Four classic errors: missing indent · escaped body line · unexpected indent · missing colon — three crash, one misbehaves. , Unindented lines after the loop run exactly once , when the loop completes. , ]} />

Quiz 1 format · the fundamentals lap · rehearsal. digits = list(range(1, 8)) # ① what is digits? print(len(digits)) # ② print(max(digits) - min(digits)) # ③ print(sum(digits)) # ④ words = ["mumbai", "delhi", "chennai"] words.sort() # ⑤ what order now? print(words[0]) age = 17 print(age >= 18 or age > 15) # ⑥ True or False? checkpoint-1 Lecture 14 · checkpoint grad-text Half the foundations, one guided lap. This is the deck's own consolidation lecture: the syllabus for Quiz One, the exam format, and a predict-the-output drill that is exactly the kind of question the paper asks. 1 The format & the stakes 60 MCQs · 20 minutes · the whole foundations lap so far grid gap-5 md:grid-cols-3 card-warm p-5 h-5 w-5 #c2410c mt-2 text-2xl font-black text-[#3e2c1d] text-[.85rem] text-muted-warm card-warm p-5 h-5 w-5 #c2410c mt-2 text-2xl font-black text-[#3e2c1d] text-[.85rem] text-muted-warm card-warm p-5 h-5 w-5 #c2410c mt-2 text-2xl font-black text-[#3e2c1d] text-[.85rem] text-muted-warm mt-6 insight Syllabus & stakes mt-3 text-[.72rem] font-semibold leading-relaxed text-[#a08568] 2 The lap — everything so far in ten cards Skim each station; if one feels foggy, jump back to that lecture before Saturday mt-6 card-warm p-6 eyebrow mt-4 grid gap-4 md:grid-cols-2 rounded-xl border border-[#f3e2c8] bg-[#fffaf1] p-4 font-bold text-[#3e2c1d] mt-1 text-[.82rem] leading-relaxed text-muted-warm rounded-xl border border-[#f3e2c8] bg-[#fffaf1] p-4 font-bold text-[#3e2c1d] mt-1 text-[.82rem] leading-relaxed text-muted-warm rounded-xl border border-[#f3e2c8] bg-[#fffaf1] p-4 font-bold text-[#3e2c1d] mt-1 text-[.82rem] leading-relaxed text-muted-warm rounded-xl border border-[#f3e2c8] bg-[#fffaf1] p-4 font-bold text-[#3e2c1d] mt-1 text-[.82rem] leading-relaxed text-muted-warm font-mono-warm font-mono-warm 3 Predict the output — the quiz, rehearsed Cover the output panel, write your prediction on paper, then run the block quiz_rehearsal.py [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7] 7 6 28 ['chennai', 'delhi', 'mumbai'] chennai True ① [1..7] — range stops before 8 · ② seven items · ③ 7−1=6 · ④ 1+2+…+7=28 · ⑤ sort() is permanent, 'chennai' is first · ⑥ False or True → True. Every one of these is a Quiz-One-style question. mt-6 <SectionHead eyebrow= title={ Checkpoint — Quiz One } lead= /> 60 MCQs ≈ 20 seconds per question — pace is part of the test 20 minutes next Saturday, 8:00 AM sharp Best of three the best quiz score counts — one bad day never defines you Everything recorded up to September 20th — including "Working with Lists Part 2" . The evaluation scheme at this point in the course: class participation 10% · quizzes 30% (best of three recorded, 15% each) · final exam 60%, held offline, pen and paper — with real Python code writing, so practise writing code by hand, not just reading it. Note: Lecture 34 later finalizes the assessment — 40% quizzes with the best score of the two actually conducted, 60% final exam, and no participation weightage. See the final word before the end term. The details Quiz One loves Quant vs qual — context decides Discrete counts (number of students = 102); continuous ranges (height 100–190 cm, temperature). Square feet of a house and its price are continuous quantitative because they fall within specific ranges — classification depends on context, not just the numbers. Primary vs secondary — credibility decides Primary: collected by you or your team for the analysis (surveys, Google Forms, sensors, interviews). Secondary: World Bank, IMF, NSSO, Wikipedia, stock-exchange data — World Bank data is more reliable than unknown private sources. Metadata is data about data (the library catalog, not the books). Interpreter vs compiler Interpreter (Python): translates line by line at runtime, errors appear progressively. Compiler (C, C++): translates the whole program before execution — no output until every error is fixed. Methods, nested Dot notation runs the method on the variable: name.title() . Functions nest inside functions — print(name.title()) converts first, prints second. Variables are case-sensitive; spelling matters. <Takeaways items={[ Quiz One: 60 MCQs · 20 minutes · the best quiz score counts toward the final evaluation (the deck's initial scheme was best of three at 15% each; Lecture 34 finalizes it). , Syllabus: all recorded lectures up to September 20th , including Working with Lists Part 2. , The final exam is offline pen-and-paper with code writing — practise writing code by hand. , The evaluation rewards interpretation, not memorization : trace the code, predict the output, explain the logic. , ]} />

chapters.label: Numeric lists
chapters.text: Lecture 15 · Numeric lists. range · comprehensions · statistics · slices. for value in range(1, 5): # 1,2,3,4 — stops BEFORE 5 print(value) even = list(range(2, 11, 2)) # start, stop, step print(even) # [2,4,6,8,10] odds = list(range(1, 21, 2)) # odd numbers 1..20 threes = list(range(3, 31, 3)) # multiples of 3 digits = list(range(1, 10)) print(min(digits), max(digits), sum(digits)) # 1 9 45 cubes = [n**3 for n in range(1, 11)] # 2**3 means 2 cubed print(cubes) # The traditional way — 3 lines: squares = [] for value in range(1, 11): squares.append(value ** 2) print(squares) # The comprehension — 1 line, same result: squares = [value ** 2 for value in range(1, 11)] print(squares) digits = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 0] print("min:", min(digits)) # 0 print("max:", max(digits)) # 9 print("sum:", sum(digits)) # 45 players = ['charles', 'martina', 'michael', 'florence', 'eli'] print(players[0:3]) # first three print(players[1:4]) # middle three print(players[-3:]) # last three print(players[:3]) # from start print(players[3:]) # to the end players = ['charles', 'martina', 'michael', 'florence', 'eli'] print("Here are the first three players on my roster:") for player in players[:3]: print(player.title()) numeric-lists Lecture 15 · numerical lists grad-text Half of all programming is generating numbers and looking at parts of them. range() is the number factory, list comprehensions fold four lines into one, min/max/sum do the maths, and slices cut lists without wounding them. card-warm p-6 md:p-8 eyebrow mt-2 text-2xl font-bold mt-5 grid gap-5 lg:grid-cols-2 range_basics.py 1 2 3 4 [2, 4, 6, 8, 10] 1 9 45 [1, 8, 27, 64, 125, 216, 343, 512, 729, 1000] insight Off-by-one, memorized once font-mono-warm font-mono-warm why Million-element lists are fine font-mono-warm 2 List comprehensions — four lines into one The for loop and the list birth, fused into a single readable line grid gap-5 lg:grid-cols-2 squares.py — the same list, two ways [1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, 49, 64, 81, 100] [1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, 49, 64, 81, 100] Read a comprehension out loud: 'give me value squared, for each value in range 1 to 10.' The expression comes FIRST — and note: no colon at the end. That's the grammar. grid content-start gap-4 insight Why Pythonists love these warn Two grammar traps mt-6 3 Simple statistics — min, max, sum Three functions that answer three questions every dataset gets asked digits.py — the one-liner statistics kit min: 0 max: 9 sum: 45 These scale from ten digits to ten million — the million-element list from the checkpoint drill? min, max and sum still answer instantly. 4 Slices — working with part of a list [start:stop] includes start, excludes stop — the same off-by-one rule as range() grid gap-5 lg:grid-cols-2 players.py — slicing ['charles', 'martina', 'michael'] ['martina', 'michael', 'florence'] ['michael', 'florence', 'eli'] ['charles', 'martina', 'michael'] ['florence', 'eli'] A slice [start:stop] includes start, excludes stop — same off-by-one rule as range(). chunks.py — looping a slice Here are the first three players on my roster: Charles Martina Michael Looping through a slice processes a PORTION of a list — chunks of a dataset, one page of results at a time — without ever touching the original. mt-6 mt-6 why Where this pays off mt-8 grid gap-5 md:grid-cols-2 Concept check What does list(range(2, 11, 2)) produce? [2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 11] [2, 4, 6, 8, 10] [2, 3, 5, 7, 9, 11] [4, 6, 8, 10] Start 2, stop 11 (excluded), step 2 → [2, 4, 6, 8, 10]. The step skips between values; the stop is never included. Concept check Which one line replaces the loop form: squares = []; for v in range(1, 6): squares.append(v**2)? squares = [v**2 for v in range(1, 6):] squares = [v**2 for v in range(1, 6)] squares = for v**2 in range(1, 6) squares = (v**2 for v in range(1, 6):) Expression first, then for, then the range — and NO colon inside a comprehension. [v**2 for v in range(1, 6)] → [1, 4, 9, 16, 25]. mt-6 Try It Yourself — numeric-list drills range(1, 21) range(1, 21, 2) range(3, 31, 3) [n**3 for n in range(1,11)] cars[:3], cars[3:6], cars[-3:] mt-6 <SectionHead dark eyebrow= title={ Numeric lists, ranges & slices } lead= /> Making numerical lists range() — Python's number factory range(1, 5) gives 1, 2, 3, 4 — it stops before the second number . To reach 5, write{ } range(1, 6) . This habit will save you a hundred bugs. list(range(1, 1_000_001)) is a million numbers — Python builds it in a blink. Printing them takes a while; press Ctrl-C (or stop the cell) if the output floods. Comprehensions are the signature "Pythonic" move: concise, readable, and faster to write than the loop they replace. You will use them in the data-visualization and sentiment-analysis chapters constantly. No colon after the for inside a comprehension, and the expression sits before the for — the reverse of the loop order. Both feel wrong for exactly one day, then forever natural. Chunks of a specific size = batch processing . Controlled amounts per view ={ } pagination . Subsets without modifying the original = safe analysis . In machine learning you will slice datasets into training and testing sets exactly this way. <Practice title= items={[ { q: Use a for loop to print numbers 1 to 20, inclusive. , hint: }, { q: Make a list of 1 → 1,000,000 and verify it with min() (1), max() (1,000,000) and sum(). }, { q: Use range()'s third argument to list the odd numbers 1–20; print each. , hint: }, { q: Make a list of multiples of 3 from 3 to 30; loop and print. , hint: }, { q: Build the first ten cubes — once with a loop, once with a comprehension. (2**3 is 2 cubed.) , hint: }, { q: With a 9-car list, slice and print the first three, middle three and last three — with a message before each. , hint: }, { q: Loop through a slice of your favourite players and print them in title case — the original list must not change. }, ]} /> <Takeaways dark items={[ range(start, stop, step) stops BEFORE stop; wrap in list() to materialize it. , List comprehensions fuse the loop and the append into one line — expression first, no c

chapters.label: Copies & tuples
chapters.text: Lecture 16 · Copies & tuples. Copy vs reference · immutable tuples. my_foods = ['pizza', 'falafel', 'carrot cake'] # CORRECT — a real, independent copy: friend_foods = my_foods[:] my_foods.append('cannoli') friend_foods.append('ice cream') print(my_foods) # both lists grow independently print(friend_foods) # THE TRAP — this is NOT a copy: alias = my_foods # two names, ONE list alias.append('sprouts') print(my_foods) # sprouts appears here too! my_foods = ['pizza', 'falafel', 'carrot cake'] friend_foods = my_foods # no slice — a REFERENCE my_foods.append('cannoli') # via my_foods… print(friend_foods) # …cannoli is HERE too friend_foods.append('ice cream') print(my_foods) # …and ice cream lands here print(my_foods is friend_foods) # True: same object! is dimensions = (200, 50) # parentheses, not brackets print(dimensions[0]) print(dimensions[1]) dimensions[0] = 250 # try to change one item menu = ('rice', 'dal', 'paneer', 'salad', 'curd') for food in menu: print(food) # The restaurant changes its menu: # you can't edit an item, but you CAN # redefine the whole tuple: menu = ('rice', 'dal', 'biryani', 'halwa', 'lassi') print("\\nRevised menu:") for food in menu: print(food) copies-tuples Lecture 16 · working with lists & tuples grad-text Sometimes you want a real second list — and sometimes Python quietly gives you the same list wearing a second name tag. Then meet the tuple: the immutable list whose TypeError is a feature, not a bug. 1 The slice that copies — and the assignment that doesn't Same words, nearly: my_foods[:] versus my_foods — two utterly different universes mt-6 grid gap-5 lg:grid-cols-2 foods.py — copying lists ['pizza', 'falafel', 'carrot cake', 'cannoli'] ['pizza', 'falafel', 'carrot cake', 'ice cream'] ['pizza', 'falafel', 'carrot cake', 'cannoli', 'sprouts'] Omitting the slice (my_foods[:] vs my_foods) is one of the most common beginner bugs. Always copy with [:]. reference_problem.py — the bug, staged ['pizza', 'falafel', 'carrot cake', 'cannoli'] ['pizza', 'falafel', 'carrot cake', 'cannoli', 'ice cream'] True The check proves it: both names point to ONE list object in memory. This is why the deck says the two variables are aliases, not copies. 2 Tuples — the immutable list Parentheses instead of brackets; Python enforces the promise card-warm p-6 md:p-8 mt-2 max-w-4xl text-[.9rem] text-[#e9d7bf] mt-5 grid gap-5 lg:grid-cols-2 dimensions.py 200 50 Traceback (most recent call last): TypeError: 'tuple' object does not support item assignment Python rejects the change — exactly what we wanted: protection. buffet.py — rewriting a tuple rice dal paneer salad curd Revised menu: rice dal biryani halwa lassi Assigning a NEW tuple to the same variable is legal — mutating the existing one is not. mt-6 grid gap-4 md:grid-cols-3 List [ ] mutable — users, scores, carts: anything that grows and shrinks Tuple ( ) immutable — rectangle dimensions, config values: data that must not drift Looping identical syntax for both — for item in structure: works the same mt-8 grid gap-5 md:grid-cols-2 Concept check friend_foods = my_foods (no slice). You append 'cannoli' to my_foods. What does friend_foods hold? The original three items only The original plus cannoli — same underlying list An empty list A TypeError is raised Without the slice you created a second NAME, not a second list — both variables are aliases for the same object, so the append shows through both names. Concept check dimensions = (200, 50); dimensions[0] = 250 — what happens? dimensions becomes (250, 50) TypeError: 'tuple' object does not support item assignment The tuple gains a third item 250 silently replaces 200 Tuples are immutable — item assignment raises TypeError. You may, however, redefine the ENTIRE tuple: dimensions = (400, 100) is legal. mt-6 Try It Yourself — copies & tuples drills cars[:3], cars[3:6], cars[-3:] mt-6 font-mono-warm <SectionHead dark eyebrow= title={ Copies & tuples } lead= /> Lists work well for sets of items that can change throughout the life of a program — users on a website, characters in a game. But sometimes we want a list of items that cannot change . Python calls values that cannot change immutable , and an immutable list is called a tuple . Write it with parentheses instead of brackets. <Practice title= items={[ { q: Pizzas: loop your pizza list; copy with [:] into friend_pizzas; add different pizzas to each; prove the two lists are separate with two loops. }, { q: Now repeat the pizza program WITHOUT the slice and watch the contamination — then fix it. }, { q: Store five basic foods in a tuple; loop and print each. }, { q: Try to modify one item — meet the TypeError on purpose; read it aloud. }, { q: Rewrite the whole tuple with a new menu and loop again — the legal way to "change" a tuple. }, { q: Nine cars: slice and print the first three, middle three and last three. , hint: }, ]} /> <Takeaways dark items={[ list[:] creates an independent copy ; plain assignment creates a reference — one list, two names. , Changes through either alias affect the same object — prove it with a is b . , Tuples are immutable : item assignment raises TypeError; redefining the whole tuple is allowed. , Choose lists for dynamic data , tuples for fixed data — loops work identically on both. , ]} />

chapters.label: If / Else
chapters.text:
Lecture 17 · If / Else. Conditional tests, comparisons, logic. age = 19 if age >= 18: print("You are old enough to vote!") print("Have you registered yet?") print("(this line is not indented — it always runs)") cars = ['audi', 'bmw', 'ferrari', 'jaguar', 'tesla'] for car in cars: if car == 'bmw': print(car.upper()) # test is True → this indented block runs else: print(car.title()) # test is False → this indented block runs # Single = assigns a value; double == compares two values car = 'BMW' # assignment print(car == 'BMW') # comparison → True (values match) print(car == 'Audi') # comparison → False # The exercise pattern: print a prediction, then the test car = 'subaru' print("Is car == 'subaru'? I predict True.") print(car == 'subaru') # True print("\\nIs car == 'audi'? chapters.text: Lecture 20 · If × lists. Special items · empty checks · multiple lists. # Special items inside a loop requested_toppings = ['mushrooms', 'green peppers', 'extra cheese'] for topping in requested_toppings: if topping == 'green peppers': print("Sorry, we are out of green peppers right now.") else: print(f"Adding {topping}.") # Checking that a list is NOT empty requested_toppings = [] if requested_toppings: # empty list is False! for topping in requested_toppings: print(f"Adding {topping}.") else: print("Are you sure you want a plain pizza?") available_toppings = ['mushrooms', 'olives', 'green peppers', 'pepperoni', 'pineapple', 'extra cheese'] requested_toppings = ['mushrooms', 'french fries', 'extra cheese'] for requested in requested_toppings: if requested in available_toppings: print(f"Adding {requested}.") else: print(f"Sorry, we don't have {requested}.") current_users = ['john', 'admin', 'maria', 'priya', 'sam'] new_users = ['MARIA', 'rahul', 'SAM', 'zoe', 'kiran'] for new_user in new_users: if new_user.lower() in [u.lower() for u in current_users]: print(f"Sorry, {new_user} — that name is taken.") else: print(f"Good news, {new_user} — the name is available.") if-lists Lecture 20 · if statements with lists grad-text The third act of the if chapter: conditional statements wrapped around lists. Special items that need apologies, the empty list that is secretly False, and two lists checked against each other before the kitchen fires up. 1 Special items & the empty-list guard An if INSIDE the loop treats one topping differently; the list name itself IS the emptiness test card-warm p-6 md:p-8 grid gap-5 lg:grid-cols-2 special_items_and_empty.py Adding mushrooms. Sorry, we are out of green peppers right now. Adding extra cheese. Are you sure you want a plain pizza? grid content-start gap-4 insight A list name is a truth test font-mono-warm why Why guard at all? 2 Multiple lists — validate before you cook Compare what was REQUESTED against what is AVAILABLE before committing grid gap-5 lg:grid-cols-2 available_toppings.py — the availability check Adding mushrooms. Sorry, we don't have french fries. Adding extra cheese. Nested loop + membership test: every requested item is checked against the available list. The 'in' operator you met in Lecture 17, doing real kitchen management. unique_usernames.py — multiple lists Sorry, MARIA — that name is taken. Good news, rahul — the name is available. Sorry, SAM — that name is taken. Good news, zoe — the name is available. Good news, kiran — the name is available. Real systems compare case-insensitively: if 'John' exists, 'JOHN' must be rejected too — that's why we lower() both sides before comparing. mt-6 mt-6 story Chapter closed — where the course goes next mt-8 grid gap-5 md:grid-cols-2 Concept check if requested_toppings: — what does this test when the list is empty? True — an empty list is truthy False — an empty list is falsy SyntaxError It depends on the toppings An empty list evaluates to False. That one line is the idiomatic Python guard for 'does the list actually contain anything?' Concept check requested = ['french fries']; available has no french fries. What prints? Adding french fries. Nothing — the loop skips it Sorry, we don't have french fries. IndexError 'french fries' in available_toppings is False, so the else branch runs and apologizes. This is data validation: requests checked against reality before processing. mt-6 Try It Yourself — if × lists drills mt-6 font-mono-warm <SectionHead dark eyebrow= title={ If × lists — filtering the real world } lead= /> if requested_toppings: — Python returns{ } True if the list holds at least one item , False if it is empty. That one line is the idiomatic guard before any "process the list" loop. User input arrives empty more often than anyone expects. Without the guard, an empty order would loop zero times and print nothing — a silent failure. With it, the program asks: plain pizza, really? Conditional tests evaluate to true or false; simple if, if-else and if-elif-else chains handle the roads; combined with loops they filter real data.
