Key–value pairs, add/modify/delete. alien_0 = {'color': 'green', 'points': 5} print(alien_0['color']) # green print(alien_0['points']) # 5 # ADD new key-value pairs at any time alien_0['x_position'] = 0 alien_0['y_position'] = 25 # Start with an empty dictionary and fill it alien = {} alien['color'] = 'green' alien['points'] = 5 # MODIFY a value alien_0['color'] = 'yellow' # DELETE a pair del alien_0['points'] # A dictionary of similar objects (one key → one value per person) favorite_languages = { 'jen': 'python', 'sarah': 'c', 'edward': 'rust', 'phil': 'python', } language = favorite_languages['sarah'].title() print(f"Sarah's favorite language is {language}.") alien_0 = {'color': 'green', 'speed': 'slow'} # This CRASHES if the key is missing: # print(alien_0['points']) → KeyError # get() returns a default instead: point_value = alien_0.get('points', 'No point value assigned.') print(point_value) # get() with no default returns None # (None means "the absence of a value") speed = alien_0.get('speed') print(speed) dicts Python · chapter 4 grad-text You already know lists — but list[0] forces you to memorise what position 0 means. A dictionary replaces positions with labels: alien_0['color'] reads like English. One structure that models users, games, glossaries, entire databases. Four steps and it clicks. card-warm p-6 md:p-8 text-[.95rem] leading-relaxed text-[#e9d7bf] mt-5 rounded-2xl p-4 #fbf3e3 1px dashed #e5c79d 2 Build it — create · read · add · modify · delete A dictionary starts empty or full, and every pair can be added, changed or removed at any time mt-6 grid gap-5 lg:grid-cols-2 alien.py — add · modify · delete green 5 Sarah's favorite language is C. get() — the safe lookup No point value assigned. slow get() is the difference between a program that crashes on missing data and one that handles it gracefully. story Where dictionaries go next mt-8 grid gap-5 md:grid-cols-2 Concept check What does alien_0.get('points', 0) do if 'points' is missing? Crashes with KeyError Returns None Returns 0 instead of crashing Adds the key with value 0 get() looks up the key and returns your provided default (0) when it’s absent — graceful handling instead of a KeyError. Concept check del alien_0['points'] — what happens to the pair? It is hidden until needed It is permanently removed — unrecoverable Its value becomes None A KeyError is raised del permanently removes the key-value pair; a later lookup of 'points' would raise KeyError (that's what get() protects against). mt-8 grid gap-5 md:grid-cols-2 Concept check What does alien_0.get('points', 0) do if 'points' is missing? Crashes with KeyError Returns None Returns 0 instead of crashing Adds the key with value 0 get() looks up the key and returns your provided default (0) when it’s absent — graceful handling instead of a KeyError. mt-6 Try It Yourself — dictionary drills mt-6 {} <SectionHead dark eyebrow= title={ Dictionaries — connecting pieces of information } lead= /> The one idea before any syntax: a list finds things by position, a dictionary finds things by label . Same data, two very different shapes — and the shape on the right is the one that scales to real programs, because “which label?” is a question you can actually answer while writing code: You can build, read, modify and delete pairs. chapters.label: Dict loops
chapters.text: Lecture 22 · Dict loops. items · keys · sorted · values · sets. user_0 = { 'username': 'efermi', 'first': 'enrico', 'last': 'fermi', } # ALL key-value pairs — .items() for key, value in user_0.items(): print(f"\\nKey: {key}") print(f"Value: {value}") # ALL keys — .keys() (default!) for name in favorite_languages.keys(): print(name.title()) # Keys in order — sorted() for name in sorted(favorite_languages.keys()): print(f"{name.title()}, thank you for taking the poll.") # ALL values — .values() print("Languages chosen:") for language in favorite_languages.values(): print(language.title()) # Repetition is natural ('python' appears twice). # Use set() when each item should appear ONCE: print("\\nThe following languages have been chosen:") for language in set(favorite_languages.values()): print(language.title()) # Polling: who already responded vs who to invite if 'erin' not in favorite_languages.keys(): print("Erin, please take our poll!") dict-loops Lecture 22 · looping dictionaries grad-text A dictionary can hold a few pairs or a few million. Python gives you three lenses — pairs, keys, values — and one deduplicator. Pick the lens that matches the question you're asking. rounded-2xl p-4 #fbf3e3 1px dashed #e5c79d mt-6 card-warm p-6 md:p-8 grid gap-5 lg:grid-cols-2 loop_all_pairs.py Key: username Value: efermi ... Two variables in the loop header — .items() hands you the key AND its value each pass. Name them for meaning (name, language) rather than key, value. And note: for name in dictionary: is identical to .keys() — the keys ARE the default. loop_values_and_set.py Languages chosen: Python C Rust Python The following languages have been chosen: C Python Rust Erin, please take our poll! A set is a collection in which each item must be unique — a list wrapped in set() loses duplicates. One honest caveat: the order of a set's output is the machine's choice, not yours — the values above could print in any order from run to run. Sets guarantee uniqueness, never sequence. mt-6 grid gap-4 md:grid-cols-3 insight .items() — the pair lens insight sorted(.keys()) — the order lens insight set(.values()) — the dedupe lens mt-8 grid gap-5 md:grid-cols-2 Concept check Why wrap favorite_languages.values() in set() before looping? To sort alphabetically To make each language appear only once To speed up the loop To convert values to keys A set keeps only unique items — so 'python' appearing for both jen and phil prints once. Use sorted(keys) when you want order instead. Concept check for name in favorite_languages: — what does this loop over? Key-value pairs The keys — .keys() is the default The values Nothing — it needs .items() Looping a dictionary directly loops its KEYS — writing .keys() explicitly is optional (though it can read more clearly). mt-6 Try It Yourself — dict-loop drills if name in favorite_languages.keys() mt-6 {’nile’: ’egypt’, ’amazon’: ’brazil’, …} <SectionHead dark eyebrow= title={ Looping through dictionaries } lead= /> For greeting every user BY their answer: "Jen's favorite language is Python." The dictionary stores pairs in insertion order; sorted() loops a sorted COPY — the original dict is untouched. Thousands of respondents, four languages: set() answers "which languages exist?" without repetition. <Practice title= items={[ { q: Glossary: five programming terms as keys, definitions as values — loop with .items() and print each neatly. Then expand to ten: the loop picks them up automatically. }, { q: Rivers: { } — print “The Nile runs through Egypt.”, then all river names, then all countries. }, { q: Polling: loop a list of people; thank those already in favorite_languages, invite the rest. , hint: }, { q: Loop the glossary keys in ALPHABETICAL order with sorted() — prove the dictionary itself kept its order. }, { q: Print the distinct languages with set() — then add a fifth person favouring python and confirm the set does not change. }, ]} /> <Takeaways dark items={[ .items() walks key-value pairs into two loop variables. , .keys() is the default lens — looping the dict directly is the same; sorted() imposes order on a copy. , .values() reads just the answers; wrap in set() to dedupe. , Combine loops + membership ( in .keys() ) for poll invitations and filters. , ]} />

chapters.label: Nesting
chapters.text: Lecture 23 · Nesting. List of dicts · dict of lists · dict of dicts. aliens = [] for n in range(3): aliens.append({ 'color': 'green', 'points': 5, 'speed': 'slow', }) for alien in aliens[:3]: print(alien) pizza = { 'crust': 'thick', 'toppings': ['mushrooms', 'extra cheese'], } print(pizza['crust']) for topping in pizza['toppings']: print(topping) users = { 'aeinstein': { 'first': 'albert', 'last': 'einstein', }, 'mcurie': { 'first': 'marie', 'last': 'curie', }, } for username, info in users.items(): print(f"\\n{username}") print(info['first'].title(), info['last'].title()) aliens = [] for alien_number in range(30): aliens.append({'color': 'green', 'points': 5, 'speed': 'slow'}) print("created:", len(aliens), "aliens") # The first three speed up and turn yellow: for alien in aliens[:3]: if alien['color'] == 'green': alien['color'] = 'yellow' alien['speed'] = 'medium' alien['points'] = 10 for alien in aliens[:5]: print(alien) nesting Lecture 23 · nesting grad-text Python lets you nest lists inside dictionaries, dictionaries inside lists, and dictionaries inside dictionaries. The moment real data shows up, structures combine — this is how you model fleets, orders and user bases. 2 The three patterns, runnable Same ideas you saw in Lecture 21 — now with room to breathe and edit grid gap-5 lg:grid-cols-3 a list of dictionaries a list in a dictionary a dictionary in a dictionary 3 Generating a fleet — 30 aliens from one loop The deck's video-game pattern: create thousands of objects, then steer them by condition grid gap-5 lg:grid-cols-2 aliens_30.py — generate, then modify created: 30 aliens {'color': 'yellow', 'points': 10, 'speed': 'medium'} {'color': 'yellow', 'points': 10, 'speed': 'medium'} {'color': 'yellow', 'points': 10, 'speed': 'medium'} {'color': 'green', 'points': 5, 'speed': 'slow'} {'color': 'green', 'points': 5, 'speed': 'slow'} range(30) iterates the loop 30 times, creating one dictionary per pass. Then a for + if combo modifies only the aliens that meet the criterion — game engines are built on exactly this beat. grid content-start gap-4 insight Why fleets, not variables why Slices + loops + conditions = management font-mono-warm mt-6 warn Nesting has a depth cost mt-8 grid gap-5 md:grid-cols-2 Concept check aliens holds 30 dictionaries. What does aliens[:3] give you? The last three aliens The first three aliens — as a slice of the list Three random aliens An error — you can't slice a list of dicts Lists of anything slice identically: [:3] is the first three ITEMS — here, three whole dictionaries, which you can then modify key by key. Concept check In users = {'aeinstein': {'first': 'albert', ...}}, how do you reach 'albert'? users.first users['first'] users['aeinstein']['first'] users['aeinstein.first'] Two lookups in sequence: the outer key 'aeinstein' returns the INNER dictionary, then ['first'] reads from it — that's dictionary-in-dictionary access. mt-6 Try It Yourself — nesting drills sum(1 for a in aliens if a['color'] == 'green') mt-6 { } <SectionHead eyebrow= title={ Nesting — structures inside structures } lead= /> Thirty dictionaries hand-typed is bureaucracy; thirty generated by one loop is{ } data engineering . Change the blueprint once and every alien in the fleet changes with it. aliens[:3] picks the front of the fleet, the if filters by colour, the assignments steer. The same trio later powers the records-lab in Lecture 24. Two levels (a dict of dicts, a list of dicts) models most of reality cleanly. Three-plus levels get hard to read — when you feel that pain, that's your cue for{ } classes , waiting at the end of the course. <Practice title= items={[ { q: Pets: several dictionaries (kind of animal + owner's name) inside a list called pets; loop and print everything about each. }, { q: favorite_places: three people as keys, one to three favorite places each as lists; loop and print. }, { q: Cities: three cities as keys, each mapping to a nested dictionary { }country, population, fact{ }; print each city with all its information. }, { q: Scale the fleet: generate 50 aliens, promote the first 5 to yellow, the next 5 to red — then count how many remain green. , hint: }, { q: Pizza orders: a list of pizza dictionaries (crust + toppings list) — loop the orders, then loop each order's toppings. }, ]} /> <Takeaways items={[ List of dicts — fleets and rosters: many objects, one shape, generated by a loop. , Dict with a list value — one key, many values: pizza toppings, favourite languages. , Dict of dicts — hierarchical records: username → profile. , Access nests the same way the data does: outer[key][innerKey] ; loops nest to match. , ]} />

chapters.label: Records lab
chapters.text: Lecture 24 · Records lab. Filter · reward · insert · sort. student_records = [ ['Alice', [75, 88, 92]], ['Bob', [65, 70, 72]], ['Charlie', [88, 90, 95]], ['David', [78, 82, 85]], ['Eve', [45, 50, 55]], ] # 1 — FILTER: keep students whose average is at least 60 eligible = [] for name, scores in student_records: avg = sum(scores) / len(scores) if avg >= 60: eligible.append([name, scores]) student_records = eligible # reassign, don't mutate while looping print("after filter :", student_records) # 2 — REWARD: any paper at 90+ earns 'distinction' for name, scores in student_records: if max(scores) >= 90: scores.append('distinction') # 3 — INSERT: a new student joins at the FRONT student_records.insert(0, ['Zoya', [91, 84, 88]]) # 4 — SORT: alphabetically by name (the lambda picks the key) student_records.sort(key=lambda x: x[0]) for record in student_records: print(record) names = ['charlie', 'alice', 'bob'] names.sort() # permanent sort print(names) print(sorted(names, reverse=True)) # temporary, reversed print(names[:2]) # slice — first two copied = names[:] # deep copy copied.append('zoya') print(names, "|", copied) point = (200, 50) # tuple: immutable print(point[0]) eligible records-lab Lecture 24 · the records lab grad-text Five students, three scores each, four operations. This is the deck's interpretation-over-syntax finale: read the nested structure, run the pipeline, and understand every line — not memorize it. grid gap-4 md:grid-cols-2 lg:grid-cols-4 card-warm p-4 mt-2 font-bold leading-tight text-[#3e2c1d] mt-1 text-[.82rem] leading-relaxed text-muted-warm mt-8 student_records.py — the full pipeline after filter : [['Alice', [75, 88, 92]], ['Bob', [65, 70, 72]], ['Charlie', [88, 90, 95]], ['David', [78, 82, 85]]] ['Alice', [75, 88, 92, 'distinction']] ['Bob', [65, 70, 72]] ['Charlie', [88, 90, 95, 'distinction']] ['David', [78, 82, 85]] ['Zoya', [91, 84, 88]] Trace it: Eve averages 50 → filtered out. Alice (92) and Charlie (95) hit 90+ → distinction. Zoya lands at the front via insert(0, …). The sort's lambda x: x[0] says 'rank by element 0 of each record' — the name. mt-6 records mt-6 grid gap-4 md:grid-cols-2 why Why build a new list instead of removing while looping? insight Reading vs writing code mt-4 story Course logistics straight from the deck mt-6 eyebrow mb-3 toolbox_recap.py ['alice', 'bob', 'charlie'] ['charlie', 'bob', 'alice'] ['alice', 'bob'] ['alice', 'bob', 'charlie'] | ['alice', 'bob', 'charlie', 'zoya'] 200 Sort, sorted-reverse, slicing, deep copy, tuple indexing — every Lecture 11–16 tool, one screen. If any line surprises you, that lecture is your revision spot. mt-8 grid gap-5 md:grid-cols-2 Concept check Why does the lab build and reassign, instead of removing entries from student_records during the loop? It looks tidier Removing items while iterating skips elements — the loop's ground shifts del cannot be used inside loops It is faster Python iterates by index; removing items mid-loop shifts positions and skips elements. Collect survivors into a new list, then reassign — the deck's explicit rule. Concept check What does sort(key=lambda x: x[0]) rank by, for records like ['Alice', [75, 88, 92]]? The scores list The first score (75) Element 0 of each record — the name The record's length The lambda receives each record and returns x[0] — the name — so the sort is alphabetical by name. Without the key, Python would try comparing lists against strings and fail. mt-6 Lab extensions — own the pipeline f-string with :.1f key=lambda x: max(x[1]), reverse=True mt-6 <SectionHead eyebrow= title={ The records lab — a complete data pipeline } lead= /> {LAB_OPS.map((o, i) => ( {o.icon} {o.title} {o.detail} ))} Modifying a list while iterating it shifts the ground under Python's feet — items get skipped. The safe pattern: collect survivors into a new list, then{ } reassign . The deck calls this out explicitly; the exam will too. The final exam cares more about interpretation than syntax memory: given this pipeline, explain what each operation does, spot the indentation and logical errors, and write small programs with the logic right — pen and paper, flexible syntax. One more quiz is scheduled for the end of October — and{ } no third quiz , so every assessment counts double. Assignments will ask for both code and a detailed explanation ; the descriptive questions come primarily from the foundational topics, while the coding sections test how well you interpret and trace programs like this one. The toolbox this lab leaned on — all re-run, one page <Practice title= items={[ { q: Add operation 5: print each student's average next to their name, rounded to one decimal. , hint: }, { q: Change the filter to 65 and predict WHO leaves before running. Eve goes — anyone else? }, { q: Insert TWO new students at the front, in reverse priority order — then sort and explain why the order they were inserted doesn't matter. }, { q: Reward differently: distinction only if the AVERAGE is 90+ (not any single paper). Who keeps it? }, { q: Sort by best score instead of name — rewrite the lambda. , hint: }, ]} /> <Takeaways items={[ Filter with sum/len + a new list ; never mutate while iterating. , max(scores) ≥ 90 → append the distinction marker to the record itself. , insert(0, …) puts arrivals first; append() would bury them last. , sort(key=lambda x: x[0]) — lambdas tell sort() what to rank by; here, the name. , The exam rewards interpretation and explanation — trace the pipeline on paper. , ]} />

chapters.label: While loops
chapters.text: Lecture 25 · While loops. input() · int() · modulo · repeat until done. name = input("Please enter your name: ") print(f"\\nHello, {name}!") # Multi-line prompt with += prompt = "If you share your name, we can personalize it. " prompt += "\\nWhat is your first name? " name = input(prompt) # input() ALWAYS returns a string! age = input("How old are you? ") # "21" not 21 # age >= 18 would crash — str vs int # Convert with int(): age = int(input("How old are you? ")) if age >= 18: print("You are old enough to vote!") # The modulo operator % — the remainder number = int(input("Enter a number: ")) if number % 10 == 0: print(f"{number} is a multiple of 10.") else: print(f"{number} is not a multiple of 10.") print(4 % 3) # 1 (odd/even check uses % 2) current_number = 1 while current_number <= 5: print(current_number) current_number += 1 # the update is ESSENTIAL # 1) where the variable starts runs = 0 # 2) the condition that decides to keep going while runs < 3: print(f"lap {runs + 1}") # 3) the change that moves toward False runs += 1 print("done — the condition finally failed") while Python · chapter 5 grad-text Until now your programs ran top to bottom and finished. input() makes them listen; while makes them persist. This chapter is one conversation: ask the user something, keep responding until they say stop. Two steps here — the exits live in Lecture 26. card-warm p-6 md:p-8 text-[.95rem] leading-relaxed text-[#2b2014] mt-5 rounded-2xl p-4 #fbf3e3 1px dashed #e5c79d mt-5 grid gap-5 lg:grid-cols-2 greeter.py — clear prompts Please enter your name: Eric Hello, Eric! rollercoaster.py — int() for numbers How old are you? 21 You are old enough to vote! Enter a number: 40 40 is a multiple of 10. 1 2 while — repeat until the job is done A for loop counts items; a while loop keeps going as long as its condition stays True card-warm p-6 md:p-8 mb-5 max-w-4xl text-[.92rem] leading-relaxed text-[#2b2014] rounded-2xl p-4 #fbf3e3 1px dashed #e5c79d mt-6 grid gap-5 lg:grid-cols-2 counting.py — the while loop in action 1 2 3 4 5 Forget current_number += 1 and the condition stays True forever — an infinite loop. (In a terminal: Ctrl-C to stop; in Colab: interrupt the cell.) the three moving parts — name them in every while you write lap 1 lap 2 lap 3 done — the condition finally failed Every correct while loop answers three questions: where does the variable start, what must stay True, and what changes it each pass? Miss the third and you loop forever. warn Avoiding infinite loops story Four ways out — next lecture mt-8 grid gap-5 md:grid-cols-2 Concept check Why does age = input('How old are you? ') followed by age >= 18 crash? input() cannot store numbers input() returns a string; comparing str >= int raises TypeError The prompt must not contain a question mark It doesn’t crash input() always returns a string ('21', not 21). Wrap with int() to convert before numerical comparison — and remember the modulo % for remainder tests like multiples of 10. mt-6 Try It Yourself — input & while drills number % 10 == 0 mt-6 quit <SectionHead eyebrow= title={ User input & while loops — interactive programs } lead= /> input() takes one argument — the prompt — prints it, then freezes the whole program until the user presses Enter. Whatever they typed comes back as a string , and you store it in a variable. Follow the value on its journey — and watch the trap at the bottom of the diagram: Use a while loop when you don’t know in advance how many times to repeat — how many users will log in? how many toppings will they ask for? Python tests the condition, runs the body, tests again… The diagram is the whole story: Every while loop needs something that can make its condition False: a counter that increments, a flag that flips, a break. If the loop never ends, trace the variable the condition depends on — is anything changing it? The exit toolkit — flags, break, continue — and while loops that drain lists and fill dictionaries are the whole of Lecture 26, "Flags, Break & Continue". First, make the counting loop below second nature. <Practice title= items={[ { q: Ask what kind of rental car the user would like; print “Let me see if I can find you a Subaru.” }, { q: Ask how many people are in their dinner group: more than eight → wait for a table; otherwise → table is ready. }, { q: Ask for a number and report whether it is a multiple of 10. , hint: }, { q: While loop for pizza toppings until ; confirm each topping: “I’ll add that topping to their pizza.” }, ]} /> <Takeaways items={[ input() shows a prompt and returns a string ; convert with int() for math; % modulo gives remainders. , while condition: repeats while True — the counter, flag or break must guarantee eventual False, or you have an infinite loop. , ]} />

chapters.label: Loop control
chapters.text: Lecture 26 · Loop control. Flags · break · continue · while with data. # 1) Let the user choose when to quit prompt = "\\nTell me something, and I will repeat it back. " prompt += "\\nEnter 'quit' to end. " message = "" while message != 'quit': message = input(prompt) if message != 'quit': print(message) # 2) Using a FLAG — one variable governs the loop active = True while active: message = input(prompt) if message == 'quit': active = False # flips the flag else: print(message) # 3) break — exit the loop immediately while True: city = input("\\nWhich city? ('quit' to stop) ") if city == 'quit': break print(f"{city.title()} — great choice!") current = 0 while current < 10: current += 1 if current % 2 == 0: continue # skip the print for evens print(current) sandwich_orders = ['tuna', 'pastrami', 'pastrami', 'veg', 'pastrami', 'grilled cheese'] finished_sandwiches = [] # The deli ran out of pastrami — remove ALL of them: while 'pastrami' in sandwich_orders: sandwich_orders.remove('pastrami') while sandwich_orders: # while list not empty sandwich = sandwich_orders.pop() print(f"I made your {sandwich} sandwich.") finished_sandwiches.append(sandwich) print("\\nAll sandwiches made:") for s in finished_sandwiches: print(f" · {s}") responses = {} polling_active = True # the flag again while polling_active: name = input("\\nWhat is your name? ") response = input("Which mountain would you like to climb someday? ") responses[name] = response # store key → value repeat = input("Another responder? (yes/ no) ") if repeat == 'no': polling_active = False print("\\n--- Poll Results ---") for name, mountain in responses.items(): print(f"{name} would like to climb {mountain}.") pets = ['dog', 'cat', 'dog', 'goldfish', 'cat', 'rabbit', 'cat'] print(pets) while 'cat' in pets: pets.remove('cat') print(pets) # cats: gone. All of them. loop-control Lecture 26 · loop control grad-text Lecture 25 taught the while loop; this lecture hands you the steering wheel. One Boolean to rule the loop, break to leave mid-stride, continue to skip a beat — then while loops that safely drain lists and fill dictionaries. mt-6 card-warm p-6 md:p-8 mb-5 text-[.92rem] leading-relaxed text-[#e9d7bf] grid gap-5 lg:grid-cols-2 quit_flag_break_continue.py — three ways to stop All three produce the same conversation — the difference is WHO decides to stop: the while test itself, a variable you flip, or an emergency exit. Pick whichever reads clearest. continue — skip one, keep the loop 1 3 5 7 9 continue never exits — it only abandons the rest of THIS pass and jumps back to the test. break exits; continue skips. That pair is all you need to remember. 2 while + lists — where it beats the for loop Drain a list, purge an item — while loops can safely modify the list they're watching card-warm p-6 md:p-8 grid gap-5 lg:grid-cols-2 sandwich_shop.py — moving between lists I made your grilled cheese sandwich. I made your veg sandwich. I made your tuna sandwich. All sandwiches made: · grilled cheese · veg · tuna Two idioms to memorize: while x in list: list.remove(x) purges every occurrence; while list: pop() drains it. mountain_poll.py — filling a dictionary --- Poll Results --- Eric would like to climb Denali. Lynn would like to climb Devil's Thumb. A while loop + a dictionary = a program that collects data until you tell it to stop. This tiny pattern is the seed of every survey app. mt-6 grid gap-5 lg:grid-cols-2 pet_purge.py — remove ALL instances ['dog', 'cat', 'dog', 'goldfish', 'cat', 'rabbit', 'cat'] ['dog', 'dog', 'goldfish', 'rabbit'] remove() alone kills only the FIRST occurrence — the deck flagged that in Lecture 11. Wrap it in while x in list: and every instance falls. When remove() finds nothing, the condition goes False and the loop ends. grid content-start gap-4 insight Why while, not for, here? warn Infinite loops & the stop button mt-6 mt-8 grid gap-5 md:grid-cols-2 Concept check What is the difference between break and continue inside a while loop? They are identical break exits the loop entirely; continue jumps back to the condition test continue exits; break skips one iteration Only for-loops can use break break abandons the loop and moves to the code after it; continue abandons only the current iteration and returns to the while test. Concept check pets = ['dog', 'cat', 'dog', 'cat'] — after while 'cat' in pets: pets.remove('cat'), pets holds… ['dog', 'cat', 'dog'] ['dog', 'dog'] ['dog', 'dog', 'cat'] An infinite loop runs Each pass removes ONE 'cat' and re-tests. When the last 'cat' is gone, 'cat' in pets is False and the loop ends — leaving ['dog', 'dog']. mt-6 Try It Yourself — control drills mt-6 <SectionHead dark eyebrow= title={ Flags, break & continue } lead= /> All four exits, side by side in runnable code — read them in order and the escalation makes sense: sentinel → flag → break, with continue as the "skip one" companion: A for loop iterates by position — remove items mid-loop and elements get skipped. A while loop re-tests its condition each pass : pop from the list, append to the new one, and Python never loses track. That is why unverified→verified user pipelines are written with while. No exit condition, no counter update, no flag flip — the loop never ends. In Colab, press the pause/interrupt button ; in a terminal, Ctrl-C. Then re-read the three moving parts from Lecture 25: initialize, condition, update. <Practice title= items={[ { q: Pizza toppings until 'quit'; confirm each: "I'll add that topping." }, { q: Movie tickets: while loop asking age — under 3 free, 3–12 $10, over 12 $15. }, { q: Three versions of one exit: a conditional test in the while statement · an active flag · a break. }, { q: Write a loop that never ends — run it, stop it (Ctrl-C / interrupt), then explain exactly why it never stopped. }, { q: Dream-vacation poll: name → place into a dictionary while polling; print the results block. }, { q: Unconfirmed → confirmed users: while unconfirmed_users: pop from one list, append to the other — then print both. }, ]} /> <Takeaways dark items={[ A flag is one Boolea

chapters.label: Functions
chapters.text: Lecture 27 · Functions. Define, call, reuse — first steps. def greet_user(username): """Display a simple greeting.""" print(f"Hello, {username.title()}!") greet_user('jesse') # call it — reuse forever greet_user('arpit') functions Python · functions · chapter 6 grad-text You have already felt the pain of repetition: the same greeting logic, the same printing pattern, again and again. A function lets you write a job ONCE, give it a name, and summon it by that name forever after. Three steps — the machine, the shape, the call — and it clicks. card-warm p-6 md:p-8 text-[.95rem] leading-relaxed text-[#e9d7bf] mt-5 rounded-2xl p-4 #fbf3e3 1px dashed #e5c79d 2 See the shape — anatomy of a definition Two lines of vocabulary — def, parameter, docstring, call — carry the entire chapter rounded-2xl p-4 #fbf3e3 1px dashed #e5c79d mt-6 greeter.py — your first function Hello, Jesse! Hello, Arpit! def names the function · the string is a docstring describing what it does · parentheses pass information in. 3 What a call actually does — four beats Follow the jump: call → bind → run → return. This rhythm never changes, no matter how big the function You call greet_user('jesse') — Python pauses this line h-5 w-5 #c2410c Python jumps to the def; 'jesse' is copied into username h-5 w-5 #c2410c The body runs the indented steps do their job h-5 w-5 #c2410c Back you go to the line after the call, as if nothing happened h-5 w-5 #c2410c mt-6 grid gap-5 lg:grid-cols-2 card-warm p-6 flex items-center gap-2 h-5 w-5 #f5c889 text-lg font-bold mt-3 grid gap-2 text-[.88rem] leading-relaxed text-[#cbb392] grid content-start gap-4 insight Connect it back to Pillar 2 story Where the story goes next <SectionHead dark eyebrow= title={ Functions — named blocks that do one job } lead= /> The mental model first: a function is a machine with a name . You feed it inputs ( arguments ), it does its job (the body ), and it hands a result back. Define the machine once — then call it a hundred times with different inputs: <StepsFlow steps={[ { label: , sub: , icon: , }, { label: , sub: , icon: , }, { label: , sub: , icon: , }, { label: , sub: , icon: , }, ]} /> Why functions matter • They break programs into small parts , each doing one specific job • You can call a function as many times as you want , and store functions in separate files • The result: more efficient code that is easier to troubleshoot and maintain — and reusable across many different programs A function is an algorithm with a name — it has input (parameters), defined steps (the body) and output (return values). All five properties still apply. You’ve been training for this since the flowchart. This page is the shape of the idea. The next two chapters go deeper: arguments & return values (positional vs keyword, defaults, what return really does), then functions at scale (passing lists, *args/**kwargs, modules). Master the machine here and they’ll feel easy.

chapters.label: Arguments
chapters.text: Lecture 27 · Arguments. Positional, keyword, defaults & errors. def greet_user(): # defining a function """Display a simple greeting.""" print("Hello!") # the body of the function greet_user() # a function call def greet_user(username): # parameter """Display a simple greeting.""" print("Hello, " + username.title() + "!") greet_user('Arun') # calling the function — 'Arun' is the argument def describe_pet(animal_type, pet_name): # defining with arguments """Display information about a pet.""" print("\\nI have a " + animal_type + ".") # the body print("My " + animal_type + "'s name is " + pet_name.title() + ".") describe_pet('hamster', 'harry') # function call describe_pet('Brad', 'Cow') # same order: type first, name second def describe_pet(animal_type, pet_name): # same definition """Display information about a pet.""" print("\\nI have a " + animal_type + ".") print("My " + animal_type + "'s name is " + pet_name.title() + ".") describe_pet(pet_name='Kyle', animal_type='Parrot') describe_pet(pet_name='Sachin', animal_type='Goat') def describe_BSMT(course_name, instructor_name='aman'): """Display information.""" print("\\nI am enrolled in the " + course_name + " course.") print("The instructor for the " + course_name + " is " + instructor_name.title() + ".") describe_BSMT(course_name='Foundations of Computing') # default used describe_BSMT(course_name='AI in Business', instructor_name='hari') # default ignored def describe_student(student_name, course_name, instructor_name='aman'): """Display information.""" print("\\nMy name is " + student_name + " .") print("I am enrolled in the " + course_name + " course.") print("The instructor for the " + course_name + " is " + instructor_name.title() + ".") describe_student(student_name='Hardavi', course_name='Foundations of Computing') describe_pet() describe_pet('harry', 'hamster', 'good') args Python · functions · the full chapter — part 1 grad-text grad-text You've seen a function defined and called. The argument toolkit: passing information in three styles, letting defaults do quiet work, and catching argument errors. The return keyword that sends answers back lives in Lecture 28. card-warm p-6 md:p-8 flex items-center gap-3 h-6 w-6 #c2410c text-2xl font-bold mt-5 grid gap-5 lg:grid-cols-2 greet.py — no information needed Hello! greet_user() illustrates the simplest possible structure — definition, body, call. grid content-start gap-3 text-[.9rem] leading-relaxed text-[#2b2014] flex gap-3 rounded-xl border border-[#f3e2c8] bg-[#fffaf1] px-4 py-3 term shrink-0 flex gap-3 rounded-xl border border-[#f3e2c8] bg-[#fffaf1] px-4 py-3 term shrink-0 flex gap-3 rounded-xl border border-[#f3e2c8] bg-[#fffaf1] px-4 py-3 term shrink-0 flex gap-3 rounded-xl border border-[#f3e2c8] bg-[#fffaf1] px-4 py-3 term shrink-0 mt-8 card-warm p-6 md:p-8 flex items-center gap-3 h-6 w-6 #c2410c text-2xl font-bold grad-text mt-5 grid gap-5 lg:grid-cols-2 greet.py — greeting by name Hello, Arun! By adding username in the definition, the function now expects a value each time it's called. grid content-start gap-3 parameter The variable username in the definition — a piece of information the function needs to do its job. argument The value 'Arun' in greet_user('Arun') — information passed from a function call to a function. the handshake The argument 'Arun' was passed to greet_user() and stored in the username parameter. while True: # condition is always True print("\\nPlease tell me your name:") f_name = input("First name: ") l_name = input("Last name: ") def get_formatted_name(first_name, last_name): """Return a full name, neatly formatted.""" full_name = first_name + ' ' + last_name return full_name.title() while True: print("\\nPlease tell me your name:") print("(enter 'q' at any time to quit)") f_name = input("First name: ") if f_name == 'q': break l_name = input("Last name: ") if l_name == 'q': break formatted_name = get_formatted_name('aman', 'pathak') print("\\nHello, " + formatted_name + "!") def greet_users(names): """Print a simple greeting to each user in the list.""" # docstring for name in names: msg = "Hello, " + name.title() + "!" print(msg) usernames = ['priyanka', 'unnati', 'anaaya'] # function call greet_users(usernames) # Start with some designs that need to be printed. unprinted_designs = ['iphone case', 'robot pendant', 'dodecahedron'] completed_models = [] # Simulate printing each design, until none are left. # Move each design to completed_models after printing. while unprinted_designs: current_design = unprinted_designs.pop() # Simulate creating a 3D print from the design. print("Printing model: " + current_design) completed_models.append(current_design) # Display all completed models. print("\\nThe following models have been printed:") for completed_model in completed_models: print(completed_model) def print_models(unprinted_designs, completed_models): """ Simulate printing each design, until none are left. Move each design to completed_models after printing. """ while unprinted_designs: current_design = unprinted_designs.pop() # Simulate creating a 3D print from the design. print("Printing model: " + current_design) completed_models.append(current_design) def show_completed_models(completed_models): """Show all the models that were printed.""" print("\\nThe following models have been printed:") for completed_model in completed_models: print(completed_model) unprinted_designs = ['iphone case', 'robot pendant', 'dodecahedron'] completed_models = [] print_models(unprinted_designs, completed_models) show_completed_models(completed_models) unprinted_designs # → [] — permanently emptied! unprinted_designs = ['ferrari', 'honda', 'ford'] completed_models = [] print_models(unprinted_designs[:], completed_models) # passing a copy of the original list show_completed_models(completed_models) unprinted_designs # → ['ferrari', 'honda', 'ford'] — still intact! returns Lecture 28 · return values grad-text Lecture 27 taught functions to take; this lecture teaches them to give back. A function can process data internally and return the result — to be stored, reused, or passed on. This is where functions stop being shortcuts and start being building blocks. 1 return, not print print() is a dead end; return is a doorway card-warm p-6 md:p-8 mt-2 max-w-3xl text-[.92rem] leading-relaxed text-muted-warm font-mono text-[.84rem] font-bold text-[#b45309] mt-5 grid gap-5 lg:grid-cols-2 names.py — return, don't print Agastya Gupta The function combines the names, converts to title case and returns the result. Your Pizza is ready." #pizza.greet("Neha") # ← the dot would have kept yours safe funcs3 Lecture 30 · arbitrary arguments & modules grad-text The power moves: when you can't know in advance how many arguments will arrive, *toppings packs every one into a tuple and **user_info builds a dictionary from whatever key-value pairs show up — then the whole toolbox moves into pizza.py and imports itself back, five ways. 1 Passing an arbitrary number of arguments The asterisk makes an empty tuple and packs whatever the call sends — even a single value card-warm p-6 md:p-8 flex items-center gap-3 h-6 w-6 #f5c889 text-2xl font-bold grad-text mt-2 max-w-3xl text-[.92rem] leading-relaxed text-[#cbb392] mt-5 grid gap-5 lg:grid-cols-2 pizzas.py — the asterisk packs a tuple ('pepperoni',) ('mushrooms', 'green peppers', 'extra cheese') The asterisk tells Python: make an empty tuple called toppings and pack whatever values arrive into it. chapters.label: Classes I
chapters.text: Lecture 31 · Classes I. Dog class · instances · self · methods. class Dog(): """A simple attempt to model a dog.""" def __init__(self, name, age): # Initializing values """Initialize name and age attributes.""" self.name = name self.age = age # __init__() has no explicit return — Python # automatically returns an instance representing this dog. def sit(self): """Simulate a dog sitting in response to a command.""" print(self.name.title() + " is now sitting.") def roll_over(self): """Simulate rolling over in response to a command.""" print(self.name.title() + " rolled over!") my_dog = Dog('willie', 6) # Python reads this line → calls __init__() in Dog # with arguments 'willie' and 6 → sets name and age # → automatically RETURNS an instance → stored in my_dog # Accessing instance attributes print("My dog's name is " + my_dog.name.title() + ".") print("My dog is " + str(my_dog.age) + " years old. \\n") # Calling instance methods my_dog.sit() my_dog.roll_over() my_dog = Dog('willie', 6) your_dog = Dog('lucy', 3) t_dog = Dog('willie', 6) # same values as my_dog! print("My dog's name is " + my_dog.name.title() + ".") print("My dog is " + str(my_dog.age) + " years old.") my_dog.sit() print("\\nYour dog's name is " + your_dog.name.title() + ".") print("Your dog is " + str(your_dog.age) + " years old.") your_dog.sit() your_dog.roll_over() t_dog.sit() class Car(): """A simple attempt to represent a car.""" def __init__(self, make, model, year): """Initialize attributes to describe a car.""" self.make = make self.model = model self.year = year def get_descriptive_name(self): """Return a neatly formatted descriptive name.""" long_name = str(self.year) + ' ' + self.make + ' ' + self.model return long_name.title() my_new_car = Car('audi', 'a4', 2016) # creating an instance print(my_new_car.get_descriptive_name()) oop-intro Lecture 31 · classes & objects grad-text Object-oriented programming is one of the most effective approaches to writing software — and it starts with one image: a class is an architectural blueprint, an instance is the actual house built from it, with its own paint, occupants and address. One blueprint, many houses. Today the Dog and Car classes make that real. 1 Objects from blueprints — the OOP mental model Class = the architectural drawing · instance = the actual house card-warm p-6 md:p-8 text-[.95rem] leading-relaxed text-[#2b2014] mt-6 grid items-stretch gap-3 lg:grid-cols-[1fr_auto_1fr] rounded-2xl border-2 border-[#e8cfa5] bg-gradient-to-b from-[#fffaf1] to-[#fdeed6] p-5 flex items-center gap-2 h-6 w-6 #b45309 font-mono text-[.9rem] font-black text-[#3e2c1d] mt-1 text-[.7rem] font-bold uppercase tracking-widest text-[#8a5a10] mt-2 text-[.82rem] leading-relaxed text-muted-warm 0 0 60 24 mx-auto h-6 w-14 self-center lg:h-8 lg:w-20 M2 12 H50 flow-arrow-line #c2410c 2.5 none M46 5 L56 12 L46 19 #c2410c 2.5 none round round grid content-start gap-3 ivory white the Sharmas Jodhpur sea green the Iyers Pune rounded-2xl border-2 border-[#e8cfa5] bg-gradient-to-b from-[#fdeed6] to-[#fbd9a8] p-4 flex items-center gap-2 h-5 w-5 #c2410c font-mono text-[.82rem] font-black text-[#3e2c1d] mt-1 text-[.8rem] leading-relaxed text-[#6f5438] mt-3 text-center text-[.8rem] font-semibold text-muted-warm mt-5 grid gap-3 class Defines the general behavior and characteristics that a whole category of objects can share. instance An object built from the class — it automatically has the general behavior, plus unique traits of its own. instantiation The act of making an individual object from a class — one class, as many instances as you need. 2 Creating and using a class — Dog The class keyword · capitalized names · __init__ runs automatically · self arrives on its own card-warm p-6 md:p-8 flex items-center gap-3 h-6 w-6 #c2410c text-2xl font-bold mt-2 max-w-3xl text-[.92rem] leading-relaxed text-muted-warm mt-5 grid gap-5 lg:grid-cols-2 dog.py — 1. THE CLASS (Blueprint) grid content-start gap-3 convention By convention, capitalized names refer to classes in Python — Dog, not dog. empty ( ) The parentheses in the class definition are empty because we're creating this class from scratch. The docstring describes what the class does. __init__() A special method Python runs automatically whenever we create a new instance. Two leading + two trailing underscores prevent conflicts with your own method names. method A function that's part of a class. Everything you know about functions applies — the only difference (for now) is how we call them. self Required in the method definition, first in the parameter list. Python passes it automatically — a reference to the instance itself, giving it access to the class's attributes and methods. attributes Variables prefixed with self (self.name, self.age) are available to every method in the class and accessible through any instance. self.name = name attaches the value to the instance being created. mt-6 max-w-3xl rounded-2xl border border-[#f3e2c8] bg-[#fffaf1] p-5 text-[.72rem] font-extrabold uppercase tracking-[.18em] text-[#8a5a10] mt-2 text-[.88rem] leading-relaxed text-[#2b2014] font-mono text-[.8rem] font-mono text-[.8rem] font-mono text-[.8rem] font-mono text-[.8rem] mt-8 text-xl font-bold grad-text mt-2 max-w-3xl text-[.92rem] leading-relaxed text-muted-warm mt-5 my_dog.sit() you call the method on one instance h-5 w-5 #c2410c my_dog → self Python passes the instance automatically — no argument from you h-5 w-5 #c2410c self.name → 'willie' the attribute read belongs to THIS instance h-5 w-5 #c2410c 'Willie is now sitting.' printed with that instance's own data h-5 w-5 #c2410c 3 Making an instance — instantiation Dog('willie', 6) runs __init__ and hands back a real object · then make several card-warm p-6 md:p-8 text-2xl font-bold grad-text mt-2 max-w-3xl text-[.92rem] leading-relaxed text-muted-warm mt-5 grid gap-5 lg:grid-cols-2 dog.py — 2. Attributes · inheritance · composition. class Car(): def __init__(self, make, model, year): """Initialize attributes to describe a car.""" self.make = make self.model = model self.year = year self.odometer_reading = 0 # default, not a parameter def read_odometer(self): """Print a statement showing the car's mileage.""" print("This car has " + str(self.odometer_reading) + " miles on it.") my_new_car = Car('audi', 'a4', 2016) print(my_new_car.get_descriptive_name() + '\\n') my_new_car.read_odometer() def update_odometer(self, mileage): """ Set the odometer reading to the given value. Reject the change if it attempts to roll the odometer back. """ if mileage >= self.odometer_reading: self.odometer_reading = mileage else: print("You can't roll back an odometer!") # --- driving it --- my_new_car1 = Car('audi', 'a4', 2016) my_new_car1.update_odometer(20) # set to 20 my_new_car1.read_odometer() my_new_car1.update_odometer(18) # 18 < 20 → rejected! my_new_car1.read_odometer() my_new_car1.update_odometer(25) # 25 >= 20 → accepted my_new_car1.read_odometer() def increment_odometer(self, miles): """Add the given amount to the odometer reading.""" self.odometer_reading += miles # --- the used-car story --- my_used_car = Car('subaru', 'outback', 2013) print(my_used_car.get_descriptive_name()) my_used_car.update_odometer(23500) my_used_car.read_odometer() # We buy it and put 100 miles on it # between buying and registering: my_used_car.increment_odometer(100) my_used_car.read_odometer() class ElectricCar(Car): """Represent aspects of a car, specific to electric vehicles.""" def __init__(self, make, model, year): """Initialize attributes of the parent class.""" super().__init__(make, model, year) my_tesla = ElectricCar('tesla', 'model s', 2016) print(my_tesla.get_descriptive_name()) class ElectricCar(Car): """Represent aspects of a car, specific to electric vehicles.""" def __init__(self, make, model, year): """ Initialize attributes of the parent class. The profit line they are tied to — and how it is built. card-warm lift h-full p-5 flex h-9 w-9 items-center justify-center rounded-xl text-white shadow-md h-4.5 w-4.5 mt-3 text-[.95rem] font-extrabold text-[#3e2c1d] mt-1 text-[.8rem] font-semibold mt-2 text-[.8rem] leading-relaxed text-muted-warm mt-4 insight So what is financial accounting, really? 04 Would you lend them money? \u20B950 crore of revenue each — very different profits grid gap-3 md:grid-cols-2 card-warm lift h-full p-5 font-mono text-[.68rem] font-bold uppercase tracking-[.2em] text-[#b3402c] mt-2 text-[.9rem] leading-relaxed text-[#2b2014] card-warm lift h-full p-5 font-mono text-[.68rem] font-bold uppercase tracking-[.2em] mt-2 text-[.9rem] leading-relaxed text-[#2b2014] mt-4 The lending decision Your \u20B910 crore loan application is on the desk of one of these two. Which profit figure would you rather be judged by — and why? Company X's \u20B98 crore — bigger is better Company Y's \u20B92 crore — it repeats, X's does not Neither — profit is irrelevant to lending Whichever company has more factories Lending is repaid out of the business a company can repeat tomorrow. X's gain is a one-time event — sell the factory once and it is gone (the core actually lost money). Y's smaller profit is recurring and growing, which is exactly what services debt. One number is bigger; the other is better. 05 Profitable — and out of cash The gap between the income statement and the bank account story The case mt-4 warn Profit is an opinion about a period — cash is a fact at a moment mt-8 mt-8 Seminar drills — argue it out How can two people looking at the same year of the same business reach opposite conclusions about performance? Each privately chose a different measurement rule for the machine and the wear-and-tear — the number follows the rule. What would prevent this disagreement in a company with professionally prepared statements? Agreed conventions + a measurement framework applied by someone other than the winner of the argument. Why does accounting rely on agreed-upon rules at all, instead of everyone calculating profit their own way? Think of Ramesh's investor and Vasudha's three meetings — numbers only trade value when strangers can trust how they were built. <SectionHead eyebrow={eyebrowOf( )} /* derived — was: Module 1 · Why accounting exists */ title={ Five openings — every one ends at the{ } same question } lead= /> } Priya and Rohan jointly inherited their father's small manufacturing business. At year end they sit down to figure out how it did. Priya says it{ } "barely made anything" and wants to sell. Rohan says it{ } "did great" and wants to expand. Same transactions, same year — but Priya counted the full cost of a new machine as this year's expense, while Rohan counted no wear-and-tear on the older equipment at all. "Profit" is not a fact lying around to be picked up — it is a{ } constructed number . Until rules decide how the machine's cost is spread and how wear-and-tear is recognised every period, two honest people looking at the same year will build two different profits. That is what accounting conventions are for: one agreed way, so the argument ends. } Ramesh runs a street-food business that grew from one stall to three. He tracks everything himself — cash in, cash out — in a personal notebook, in his own shorthand. A close friend offers to invest ₹15 lakh so Ramesh can open five more stalls — but asks to see "the financials" first. Ramesh says, "It's all in my head, and in this notebook — ask me anything, I'll tell you." The friend trusts Ramesh personally — and is still hesitant to invest. Personal trust does not scale into capital. The friend is not doubting Ramesh's honesty — he is doubting a system where one person's shorthand decides what counts as income. Financial statements exist to replace "ask me anything" with numbers prepared by agreed rules, so a stranger can check them too. } Vasudha runs a small chain of three gyms. One set of statements — a balance sheet and an income statement. On the same afternoon she shows them to a bank (a loan for a fourth location), to Arjun (a friend investing "the company's profit"). She assumed one set of numbers would mean one conversation. All three meetings went completely differently. {[ { icon: Landmark, who: , want: , eye: }, { icon: HandCoins, who: , want: , eye: }, { icon: Users, who: , want: , eye: }, ].map((c, i) => ( {c.who} {c.want} {c.eye} ))} A common language for the money story of a business — prepared once, but read by lenders, investors, managers, the government. The statements are the same; the question each reader brings decides the conversation. Learning the language is learning all three meetings at once. } Company X Revenue ₹50 crore, profit ₹8 crore — but the ₹8 crore came almost entirely from selling off a factory : a one-time gain. Reporting entity — personal expenses must stay out of the business's books. (b) Car revalued after one week A car bought at auction for \u20B940,000 is re-recorded at \u20B950,000 a week later. Historical cost — assets stay at original purchase price, not fluctuating market values. (c) Personal smartphone as business asset A smartphone bought for the owner's personal use is recorded as a business asset. Reporting entity again — only business-related items belong in the company's books. card-warm lift flex h-full flex-col p-5 font-mono text-[.7rem] font-black tracking-[.2em] mt-1 text-[.95rem] font-extrabold leading-snug text-[#3e2c1d] mt-2 text-[.84rem] leading-relaxed text-muted-warm mt-3 rounded-xl border p-3 text-[.8rem] font-semibold leading-relaxed mt-8 mt-8 December sales, January commission Commission is paid to a salesman in January 2011 for sales made in December 2010. The commission expense belongs to\u2026 January 2011 — that is when cash left December 2010 — the period whose sales it earned Split 50/50 across both months Whichever year the auditor prefers Periodic matching: revenues of a period must be matched with the costs incurred to earn those revenues — when payment was made is irrelevant. December's sales carry December's commission, paid or not. Periodicity requires activities to be divided into artificial time periods : usually a year, sometimes as short as a quarter. Artificial periods create real difficulties — the equipment bought today must serve for years, so its useful life has to be estimated . Those estimates ride on management's judgment and are often subjective. This assumption is the{ } root cause of many accounting controversies — including the dinner-table one. } } REVENUE Sales made in December 2010 earned in this period } COST Commission paid to salesman in January 2011 — for December 2010 sales — cost of earning THAT revenue } MATCH } } When payment was received or made is irrelevant — this is why year-end adjustments exist. On account of this one concept, year-end adjustments are made for{ } outstanding expenses, accrued incomes, prepaid expenses and unearned incomes . Module 4 of this course builds every one of them — they are all this diagram wearing different clothes. Revenue is recognized when a sale is made — specifically when property in the goods passes to the buyer and the buyer becomes legally liable to pay. The moment of delivery, not the order and not the payment, owns the revenue. Hire purchase: ownership passes only at the final installment — yet sellers record revenue progressively as installments fall due, because waiting would misstate every interim period. Long-term construction: profit is recorded yearly on work certified, not only at completion — a bridge billed over five years cannot hide four years of results. Both exceptions exist for one reason: waiting for legal completion gives a misleading picture of the period. Under the money measurement assumption, all business transactions are expressed and recorded in terms of money . Money is the only common denominator that lets a factory, a bank loan and a cartage bill sit in one statement — in India, the rupee is the monetary unit. Anything that cannot be measured monetarily has no place in accounting : a loyal workforce, the owner's reputation, a perfect location. Real advantages — but not numbers, so not in the books. Every discipline buys its power with a boundary; this is accounting's. {[ { tag: , t: , d: , v: , }, { tag: , t: , d: , v: , }, { tag: , t: , d: , v: , }, ].map((c, i) => ( {c.tag} {c.t} {c.d} {c.v} ))} <Takeaways items={[ Accounting measures only

chapters.label: Four conventions
chapters.text: Lecture 07 · Four conventions. Conservatism · disclosure · consistency · materiality. conventions mx-auto max-w-5xl px-4 py-20 sm:px-6 md:py-28 conventions Concepts are the assumptions accounting stands on. Conventions are the customs and traditions accountants follow when preparing statements — developed over time to ensure consistency and fairness. 01 Convention 1 — conservatism Anticipate no profit; provide for all possible losses mt-4 warn The cost of playing safe 02 Conventions 2, 3, 4 Disclosure · consistency · materiality grid gap-3 md:grid-cols-3 Full disclosure Statements must fully and fairly disclose what they purport to represent. Born of joint-stock companies: owners separated from managers rely entirely on the statements. The Companies Act legally requires a true and fair view — notes to accounts (contingent liabilities, investment values) are part of the deal. Consistency Practices must stay consistent period to period, or year-on-year comparison collapses. But not rigid inflexibility: better techniques may be adopted — provided the change and its profit impact are explicitly disclosed. Switching depreciation methods? Say so, and quantify it. Materiality Attach importance to significant details; ignore insignificant ones. Highly context-dependent: a debtor's ledger needs exact paise, a board report may round to hundreds. Judgment, permitted under the Companies Act, keeps statements free of useless clutter. card-warm h-full p-5 h-5 w-5 mt-2 text-[.98rem] font-extrabold text-[#3e2c1d] mt-1.5 text-[.83rem] leading-relaxed text-muted-warm 03 The sorting drill The lecture's four scenarios — pick the convention, then reveal grid gap-3 overflow-hidden rounded-2xl border border-[#e0ece6] bg-[#fffdf9] button flex w-full items-center justify-between gap-3 px-4 py-3.5 text-left text-[.88rem] font-bold text-[#3e2c1d] shrink-0 rounded-full px-2.5 py-1 text-[.62rem] font-black uppercase tracking-[.12em] text-white #d6e8de Which convention? auto overflow-hidden border-t border-[#e4f1ea] bg-white px-4 py-3 text-[.84rem] leading-relaxed text-[#2b2014] mt-10 grid gap-4 md:grid-cols-2 Lecture 7 · check yourself Goods cost ₹1,00,000; market price has fallen to ₹80,000. At what value does inventory appear — and which convention says so? ₹1,00,000 — cost, because that is what was paid (consistency) ₹80,000 — the lower of cost and market (conservatism) ₹1,40,000 — replacement value (going concern) ₹90,000 — an average of the two (materiality) Conservatism: anticipate no profit, provide for all possible losses. Had market risen to ₹1,40,000 the goods would stay at ₹1,00,000 — the unrealized gain is never booked. The loss, though, is recognized the moment it appears. Lecture 7 · check yourself A company switches depreciation methods and says nothing. Even if the new method is genuinely better, what has it violated? Materiality only — the amount is small Nothing — better techniques are always allowed Consistency and full disclosure — changes are allowed but must be disclosed with their profit impact Conservatism — the new method must be more pessimistic Consistency does not mean rigid inflexibility — improved techniques may be adopted. But stakeholders must see the change and its financial impact in explanatory notes. Silence breaks full disclosure; arbitrary switches that flatter profit also break conservatism. mt-10 <SectionHead eyebrow={eyebrowOf( )} /* derived — was: Lecture 7 · Conventions */ title={ Not rules — evolved customs that keep statements fair. } lead= /> Conservatism has critics: it can create secret reserves , understate assets, overstate liabilities and show artificially low net income — so the statements may not reflect the true and fair value of the business. That tension is exactly why the next three conventions exist. {[ { icon: Eye, t: , d: , }, { icon: RotateCcw, t: , d: , }, { icon: Ruler, t: , d: , }, ].map((c, i) => { const Icon = c.icon; return ( {c.t} {c.d} ); })} {CONVENTION_SCENARIOS.map((sc, i) => { const isOpen = open === i; return ( setOpen(isOpen ? null : i)} aria-expanded={isOpen} className= > {sc.s} {isOpen ? sc.a : } {isOpen ? Meet the patterns, then drive them. 01 Pattern (a) — capital and asset rise together Commenced business with cash ₹1,00,000 Effects 02 Pattern (b) — one asset in, another out Bought furniture costing ₹5,000 by paying cash Effects 03 Pattern (d) — liability and asset fall together Paid creditors ₹10,000 Effects 04 Now drive the machine Rani's automobile business — the lecture's own running example, transaction by transaction mt-6 grid gap-3 md:grid-cols-2 insight What the machine is whispering why Exam instinct mt-8 mt-8 Pattern recognition Rani pays ₹8,000 to her creditors. In the machine's language, that transaction is\u2026 \u2191 Asset · \u2191 Liability \u2193 Asset · \u2193 Liability — the equation shrinks on both sides equally \u2191 Asset · \u2193 Asset \u2193 Asset · \u2191 Capital Cash (asset) goes out; creditors (liability) are settled. Both sides of the equation fall by the same 8,000 — the equation shrinks but never breaks. Settling a debt is the only pattern that makes the business smaller without taking anything from the owner. <SectionHead eyebrow={eyebrowOf( )} /* derived — was: Module 2 · Transactions in action */ title={ The four moves —{ } run them yourself } lead= /> { } { } { } Step 3 changed nothing on the claims side; step 4 shrank{ } both sides by the same 8,000 . Two assets can trade places all day; only capital and liabilities move the size of the business. For every transaction, ask exactly two questions: which two families are touched, and which way does each move? Write the two effects before touching any account — the entries then write themselves. <Takeaways items={[ Dual aspect: every transaction has two effects — the equation is book-keeping's law of gravity. , Debits grow the asset / expense / drawings family; credits grow liability / capital / revenue . , An asset needs control + future benefit — miss either and it is out. , Equity is the residual : investments and profits raise it, distributions and losses lower it. , The equation holds after every single transaction — Rani's four steps prove it. , ]} />

chapters.label: Entity & concern
chapters.text: Lecture 09 · Entity & concern. The boundary — and the promise to continue. entity-concern mx-auto max-w-5xl px-4 py-20 sm:px-6 md:py-24 entity-concern grad-emerald Two of the four assumptions do the heaviest lifting: one draws the line around the business, the other justifies how everything inside the line is valued. grid gap-4 md:grid-cols-2 card-warm h-full p-6 chip h-3.5 w-3.5 mt-4 text-[.92rem] leading-relaxed text-[#2b2014] mt-4 space-y-2 Owner's home electricity \u2192 not a business expense Owner's personal smartphone \u2192 not a business asset Owner's wedding \u2192 not business promotion flex items-start gap-2 text-[.84rem] text-muted-warm mt-0.5 h-3.5 w-3.5 shrink-0 card-warm h-full p-6 chip h-3.5 w-3.5 mt-4 text-[.92rem] leading-relaxed text-[#2b2014] mt-4 rounded-xl border p-3 text-[.8rem] leading-relaxed text-[#2b2014] 01 When the promise breaks: the Kingfisher file A going-concern case study, 2012–13 story The case mt-3 block mt-4 insight The lesson that survives the case mt-8 Violation spotting A car is bought at auction for \u20B940,000 and re-recorded at \u20B950,000 one week later \u2014 \u201Cbecause that is what it is worth now.\u201D Two assumptions are involved; what is the cleanest one-line verdict? Money measurement violated — the car cannot be valued Historical cost violated — assets stay at original purchase price while the entity is a going concern Periodicity violated — one week is not a period No violation — fair value is always allowed Going concern is what makes historical cost the right basis: the business will keep and use the car, not flip it. Re-recording at a fluctuating market estimate breaks that basis. Fair value enters only when the going-concern assumption itself collapses. <SectionHead eyebrow={eyebrowOf( )} /* derived — was: Module 1 · Assumptions, deep-dive */ title={ The boundary — and the promise to continue } lead= /> Reporting entity Accountants treat a business as a reporting entity — distinct and separate from its owners and from every other firm. The entity defines the scope of activities included in the financial statements: the owner's personal affairs stay outside, permanently. {[ , , , ].map((s) => ( {s} ))} Going concern Unless there is substantial evidence to the contrary, accountants assume the business is a continuing enterprise . This assumption is what justifies recording assets at historical cost — cost only makes sense if the business lives long enough to use the asset. Fair value — "the amount for which an asset could be exchanged, or a liability settled, between knowledgeable, willing parties in an arm's length transaction." If liquidation were imminent, cost would become irrelevant — assets would move to likely sale prices. In the wake of the 2008 financial crisis, bank auditors were faulted for{ } not issuing going-concern exceptions for any of the major banks that collapsed or needed bailouts — Lehman Brothers, Citigroup, Bear Stearns, Countrywide. Auditors do not cause corporate collapses, but staying silent at the wrong moment means failing their role as a watchdog . On Kingfisher Airlines' 2012 and 2013 statements, the auditors observed that although the accounts were prepared on a going-concern basis, there were{ } doubts : equity wiped out by losses, the air-operator permit lapsed, banks recalling loans. Management answered that it was confident of raising capital, renewing the permit and rescheduling debt. The company ceased operations in late 2012 . Going concern is an assumption with a duty attached : when the evidence turns, someone must say so — on time. Timely going-concern warnings are how the statements protect the very readers (investors, lenders, employees) the whole apparatus exists for.

The bakery wants to list 'celebrity goodwill' as an asset. Correct call? Yes — it has enormous future benefit No — control over the actor's goodwill cannot be restricted, so it fails the asset test Yes — if the auditor agrees Only if it is recorded at fair value Both conditions must hold. Future benefit is clearly there — but the bakery cannot restrict others from using the actor's charm; the resource is not controlled by the entity. No control, no asset — however valuable the endorsement feels. <SectionHead eyebrow={eyebrowOf( )} /* derived — was: Module 2 · The three elements */ title={ Assets, liabilities, equity —{ } the whole cast } lead= /> Control — the entity can restrict others from using the resource.{ } Future benefit — the resource is expected to generate economic value going forward. If either condition is missing, it is not an asset . Candidate Verdict Why Public park Not an asset You enjoy it — but you cannot control access Broken iPod Not an asset You control it — but no future benefit Cash The ideal asset Controlled — and it buys every other asset {[ { icon: Building2, t: , d: , items: [ , , ] }, { icon: Copyright, t: , d: , items: [ , , ] }, { icon: HandCoins, t: , d: , items: [ , , ] }, ].map((c, i) => ( {c.t} {c.d} {c.items.map((it) => ( {it} ))} ))} Contractual liabilities Most liabilities arise from contracts — amounts payable for electricity used, salaries owed to employees, loans payable. Typically{ } precise, known amounts . Statutory liabilities Some obligations arise from law — employer contributions to a provident fund, income tax payable. These may require estimation based on applicable rules. Equity is the residual interest in the assets after deducting all liabilities — the "leftover" value once every debt is settled. It increases through{ } owner investments and profits from operations ; it decreases through{ } distributions to owners (dividends) and losses . In a company, this is called shareholders' equity . Share capital The amount contributed by shareholders towards the company's capital, recorded in the share capital account — the foundational investment made when shares are issued. Retained earnings The cumulative net profit kept in the business rather than distributed as dividends. It grows when the company earns profits and shrinks when it incurs losses or pays dividends. {[ { n: , t: , d: }, { n: , t: , d: }, { n: , t: , d: }, ].map((c, i) => ( {c.n} {c.t} {c.d} ))}

Open one page per account, post every debit and every credit to its page, and each page ends with a balance that speaks. 01 One account to rule them all: Cash Every rupee that entered or left Vogue in June, on one T-shaped page mt-6 grid gap-3 md:grid-cols-2 insight Read the T like a story why The pipeline clicks shut 02 The ledger, grouped Exhibit 3.3 groups Vogue's June accounts into asset, liability and equity categories grid gap-3 sm:grid-cols-3 Asset accounts Cash · Equipment · Office supplies · Trade receivables · Prepaid insurance Liability accounts Trade payables · Unearned revenue Equity accounts Share capital · Dividends · Revenue · all expense accounts #7c6248 card-warm h-full p-5 font-mono text-[.64rem] font-black uppercase tracking-[.2em] mt-2 text-[.82rem] leading-relaxed text-muted-warm mt-8 Ledger mechanics Why does Vogue's Cash account end with a DEBIT balance of \u20B946,930? Because cash is revenue, and revenue carries debit balances Because total debits (58,500) exceed total credits (11,570) — and cash, an asset, keeps its balance on the debit side Because dividends were paid in cash Because the ledger always balances at zero Post everything, total both sides, subtract: 58,500 − 11,570 = 46,930. The side the balance sits on follows the account's nature — assets carry debit balances, liabilities and equity carry credit balances. Cash is an asset, so its balance is a debit. <SectionHead eyebrow={eyebrowOf( )} /* derived — was: Module 3 · Recording — the ledger */ title={ Posting — where the journal{ } grows accounts } lead= /> The debit side is the cash coming in (capital, service revenue, collections, an advance); the credit side is cash going out (supplies, rent, equipment, insurance, settling suppliers, phone, salaries, electricity, dividends). Nine outflows against five inflows — and the account still closes at ₹46,930. That ₹46,930 debit balance is exactly the Cash line in Vogue's June 30 trial balance . The ledger balance is not near the trial-balance figure — it{ } is the trial-balance figure. Which error could STILL be sitting in her books? A debit of 5,000 posted without a matching credit A purchase of machinery debited to Purchases (an error of principle) Debit totals of 1,19,000 against credit totals of 1,18,000 A cash payment entered twice on the credit side only Option A and D break the equality — the trial balance would disagree, so they are caught. Option C is impossible here. But debiting the WRONG CLASS of account (machinery into purchases) keeps both sides equal: the entry is complete and balanced — only its meaning is wrong. Errors of principle sail straight past the trial balance. <SectionHead eyebrow={eyebrowOf( )} /* derived — was: Module 3 · Checking — the trial balance */ title={ Do the columns agree? } lead= /> Under the double entry system, amounts on the debit sides of various accounts are always equal to amounts entered on the credit sides of other accounts — so the{ } totals of the debit sides must equal the totals of the credit sides . An agreeing trial balance gives reasonable confidence the work is free of{ } clerical errors . Agreement is not proof of cent-per-cent accuracy . Four error classes survive a perfect trial balance: errors of principle (wrong class of account),{ } compensating errors (two mistakes cancelling out), wholly omitted transactions (both sides missing together) and double posting (the same entry posted twice — both sides double equally). The pipeline and the day book — Vogue Company. journal mx-auto max-w-5xl px-4 py-20 sm:px-6 md:py-24 journal grad-emerald Two approaches exist for recording transactions — the accounting equation approach and the traditional approach. Both land in the same place: a journal where every event is written with its two effects, the day it happens. 01 The Vogue Company A business that supplies new designs for dresses — June, transaction by transaction story The set-up 02 The three-line ritual ANALYSIS → RULES → ENTRY — the same three moves, every single time ANALYSIS Which accounts are affected, and which way? h-5 w-5 shrink-0 RULES Debit assets/expenses to increase — credit liabilities/capital/revenues to increase. h-5 w-5 shrink-0 ENTRY Write the debits, the credits, and a narration that says why. h-5 w-5 shrink-0 03 The journal, ruled like paper Ten entries from Vogue's June — including one compound entry mt-6 grid gap-3 md:grid-cols-2 warn June 5 — the agreement that books nothing warn June 21 — the appointment that books nothing mt-8 Compound entries On June 25, Vogue completes ₹3,000 of designs for Gupta Company and receives ₹1,000 in part payment. The entry touches\u2026 Cash only — revenue is recorded when fully collected Cash Dr 1,000 + Trade receivables Dr 2,000 / To Revenue 3,000 Revenue Dr 3,000 / To Cash 3,000 Nothing until the final ₹2,000 arrives Revenue is earned in full the moment the designs are delivered — 3,000. Of that, 1,000 arrived (cash up), and 2,000 is now a claim on Gupta (trade receivables up). One event, three accounts — that is a compound entry, and the equation still closes: +3,000 assets = +3,000 equity. <SectionHead eyebrow={eyebrowOf( )} /* derived — was: Module 3 · Recording — the journal */ title={ The pipeline, and the day book } lead= /> Vogue is a business supplying new designs for dresses. The lecture records its June transactions in terms of debits and credits — and warns early:{ } not every item below is an accounting transaction . If an item does not qualify, the correct answer is to say why it does not. <StepsFlow steps={[ { label: , sub: , icon: }, { label: , sub: , icon: }, { label: , sub: , icon: }, ]} /> Vogue signs with EthniWear: a special design, fee ₹2,000 payable{ } on completion . No entry. Signing transfers no value — no asset moves, no obligation is born. Accounting records transactions , not intentions. An office manager is appointed on a monthly salary of ₹1,500. No entry. Hiring changes no asset, liability or equity — the salary becomes an expense{ } period by period , as the work is actually received and paid.

chapters.text: Lecture 16 · Cash vs accrual. Two bases, one matching principle, ₹10 split two ways. basis mx-auto max-w-5xl px-4 py-20 sm:px-6 md:py-28 basis Two ways to keep books: record cash as it moves, or record what is earned and incurred. One of them is honest about performance — and the matching principle decides which period owns which cost. 01 The opening case A software company, ₹1,000 upfront, twelve months of service 02 The two bases, face to face Where each one lives and what it costs you grid gap-3 md:grid-cols-2 h-full rounded-2xl border border-[#e8a896] bg-[#fbeae5] p-5 flex items-center gap-2 text-[.98rem] font-extrabold text-[#7c2d12] h-4.5 w-4.5 h-[18px] w-[18px] mt-2 text-[.84rem] leading-relaxed text-[#5c2a14] mt-3 grid gap-1.5 text-[.78rem] font-bold text-[#7c2d12] text-[#5c2a14] font-bold text-[#7c2d12] text-[#5c2a14] font-bold text-[#7c2d12] text-[#5c2a14] h-full rounded-2xl border p-5 #f2faf6 flex items-center gap-2 text-[.98rem] font-extrabold h-4.5 w-4.5 h-[18px] w-[18px] mt-2 text-[.84rem] leading-relaxed text-[#1d4433] mt-3 grid gap-1.5 text-[.78rem] font-bold text-[#1d4433] font-bold text-[#1d4433] font-bold text-[#1d4433] 03 The matching principle When to match, and what to match grid gap-4 md:grid-cols-2 card-warm h-full p-5 text-[.9rem] font-extrabold text-[#3e2c1d] mt-2 text-[.84rem] leading-relaxed text-[#2b2014] mt-3 rounded-xl px-3 py-2 text-[.78rem] leading-relaxed card-warm h-full p-5 text-[.9rem] font-extrabold text-[#3e2c1d] mt-2 grid gap-2 Direct (product costs) Raw materials, direct wages, machinery — matched to the specific revenue they create. Indirect (period costs) Rent, administrative salaries — matched to the period in which they are incurred. Losses Warehouse fire, theft — no product, no period, no future revenue. Recognized immediately. rounded-xl border border-[#e4f1ea] bg-white px-3 py-2 text-[.8rem] font-extrabold text-[#3e2c1d] text-[.74rem] leading-snug text-muted-warm mt-4 insight Two distinctions worth keeping 04 Operating skill vs market luck The replacement-cost lens on the same ₹10 mt-10 grid gap-4 md:grid-cols-2 Lecture 16 · check yourself Under the accrual basis, a machine built in December, shipped in March and paid for in May earns revenue in… December — when production happened March — when ownership transferred May — when cash arrived Split across all three months Realization: revenue is recognized when the goods are furnished and ownership passes — March. Manufacturing creates inventory, not revenue; cash collection is a separate event entirely. Lecture 16 · check yourself You buy stock at ₹20/kg, replace it today at ₹25/kg, and sell at ₹30/kg. Under the replacement-cost approach, how much of the ₹10 is holding gain? ₹10 — all of it ₹5 — replacement cost minus historical cost ₹2 — one fifth of the profit ₹0 — holding gains are never recognized Replacement lens: ₹30 − ₹25 = ₹5 operating profit (skill); ₹25 − ₹20 = ₹5 holding gain (inflation while you held the stock). The traditional lens shows the same ₹10 but calls it all operating — which flatters the manager and hides the market's contribution. mt-10 <SectionHead eyebrow={eyebrowOf( )} /* derived — was: Lecture 16 · Basis of accounting */ title={ Cash received is not profit earned . } lead= /> Cash basis Record revenue when cash is received; record expenses when cash is paid. Profit = cash revenues − cash payments. Accrued income, prepaid expenses, outstanding costs — none of it exists here. Where it lives Small personal businesses, non-trading entities (clubs, charitable trusts), receipt-and-payment accounts. For Simple, objective, no adjusting entries, suits cash-heavy shops. Against No fair picture of performance; ignores matching; no capital/revenue distinction; profit can be manipulated by timing cash — and reporting turns inconsistent. Accrual basis Record revenues and expenses in the period they become due — irrespective of cash. Credit sales count in the period of sale; expenses count when the service is used. Outstanding costs, prepaid expenses, accrued earnings and advance income are all recorded. Where it lives Commercial institutions everywhere — the most widely accepted basis. For Accurate period profit; true financial position; reflects all relevant transactions. Against Lengthy, complex procedures; many adjustments through the year; quick profit checks are hard. When — regular intervals, not the end of life Waiting until the business closes would make every number obsolete — and tax demands profit year by year. So business life is chopped into intervals, typically twelve months, and each period must carry its own matched result. Realization: a machine built in December, shipped in March, paid for in May — revenue is recognized in March , when ownership transfers. Not December, not May. What — three buckets of expense {[ [ , ], [ , ], [ , ], ].map(([t, d]) => ( {t} {d} ))} Expenditure vs expense: expenditure is any disbursement; only the portion consumed this period to generate revenue is an expense. Revenue vs cash: credit sales create receivables, not receipts — and manufacturing creates inventory, not revenue. Exceptions exist where a market is settled (gold is recognized when mined) and where contracts span years (revenue as work is certified). <Takeaways items={[ Cash basis: simple but blind to performance — profit moves with cash timing. , Accrual basis: record when due , not when paid — the basis commercial institutions use. , Matching: revenue is matched with the expenses of the same period — realization decides when. , Expense buckets: direct (product), indirect (period), losses (immediately). , Replacement-cost thinking splits operating skill from holding gain — both sum to the same profit. , ]} />
