Four assumptions set the rules. The dual aspect gave every rupee two stories. The journal wrote them down, the ledger grouped them, the trial balance checked the arithmetic, the adjustments made the periods honest — and the final accounts turned the whole pipeline into two answers: did we profit, and what do we own and owe? That is Financial Accounting — one equation, kept true from the first ₹10,000 to the last ₹12,00,000.

chapters.label: Balance sheet
chapters.text: Lecture 22 · Balance sheet. A photograph — current vs fixed, two orders. Assets = Liabilities + Capital ↓ always, by construction Total of one side = Total of the other If they do NOT match, it is not a mystery — it is an error in preparation. The sheet is a re-arrangement of double entry itself. balance-sheet mx-auto max-w-5xl px-4 py-20 sm:px-6 md:py-28 balance-sheet The balance sheet is a snapshot, valid only for the date it names: a single transaction can change every figure. Prepared after the P&L — together they are the final accounts — and the two sides must always agree, because capital equals assets minus liabilities. grid gap-3 md:grid-cols-2 card-warm flex h-full items-start gap-3 p-5 mt-0.5 h-5 w-5 shrink-0 text-[.95rem] font-extrabold text-[#3e2c1d] mt-1 text-[.84rem] leading-relaxed text-muted-warm card-warm flex h-full items-start gap-3 p-5 mt-0.5 h-5 w-5 shrink-0 text-[.95rem] font-extrabold text-[#3e2c1d] mt-1 text-[.84rem] leading-relaxed text-muted-warm 01 Sort the balance sheet Every item the lecture names — click its family 02 Two ways to arrange the same sheet Liquidity order or permanency order — toggle 03 The final step of the cycle Journal → ledger → trial balance → statements — and the sheet must agree grid gap-4 md:grid-cols-2 Why the two sides must always be equal card-warm h-full p-5 text-[.9rem] font-extrabold text-[#3e2c1d] mt-2 grid gap-1.5 text-[.78rem] leading-relaxed Purpose profit or loss for a period position at a date Time an interval — usually one year a point in time Items revenue & expense nature capital nature Accounts all closed to the P&L not closed — carried forward Source trial balance trial balance grid grid-cols-[64px_1fr_1fr] items-start gap-2 rounded-lg bg-white px-3 py-1.5 font-mono text-[.62rem] font-black uppercase tracking-wider text-[#9db8a9] text-[#7c2d12] mt-10 grid gap-4 md:grid-cols-2 Lecture 22 · check yourself A firm's trial balance shows assets ₹9,00,000 and liabilities ₹2,00,000. What must capital be — and what happens if the sheet shows otherwise? ₹7,00,000 — and a mismatch means an error in preparation ₹11,00,000 — assets plus liabilities ₹9,00,000 — capital equals assets It depends on the year's profit Capital = Assets − Liabilities = 9,00,000 − 2,00,000 = ₹7,00,000. Because the balance sheet simply re-arranges the accounting equation, unequal sides signal a preparation error — never a new accounting concept. Lecture 22 · check yourself Which list is arranged in liquidity order? Land → machinery → inventory → receivables → cash Cash → receivables → inventory → machinery → land Cash → land → machinery → inventory → receivables Receivables → cash → land → inventory → machinery Liquidity order puts the most convertible first — cash leads, land trails. Permanency order is its mirror image. On the liability side, liquidity order puts current liabilities before long-term; permanency order puts capital and reserves first. mt-10 <SectionHead eyebrow={eyebrowOf( )} /* derived — was: Lecture 22 · The photograph */ title={ What the firm owns and owes — on one date . } lead= /> The P&L is a video Performance over a period — revenue and expense items, every account closed after transferring to the P&L. The balance sheet is a photograph Position at a point in time — capital-nature items, balances that are not closed but carried forward to the next year. { } P&L vs balance sheet — the audit table {[ [ , , ], [ , , ], [ , , ], [ , , ], [ , , ], ].map(([k, a, b]) => ( {k} {a} {b} ))} <Takeaways items={[ A point-in-time statement — valid only for the date it names. , Current liabilities: payable within a year (creditors, overdraft, outstanding expenses, advances). Fixed: not due within a year. , Assets: current (cash, receivables, stock) · fixed (machinery, buildings) · intangible (patents, trade rights). , Two arrangements: liquidity order vs permanency order — same items, different lens. , The balance sheet completes the accounting cycle — prepared after the P&L, and its sides must always agree. , ]} />

chapters.label: The fourth pillar
chapters.text: Lecture 23 · The fourth pillar. Why profit ≠ cash — operating, investing, financing. flex items-center justify-between gap-2 rounded-xl border px-3 py-2 text-left transition-colors ${ isOpen ? c.ok ? "border-[#059669] bg-[#ecfdf5]" : "border-[#e8a896] bg-[#fbeae5]" : "border-[#e4f1ea] bg-white hover:border-[#a9dcc4]" } cashflow-intro mx-auto max-w-5xl px-4 py-20 sm:px-6 md:py-28 cashflow-intro The income statement, balance sheet and retained earnings statement each leave the same question unanswered. The cash flow statement exists to answer it — and of all the statements, it is the most honest. 01 What the other three cannot say Each statement has a blind spot grid gap-3 md:grid-cols-3 Balance sheet Shows that equipment changed — not whether it was bought with cash or credit, nor where the cash came from. Income statement Shows net income — computed on accrual, not cash. The actual cash generated by operations stays invisible. Retained earnings Shows dividends declared — not whether they were actually PAID in cash during the period. h-full rounded-2xl border border-[#e8a896] bg-[#fbeae5] p-4 text-[.9rem] font-extrabold text-[#7c2d12] mt-1.5 text-[.8rem] leading-relaxed text-[#5c2a14] mt-4 story Cathay Pacific — the paradox in one sentence 02 What counts as 'cash'? Cash in hand + demand deposits — and the equivalents test grid gap-4 md:grid-cols-2 card-warm h-full p-5 text-[.95rem] font-extrabold text-[#3e2c1d] mt-2 text-[.84rem] leading-relaxed text-[#2b2014] mt-3 text-[.8rem] leading-relaxed text-muted-warm mt-2 grid gap-1.5 button text-[.8rem] font-bold text-[#3e2c1d] h-4 w-4 shrink-0 text-[#059669] h-4 w-4 shrink-0 text-[#b3402c] text-[.62rem] font-black uppercase tracking-wider text-[#9db8a9] wait mt-2 rounded-lg px-3 py-2 text-[.76rem] leading-snug #7c2d12 flex h-full flex-col gap-3 rounded-2xl border p-5 #f2faf6 text-[.9rem] font-extrabold mt-2 grid gap-2 text-[.8rem] leading-relaxed text-[#1d4433] card-warm p-5 text-[.9rem] font-extrabold text-[#3e2c1d] mt-1.5 text-[.82rem] leading-relaxed text-[#2b2014] 03 Sort the flows The lecture's own transactions — click the family 04 Why net income ≠ operating cash Four reasons the two numbers part ways grid gap-3 md:grid-cols-2 Different bases Net income is accrual: revenue when earned, expenses when incurred. Operating cash counts only actual cash moving. Non-cash expenses Depreciation and amortization cut profit but spend nothing — added back when converting to cash. Working capital Receivables up: sales booked, cash not collected → cash flow falls. Payables up: expenses booked, cash not paid → cash flow rises. Non-operating items Gains/losses on asset sales sit in profit, but the sale proceeds belong to investing — removed from operating. card-warm h-full p-4 text-[.9rem] font-extrabold text-[#3e2c1d] mt-1 text-[.82rem] leading-relaxed text-muted-warm mt-6 insight Who reads it, and why mt-10 grid gap-4 md:grid-cols-2 Lecture 23 · check yourself A company converts ₹50 lakh of debentures into equity shares. How does this appear on the cash flow statement? As a financing inflow of ₹50 lakh As both an inflow and an outflow of ₹50 lakh It does not appear — no cash moved As an investing outflow Debt-to-equity conversion changes the capital structure entirely on paper — a balance-sheet transaction with zero cash movement. Only transactions involving actual cash appear on the statement. Lecture 23 · check yourself Interest RECEIVED on investments and interest PAID on loans — where does each belong? Both operating Received → investing; paid → financing Received → financing; paid → investing Both financing Returns on investments made (interest and dividends received) are investing inflows. The cost of financing (interest and dividends paid) belongs to financing. Memorize the pair — it recurs in every statement you will build. mt-10 <SectionHead eyebrow={eyebrowOf( )} /* derived — was: Lecture 23 · The fourth pillar */ title={ Where did the cash actually come from — and where did it go? } lead= /> {[ { t: , d: }, { t: , d: }, { t: , d: }, ].map((b, i) => ( {b.t} {b.d} ))} The airline purchased assets worth HK$9.2 billion while reporting an HK$8.6 billion loss . Neither the loss nor the balance sheet can explain how such purchases were financed. Only the cash flow statement can. (And remember Soleris from Lecture 4: 40% sales growth, and still unable to pay suppliers.) Cash & cash equivalents Cash in hand and demand deposits are cash. Cash equivalents are short-term, highly liquid investments readily convertible into cash with minimal risk of value change — think maturities around three months . Firms deploy idle cash into such instruments, staying able to pull it back for operations. ( c.ok ? : ) : ( judge )} ); })} {openTest !== null ? ( {CASH_EQUIV_TEST[openTest].d} ) : null} The three activity families Operating — the principal revenue-generating activities: receipts from sales, interest and dividends received; payments to suppliers, employees, government (tax) and lenders (interest), insurers. Investing — acquiring and disposing of long-term assets: fixed assets, shares and debt instruments of other companies, advances and loans given; proceeds from their disposal, repayments, interest and dividends received. Financing — changes in the size and composition of capital: proceeds from issuing shares, debentures, loans; repayments, interest paid, dividends paid. The non-cash trap Converting debt into equity reshapes the balance sheet — and moves no cash at all. Non-cash transactions never appear on the cash flow statement. {[ { t: , d: }, { t: , d: }, { t: , d: }, { t: , d: }, ].map((r, i) => ( {r.t} {r.d} ))} Investors and creditors assess future cash flows and their timing; employees and creditors check whether salaries, debts and declared dividends can actually be paid; every user judges the reliability of reported net income

chapters.label: Final accounts
chapters.text: Lecture 24 · Final accounts. Two questions, two statements. final-accounts mx-auto max-w-5xl px-4 py-20 sm:px-6 md:py-24 final-accounts grad-emerald Final accounts are prepared at the end of an accounting period to reveal the result of operations and the financial position. Everything the course has built — journal, ledger, trial balance, adjustments — now gets asked its purpose. grid gap-3 md:grid-cols-2 card-warm lift h-full p-6 font-mono text-[.62rem] font-black uppercase tracking-[.2em] mt-3 font-display text-xl font-bold leading-snug text-[#3e2c1d] mt-3 text-[.85rem] leading-relaxed text-muted-warm card-warm lift h-full p-6 font-mono text-[.62rem] font-black uppercase tracking-[.2em] text-[#b45309] mt-3 font-display text-xl font-bold leading-snug text-[#3e2c1d] mt-3 text-[.85rem] leading-relaxed text-muted-warm 01 From adjusted trial balance to final accounts Each adjusted trial balance item moves into one of the two statements grid gap-3 md:grid-cols-2 card-warm h-full p-5 text-[.95rem] font-extrabold text-[#3e2c1d] mt-2 text-[.84rem] leading-relaxed text-muted-warm mt-3 flex flex-wrap gap-1.5 Sales Purchases Stock Wages Rent Interest rounded-lg border px-2.5 py-1 font-mono text-[.7rem] font-bold card-warm h-full p-5 text-[.95rem] font-extrabold text-[#3e2c1d] mt-2 text-[.84rem] leading-relaxed text-muted-warm mt-3 flex flex-wrap gap-1.5 Cash Debtors Machinery Creditors Loans Capital rounded-lg border px-2.5 py-1 font-mono text-[.7rem] font-bold #e8d3ac #faf4e4 #8a5a10 mt-6 insight The sorting rule is the whole skill mt-8 Sorting round From an adjusted trial balance: closing stock ₹15,000. Where does it go? Trading account (credit side) AND balance sheet (current asset) — it does double duty Only the trading account — it is a flow Only the balance sheet — stock is an asset Nowhere — closing stock is never recorded Closing stock is the rare item that appears in BOTH statements: it credits the trading account (shrinking the cost of goods sold) and carries forward as an asset in the balance sheet. Opening stock, by contrast, appears only on the debit side of the trading account. <SectionHead eyebrow={eyebrowOf( )} /* derived — was: Module 4 · Final accounts */ title={ Two questions, two statements } lead= /> Question 1 — over the period "Did the business earn a profit or suffer a loss over the period?" Answered by the Trading & Profit and Loss Account — the statement of performance. Question 2 — at a point in time "What is the financial standing of the business at this specific point — what do we own, and what do we owe?" Answered by the Balance Sheet — the statement of position. Trading & Profit and Loss Account Revenue and expense balances: sales, purchases, stock, wages, rent, interest . Answers: did we earn a profit or suffer a loss this period? {[ , , , , , ].map((t) => ( {t} ))} Balance Sheet Asset, liability and capital balances: cash, debtors, machinery, creditors, loans, capital . Answers: what do we own and owe at the year end? {[ , , , , , ].map((t) => ( {t} ))} Look at an adjusted trial balance item and ask one question: is it{ } a flow (revenue or expense) or a stock (asset, liability or capital) ? Flows go to the Trading & P&L account; stocks go to the balance sheet. Every exam question on "prepare the final accounts" is this sorting test, then arithmetic.

chapters.label: Direct vs indirect
chapters.text: Lecture 25 · Direct vs indirect. The ₹73,000 → ₹69,700 reconciliation ladder. h-full rounded-2xl border p-4 ${i === 3 ? "border-[#e3c98f] bg-[#fbf4e4]" : "border-[#e0ece6] bg-[#fffdf9]"} text-[.9rem] font-extrabold ${i === 3 ? "text-[#8a5a10]" : "text-[#3e2c1d]"} Cash Flow Statement Jaws Photo Plus · FY… OPERATING Net cash from operating activities 69,700 INVESTING Purchases (PPE) / sales / interest rec. … FINANCING Shares, loans, interest & dividends paid … ───────────────────────────── Net increase / decrease in cash … Beginning cash & equivalents … Ending cash & equivalents … ↳ must match the balance sheet exactly cashflow-methods mx-auto max-w-5xl px-4 py-20 sm:px-6 md:py-28 cashflow-methods The statement has a fixed skeleton — three activity sections that sum to a net change, which must reconcile with the balance sheet's cash. Operating cash can be built directly from receipts and payments, or indirectly, by walking net income back to cash. 01 The skeleton Header → three sections → net change → the check grid gap-3 md:grid-cols-4 Operating daily business: receipts from customers, payments to suppliers, employees, tax Investing long-term assets: purchases and sales of PPE and investments Financing capital: shares issued, loans taken, repaid, interest & dividends paid The check beginning cash + net change = ending cash — which must equal the balance sheet's cash & cash equivalents mt-1 text-[.76rem] leading-relaxed text-muted-warm 02 Direct vs indirect Follow the cash — or walk profit back to it grid gap-3 md:grid-cols-2 h-full rounded-2xl border p-5 #f2faf6 text-[.98rem] font-extrabold mt-2 text-[.84rem] leading-relaxed text-[#1d4433] mt-3 rounded-xl px-3 py-2 text-[.78rem] font-semibold #e7f5ee h-full rounded-2xl border border-[#e3c98f] bg-[#fbf4e4] p-5 text-[.98rem] font-extrabold text-[#8a5a10] mt-2 text-[.84rem] leading-relaxed text-[#5c4a22] mt-3 rounded-xl bg-white px-3 py-2 text-[.78rem] font-semibold text-[#8a5a10] 03 The working-capital rules Four moves — current assets and current liabilities grid gap-2 sm:grid-cols-2 Current asset ↑ deduct cash is locked in (receivables, inventory grew) #b3402c Current asset ↓ add assets turned into cash Current liability ↑ add expenses booked, cash kept (payables grew) Current liability ↓ deduct old bills were paid down #b3402c flex items-center gap-3 rounded-2xl border border-[#e0ece6] bg-[#fffdf9] p-4 flex h-9 w-9 shrink-0 items-center justify-center rounded-xl text-white h-4.5 w-4.5 h-[18px] w-[18px] min-w-0 text-[.86rem] font-extrabold text-[#3e2c1d] text-[.74rem] leading-snug text-muted-warm 04 The ladder, run for real Jaws Photo Plus — ₹73,000 of profit becomes ₹69,700 of cash mt-6 The full format, condensed mt-10 grid gap-4 md:grid-cols-2 Lecture 25 · check yourself Inventory increased by ₹12,000 during the year. In the indirect method, this is… Added — inventory is an asset Deducted — cash was spent buying stock that has not sold yet Ignored — inventory is not cash Added only if sales also increased An increase in a current asset means cash was locked into it — purchases exceeded cost of goods sold. Deduct. Mirror rule: a decrease in inventory is added back. For current liabilities the signs flip. Lecture 25 · check yourself Why is the gain on disposal of plant assets DEDUCTED in the operating section? Because gains are never real Because the sale proceeds belong to investing — leaving the gain in operating would double-count Because gains are taxed separately Because the asset was bought in an earlier year The profit already includes the gain, but the cash from selling the asset is an investing inflow. Deducting the gain from operating prevents counting it twice — the full proceeds (not just the gain) show under investing. mt-10 <SectionHead eyebrow={eyebrowOf( )} /* derived — was: Lecture 25 · Building the statement */ title={ Two roads to operating cash . } lead= /> {[ { t: , d: }, { t: , d: }, { t: , d: }, { t: , d: }, ].map((s, i) => ( {s.t} {s.d} ))} Direct method Record every actual cash receipt and payment: cash from customers, less cash to suppliers, employees and operating expenses, less taxes — equals net operating cash. Sourced straight from the accounting records and cash-book analysis. Advantage: the received amounts help estimate FUTURE cash flows. Less common in practice. Indirect method Start with net income and adjust: add back non-cash expenses (depreciation, amortization, goodwill write-offs), deduct non-cash income (gains on disposal), then apply the working-capital rules. The one annual reports actually use — it reconciles profit to cash. {[ { t: , d: , why: , tone: , icon: TrendingUp }, { t: , d: , why: , tone: FA_G[700], icon: TrendingDown }, { t: , d: , why: , tone: FA_G[700], icon: TrendingUp }, { t: , d: , why: , tone: , icon: TrendingDown }, ].map((r) => { const Icon = r.icon; return ( {r.t} → {r.d} {r.why} ); })} { } <Takeaways items={[ Ending cash must reconcile exactly with the balance sheet's cash & cash equivalents. , Direct = follow actual receipts & payments; indirect = net income walked back to cash (the standard). , Adjustments: add non-cash expenses, remove non-operating gains/losses, apply the working-capital rules . , Jaws Photo Plus: 73,000 + 7,000 − 2,500 − 4,000 − 3,800 = ₹69,700 . , Negative operating cash flow = the core is spending more cash than it generates — investigate. , ]} />

chapters.label: The indirect build
chapters.text: Lecture 26 · The indirect build. Compass ₹72,000 · Ajay ₹4,32,000 → ₹3,48,000. Net Profit (or Profit Before Tax) − non-cash expenditures (depreciation, bad debts) − non-operating gains (added back if losses) − non-operating income (interest income…) − non-cash interest expenses = Operating profit before working-capital changes ± working-capital adjustments = Cash generated from operations − income tax PAID = Net cash flow from operating activities Tax paid = Tax expense + Opening tax payable − Closing tax payable Profit before tax + depreciation & bad debts (non-cash) − gains on asset sales, investment income ± inventory, receivables, payables changes − income tax actually paid ────────────────────────── Net cash flow from operating activities = ₹72,000 The full three-section statement then follows: investing (asset purchases & disposals) and financing (capital raised & returned). cashflow-build mx-auto max-w-5xl px-4 py-20 sm:px-6 md:py-28 cashflow-build The indirect method converts accrual profit into cash-based profit. Everything fits three categories: non-cash items, non-operating items, and working-capital changes — then tax paid, computed properly, and the statement is done. 01 The formula ladder Memorize the sequence — every problem is this ladder The indirect method, top to bottom 02 Category by category What moves, and which way grid gap-3 md:grid-cols-3 1 · Non-cash items Depreciation — added back Bad debts / provisions — added back Goodwill write-offs — added back They reduced profit without moving cash. 2 · Non-operating items Gain on sale of equipment — subtract Loss on sale — add back Interest income — subtract (investing) Interest expense — add back (financing) Only operating activity belongs here. 3 · Working capital Inventory ↑ subtract · ↓ add Receivables ↑ subtract · ↓ add Prepaids ↑ subtract · ↓ add Payables ↑ add · ↓ subtract Timing gaps between booking and cash. card-warm h-full p-5 text-[.92rem] font-extrabold text-[#3e2c1d] mt-2 grid gap-1.5 flex items-start gap-2 text-[.78rem] leading-relaxed text-[#2b2014] mt-[7px] h-1.5 w-1.5 shrink-0 rounded-full mt-2 text-[.74rem] italic text-muted-warm 03 Case study — Compass Company Two years of statements (2004, 2005), all three categories applied Compass Company — the verified result mt-4 04 Exercise — Ajay Company ₹4,32,000 of profit, adjusted move by move mt-6 warn Two traps the lecture warns about mt-10 grid gap-4 md:grid-cols-2 Lecture 26 · check yourself Interest income received on advances given to suppliers belongs to… Operating — it is income Investing — returns on amounts lent Financing — it involves cash It is excluded entirely Interest and dividends RECEIVED are returns on investments made — investing inflows. Interest and dividends PAID are the cost of financing — financing outflows. Income the business exists to earn (sales, service fees) is what operating captures. Lecture 26 · check yourself Tax expense for the year is ₹50,000; opening tax payable ₹30,000; closing ₹50,000. Cash paid for tax is… ₹50,000 — the expense itself ₹30,000 — 50,000 + 30,000 − 50,000 ₹70,000 — 50,000 + 30,000 − 10,000 ₹20,000 — the increase in the payable Tax paid = expense + opening payable − closing payable = 50,000 + 30,000 − 50,000 = ₹30,000. The ₹20,000 that accrued but was unpaid stays as a liability — and appears as a working-capital addition, not as tax paid. mt-10 <SectionHead eyebrow={eyebrowOf( )} /* derived — was: Lecture 26 · The indirect method at work */ title={ Three adjustment families — then the numbers land . } lead= /> { } {[ { t: , items: [ , , ], d: , }, { t: , items: [ , , , ], d: , }, { t: , items: [ , , , ], d: , }, ].map((c, i) => ( {c.t} {c.items.map((x) => ( {x} ))} {c.d} ))} { } Not everything touches cash — equipment bought on credit never appears on the statement.{ } Gains and losses on disposals are adjusted in operating, but the cash itself sits in investing — miss that and you count it twice. <Takeaways items={[ Ladder: PBT → non-cash → non-operating → working capital → cash generated → tax paid . , Compass lands at ₹72,000 ; Ajay walks ₹4,32,000 down to ₹3,48,000 . , Interest/dividends received → investing ; paid → financing . , Tax paid = expense + opening payable − closing payable. , Credit purchases of assets never touch the statement — no cash, no entry. , ]} />

Net profit: change in reserves & surplus = 1,70,000 + tax provision +50,000 + proposed dividend +50,000 = Net profit before taxation = 2,70,000 Depreciation: furniture 30,000 + equipment 15,000 = 45,000 Amortization: patent 1,00,000 → 95,000 = 5,000 Equipment: opening 2,00,000 + bought 80,000 − depreciation 15,000 − closing 2,30,000 = 35,000 sold at a 5,000 loss → proceeds = 30,000 Tax: opening provision 30,000 PAID this year; closing 50,000; the 20,000 increase is added back Operating +1,52,000 Investing −1,50,000 Financing −60,000 ──────── Net change −58,000 Opening cash 2,00,000 − 58,000 = Closing cash 1,42,000 ↳ verified against the balance sheet. The statement closes. cashflow-health mx-auto max-w-5xl px-4 py-20 sm:px-6 md:py-28 cashflow-health The three sections are the anatomy; analysis is the medicine. Compass Company's statement answers six questions about earnings quality, financing, expansion strain, flexibility — and whether the dividend can survive. 01 The six questions Compass Company, interrogated grid gap-3 md:grid-cols-2 card-warm h-full p-5 font-mono text-[.62rem] font-black uppercase tracking-[.2em] mt-1 text-[.95rem] font-extrabold leading-snug text-[#3e2c1d] mt-2 text-[.82rem] leading-relaxed text-[#2b2014] mt-6 grid gap-3 sm:grid-cols-3 3.3× interest cover — 72,000 ÷ 22,000 ₹11,41,000 → ₹72,000 profit vs operating cash — the quality gap #b3402c 12.5% → 50% dividend rate vs payout of available cash rounded-2xl border border-[#e0ece6] bg-[#fffdf9] p-4 text-center mx-auto h-5 w-5 mt-1.5 font-mono text-[1.02rem] font-black text-[#3e2c1d] mt-0.5 text-[.72rem] leading-snug text-muted-warm 02 Worked example — Pioneer Limited A full statement, built from working notes The working notes — where the numbers come from mt-4 mt-4 The closing check mt-10 grid gap-4 md:grid-cols-2 Lecture 27 · check yourself Compass earned ₹11,41,000 of profit but generated ₹72,000 of operating cash. The FIRST question an analyst asks is… Is the auditor independent? What is the quality of earnings — did profit become cash, or is it trapped in receivables and inventory? Should the dividend be raised? Is the depreciation method too aggressive? A ₹10,69,000 gap between profit and operating cash is a quality-of-earnings question: inventory +58,000 and receivables +44,000 locked cash in working capital. Profit is an opinion; the statement reveals how much of it became cash. Lecture 27 · check yourself Pioneer's equipment account: opening ₹2,00,000, purchases ₹80,000, depreciation ₹15,000, closing ₹2,30,000. Sold at a ₹5,000 loss. Sale proceeds were… ₹35,000 — the book value ₹30,000 — book value minus the loss ₹40,000 — book value plus the loss ₹50,000 — cost minus depreciation Book value at disposal = 2,00,000 + 80,000 − 15,000 − 2,30,000 = 35,000. Sold at a 5,000 loss means cash received = 35,000 − 5,000 = 30,000 — the investing inflow. The 5,000 loss is added back in operating. mt-10 <SectionHead eyebrow={eyebrowOf( )} /* derived — was: Lecture 27 · The diagnosis */ title={ Six questions turn a statement into a verdict . } lead= /> {SIX_Q.map((q, i) => ( Question {i + 1} {q.t} {q.a} ))} {[ { icon: Percent, k: , d: , tone: FA_G[700] }, { icon: TrendingDown, k: , d: , tone: }, { icon: BadgePercent, k: , d: , tone: FA_G.gold }, ].map((s) => { const Icon = s.icon; return ( {s.k} {s.d} ); })} { } { } <Takeaways items={[ Six questions: cash decline, financing sources, equity use, expansion strain, flexibility , creditor & shareholder outlook. , Profit of ₹11,41,000 vs cash of ₹72,000 = a quality of earnings flag, not necessarily fraud. , Creditors read interest cover (3.3×); shareholders read the dividend's sustainability . , Pioneer: 2,70,000 → +1,52,000 / −1,50,000 / −60,000 → net −58,000 → closing cash 1,42,000 , verified. , Working notes first, statement second: depreciation, disposal book values and tax paid must be derived. , ]} />

chapters.label: FS analysis
chapters.text: Lecture 28 · FS analysis. Four standards, four techniques, one FX red herring. fs-analysis mx-auto max-w-5xl px-4 py-20 sm:px-6 md:py-28 fs-analysis Financial statement analysis converts statements into decisions: how did the business perform, where is it strong and weak, what are the prospects? It needs standards to compare against and techniques to compare with. 01 Four standards of comparison Against what, exactly, are we judging? grid gap-3 md:grid-cols-2 card-warm h-full p-5 flex items-center gap-2 h-4.5 w-4.5 h-[18px] w-[18px] text-[.95rem] font-extrabold text-[#3e2c1d] mt-2 text-[.82rem] leading-relaxed text-muted-warm mt-4 story Kodak — the past-performance trap 02 Four techniques The analytical toolkit grid gap-3 md:grid-cols-4 h-full rounded-2xl border border-[#e0ece6] bg-[#fffdf9] p-4 font-mono text-[.6rem] font-black uppercase tracking-[.2em] mt-1 text-[.92rem] font-extrabold text-[#3e2c1d] mt-1.5 rounded-lg px-2 py-1.5 font-mono text-[.68rem] leading-snug mt-1.5 text-[.74rem] leading-snug text-muted-warm 03 Case study — Dr. Reddy's 2015-16 A profit decline that wasn't a decline mt-4 warn The distortion checklist mt-10 grid gap-4 md:grid-cols-2 Lecture 28 · check yourself A company's profit grew 10% last year. Its industry grew 30%. What is this called? Quality of earnings The illusion of growth Horizontal analysis A favorable variance Growing 10% while the industry grows 30% masks relative underperformance — the illusion of growth. Past-performance comparison without an industry (or contextual) benchmark flatters the number. Lecture 28 · check yourself Dr. Reddy's reported a 7.92% profit decline in 2015-16. What did the operating view reveal? The core business had weakened badly A one-time ₹4,621 thousand FX loss (Venezuela) explained it all — operating profit actually grew 9.23% Expenses had grown faster than revenue Tax had risen sharply Revenue +4.49%, expenses only +3.49% — core operations grew 9.23%. The entire decline came from an exceptional, non-recurring foreign-exchange loss absent in 2015. Quality of earnings analysis separates the signal from the noise. mt-10 <SectionHead eyebrow={eyebrowOf( )} /* derived — was: Lecture 28 · From preparing to interrogating */ title={ Raw data in — insight out . } lead= /> {STANDARDS.map((s, i) => { const Icon = s.icon; return ( {s.t} {s.d} ); })} Peak sales of $16 billion in 1996 , profits of $2.5 billion in 1999 — and bankruptcy in{ } 2012 . Dominating the camera market meant nothing once digital disruption redrew it. Relying solely on past performance masked the existential threat; the trend was accurate right up to the moment it stopped being the world it described. {TECHNIQUES.map((t, i) => ( 0{i + 1} {t.t} {t.f} {t.d} ))} Non-recurring and exceptional items create misleading impressions; accounting policy changes (depreciation, inventory valuation) break year-to-year comparability; different fiscal year-ends block direct comparison; and different policies across an industry complicate peer analysis. Always ask: what is the source of this number? <Takeaways items={[ Four standards: rule of thumb , past performance (Kodak's trap), internal , industry (no perfect peer). , Four techniques: horizontal , trend , vertical , ratio . , Watch for exceptional items , policy changes, fiscal-year mismatches. , Dr. Reddy's: headline −7.92% vs operating +9.23% — one FX loss, two completely different stories. , ]} />

chapters.label: Profit is an opinion
chapters.text: Lecture 29 · Profit is an opinion. Mira's shop · the student analogy · the closing argument. Concepts & conventions → the equation → journal & ledger → trial balance → adjustments → final accounts → the balance sheet → the cash flow statement → analysis that asks: can I trust this number? Answer the last question with cash first. cashflow-wrap mx-auto max-w-5xl px-4 py-20 sm:px-6 md:py-28 cashflow-wrap #b45309 A company can be profitable on paper and still run out of cash — because accrual accounting records what is earned, not what arrived. One stationery shop explains the entire lecture series. 01 Mira's stationery shop One credit sale, three months, the whole lesson 02 The three statements, one line each What each one is for grid gap-3 md:grid-cols-3 Balance sheet A snapshot: what the company owns and owes at a specific point in time. Profit & loss Performance over a period — revenue and expense, without tracking cash movement. Cash flow The fundamental question: where did cash come from, and where did it go? card-warm h-full p-5 h-5 w-5 mt-2 text-[.95rem] font-extrabold text-[#3e2c1d] mt-1 text-[.82rem] leading-relaxed text-muted-warm 03 Why profit ≠ operating cash — three sources The lecture's own numbers grid gap-3 md:grid-cols-3 Non-cash expenses ₹24,000/yr A ₹1,00,000 photocopier depreciated at ₹24,000 a year cuts profit — but the cash left two years ago. Add it back. Working capital ₹1,00,000 / ₹30,000 Mira's credit sale raises profit but not cash; her ₹30,000 credit purchase of paper cuts profit but keeps cash. Non-operating items ₹5,000 gain An old computer, book value ₹10,000, sold at ₹15,000: the ₹5,000 gain sits in profit, but the full ₹15,000 proceeds belong to investing. h-full rounded-2xl border border-[#e0ece6] bg-[#fffdf9] p-4 text-[.9rem] font-extrabold text-[#3e2c1d] mt-1 font-mono text-[1rem] font-black mt-1.5 text-[.78rem] leading-relaxed text-muted-warm 04 The student analogy You already run three cash flows grid gap-3 md:grid-cols-3 Operating Monthly pocket money in; mess charges and daily living out. Investing Buying a laptop — an asset with lasting value; parking savings in a fixed deposit. Financing Taking an education loan, and repaying it (with interest) for years. flex h-full items-start gap-3 rounded-2xl border border-[#e3c98f] bg-[#fbf4e4] p-4 mt-0.5 h-5 w-5 shrink-0 #8a5a10 text-[.9rem] font-extrabold text-[#5c4a22] mt-0.5 text-[.78rem] leading-relaxed text-[#5c4a22] mt-6 insight The four-company reality check mt-4 The course, in one balance mt-10 grid gap-4 md:grid-cols-2 Lecture 29 · check yourself Mira sells ₹1,00,000 of stock on credit in March; the coaching centre pays in May. In March, Mira's books show… ₹1,00,000 profit and ₹1,00,000 cash ₹1,00,000 profit and no cash — a receivable instead No profit until cash arrives A ₹1,00,000 liability Accrual basis: the sale is earned in March — profit and a trade receivable appear; the cash box stays empty while rent and salaries fall due. The cash flow statement is what exposes (and later explains) the gap. Lecture 29 · check yourself Why do banks and lenders read the cash flow statement before anything else? It is the shortest statement Because profit depends on accounting choices, but cash is objective — unaffected by policies Because it shows the highest profit Because tax law requires it Profit is an opinion — it moves with depreciation methods, valuation choices and accrual judgments. Cash is a fact. A lender's question ('can you actually pay me?') can only be answered in cash. mt-10 <SectionHead eyebrow={eyebrowOf( )} /* derived — was: Lecture 29 · The closing argument */ title={ Profit is an opinion . Cash is a{ } fact . } lead= /> {[ { icon: Camera, t: , d: }, { icon: LineChart, t: , d: }, { icon: Wallet, t: , d: }, ].map((s, i) => { const Icon = s.icon; return ( {s.t} {s.d} ); })} {[ { t: , n: , d: }, { t: , n: , d: }, { t: , n: , d: }, ].map((r, i) => ( {r.t} {r.n} {r.d} ))} {[ { icon: GraduationCap, t: , d: }, { icon: Laptop, t: , d: }, { icon: Banknote, t: , d: }, ].map((r, i) => { const Icon = r.icon; return ( {r.t} {r.d} ); })} Real statements from four different industries show net income and operating cash flow are never equal : for Lenovo and BP, operating cash ran below profit; for the others, above. The metrics are measured on different bases — accrual vs cash — and that is precisely why lenders scrutinize the cash flow statement first: cash is fact, whatever the accounting policies say . { } <Takeaways items={[ Accrual profit and cash move on different clocks — Mira sells in March, gets paid in May. , NI ≠ operating cash for three reasons: non-cash expenses, working capital, non-operating items . , Cash equivalents: liquid, readily convertible, minimal risk — judged from acquisition date. , The student analogy: pocket money = operating, laptop = investing, education loan = financing . , Profit is an opinion; cash is a fact — the sentence the whole course was building toward. , ]} />

chapters.label: Profitability ratios
chapters.text: Lecture 30 · Profitability ratios. Six ratios · Dr. Reddy's 15.55→13.71 · the ROA identity. h-full rounded-2xl border p-4 ${i === 0 ? "border-[#059669] bg-[#ecfdf5]" : "border-[#e0ece6] bg-[#fffdf9]"} Gross margin ↑ rose (the making-and-selling engine improved) Net margin 15.55% → 13.71% employee costs + one-time forex loss Asset turnover 0.87 → 0.81 assets +11.5% vs revenue +4.5% ROA 13.49% → 11.14% both drivers fell together ROE 26.37% → 19.96% the ROA fall, amplified by leverage EPS ₹137.18 → ₹126.15 profitability per share, down Root causes: rising salary costs · an extraordinary forex loss (₹46–61 million, one-time) · assets outgrowing revenue. ratio-profitability mx-auto max-w-5xl px-4 py-20 sm:px-6 md:py-28 ratio-profitability A ratio relates one financial figure to a base — assets, sales revenue, or shareholder value. Two firms can both earn ₹10 lakh: Firm A keeps ₹20 per ₹100 of sales, Firm B keeps ₹5. Same profit, utterly different businesses. Ratio analysis is how the story gets told. 01 Four categories — the map Profitability now; liquidity, solvency and the market next lecture grid gap-3 md:grid-cols-4 Profitability How well sales, assets or equity convert into profit. Liquidity Can the firm pay its short-term obligations on time? Solvency Can the firm survive its long-term obligations? Capital market What does the stock price say about all of it? h-5 w-5 #9db8a9 mt-2 text-[.92rem] font-extrabold text-[#3e2c1d] mt-1 text-[.76rem] leading-snug text-muted-warm 02 The six profitability ratios Click each — formula, meaning, and Dr. Reddy's 2015→2016 walk 03 The two business models ROA = Margin × Turnover — the identity that explains strategy 04 The Lipstick Index Ratios are read in context — even the recession's story Lipstick sales rose 11% during the 2001 recession 05 The gross-margin trap What moves the line — and what cannot grid gap-3 md:grid-cols-2 card-warm h-full p-5 font-extrabold text-[#3e2c1d] mt-2 text-[.84rem] leading-relaxed text-[#2b2014] #b3402c card-warm h-full p-5 font-extrabold text-[#3e2c1d] mt-2 text-[.84rem] leading-relaxed text-[#2b2014] mt-4 Dr. Reddy's 2015→2016 — the full walk, in one balance mt-10 grid gap-4 md:grid-cols-2 Lecture 30 · check yourself Dr. Reddy's gross margin rose in 2016 while its net margin fell. What does that tension reveal? The product engine improved while indirect costs grew Cost of goods sold must have collapsed Revenue must have fallen The forex loss raised the gross margin Gross margin only sees COGS — and it improved. The net-margin fall came from below the line: rising employee (indirect) costs and the one-time forex loss. That is exactly why both margins are read together. Lecture 30 · check yourself A luxury house earns a 10% margin turning assets 2×; a supermarket earns 4% turning 5×. Compare their ROAs. The supermarket's is higher — 20% vs 10% Identical at 20% — margin × turnover, two roads to one ROA The luxury house's is higher — 40% vs 20% Impossible to compare without EPS 10% × 2× = 20% and 4% × 5× = 20%. ROA is a strategy fingerprint: high-margin/slow-turning vs low-margin/fast-turning can land on the same number. mt-10 <SectionHead eyebrow={eyebrowOf( )} title={ The same profit, six different stories . } lead= /> {[ { t: , d: , icon: TrendingUp }, { t: , d: , icon: HeartPulse }, { t: , d: , icon: Building2 }, { t: , d: , icon: TrendingDown }, ].map((c, i) => { const Icon = c.icon; return ( {c.t} {c.d} ); })} While most demand collapsed, lipstick — an affordable luxury — sold 11% more. Demand for cosmetic surgeons, psychiatrists and priests also rises in downturns. The lesson the lecture draws: a profitability ratio is never read in a vacuum — smart analysts link firm performance to the wider socioeconomic weather. Ratios without context are meaningless. Gross margin = (Sales − COGS) ÷ Sales Pulls it down: raw-material costs rising without matching price increases; selling prices cut to match competitors. Below the line — invisible to gross margin Never touches it: interest expense and advertising sit{ } below the gross-margin line as indirect expenses. A stable gross margin can hide a borrowing bill quietly eating the net margin — Dr. Reddy's 2016 tension exactly. { } <Takeaways items={[ Ratios need a base — the same profit means different things per ₹100 of sales, assets or equity. , Six profitability ratios: profit margin, gross margin, asset turnover, ROA, ROE, EPS . , ROA = Margin × Turnover — luxury (10% × 2×) and supermarket (4% × 5×) both land at 20%. , Leverage amplifies ROE only while ROA > interest rate — debt is a two-edged sword. , EPS is for tracking one company over time — never cross-company comparison. , Read ratios in context: one-time events, industry norms, even the Lipstick Index . , ]} />

chapters.label: Liquidity ratios
chapters.text: Lecture 31 · Liquidity ratios. Current & quick · turnover · the 230-day cycle. ratio-liquidity mx-auto max-w-5xl px-4 py-20 sm:px-6 md:py-28 ratio-liquidity Liquidity is the ability to pay short-term obligations on time out of current assets — how quickly assets become cash. The people who care: suppliers of raw material, banks and short-term lenders, and creditors seeking assurance of payment. 01 The four liquidity ratios Formulas, thumb rules — and what each one quietly assumes 02 The operating cycle Cash → inventory → sale → cash — 140 + 90 = 230 days Buy raw material cash becomes stock Hold inventory holding period — 140 days Sell stock becomes a receivable Collect collection period — 90 days mt-3 insight 230 days — and every one of them costs money 03 The supplier-payment paradox Paying a bill can make the current ratio look BETTER 04 Evaluating receivables properly A shorter collection period is not automatically good grid gap-3 md:grid-cols-4 Credit terms What payment period did the firm actually OFFER its customers? Aging Break the receivables down by how overdue each account is. Bad-debt allowance What provision exists for the amounts that will never pay? Customer mix Retail and corporate customers pay at different speeds. h-full rounded-2xl border border-[#e0ece6] bg-[#fffdf9] p-4 text-[.88rem] font-extrabold text-[#3e2c1d] mt-1 text-[.76rem] leading-snug text-muted-warm mt-3 why The comparison rule mt-10 grid gap-4 md:grid-cols-2 Lecture 31 · check yourself Current assets ₹300, current liabilities ₹150 — ratio 2:1. The firm pays one supplier ₹50 cash. The current ratio now is… Lower — cash left the business Higher — ₹250 ÷ ₹100 = 2.5:1, the liability fell proportionally more Unchanged — one payment cannot move a ratio Zero — current assets fell Paying cash cuts current assets AND current liabilities together. Because the denominator fell proportionally more, the ratio RISES. That is the supplier-payment paradox — a low ratio can improve by paying, which is why examiners love it. Lecture 31 · check yourself Inventory turnover is 6. How long does stock sit before it sells? 6 days 60 days — 360 ÷ turnover 180 days Cannot be computed without sales Holding period = 360 ÷ turnover = 360 ÷ 6 = 60 days. The same arithmetic turns a receivable turnover of 6 into a 60-day collection period — and holding + collection is the operating cycle. mt-10 <SectionHead eyebrow={eyebrowOf( )} title={ Can the firm pay tomorrow? } lead= /> The operating cycle runs from purchasing raw material to collecting cash from customers:{ } holding period + collection period = 140 + 90 = 230 days . Shorter is better — a longer cycle inflates working-capital needs and the storage and insurance costs of stock that just sits. {[ { t: , d: }, { t: , d: }, { t: , d: }, { t: , d: }, ].map((c, i) => ( {c.t} {c.d} ))} A shorter collection period is only favorable if it aligns with or beats the credit terms the firm offered . Collecting in 45 days when you gave customers 60 is excellent; collecting in 45 when you demanded 15 is a failure — even though the raw number looks small. <Takeaways items={[ Liquidity = paying short-term obligations on time ; suppliers, banks and creditors read it first. , Current ratio thumb rule 2:1 ; quick ratio 1:1 — inventory out because it needs a sale AND a collection. , Turnover ↔ days: 360 ÷ turnover ; holding 60 + collecting 60 — and Reddy's-style cycles run 230+ days. , Operating cycle = holding + collection ; shorter cycles free working capital. , A shorter collection period is only good if it beats the terms you offered . , The supplier-payment paradox : paying cash cuts CA and CL — a low ratio can improve. , ]} />

chapters.label: Solvency & market
chapters.text: Lecture 31 · Solvency & market. D/E · interest coverage · PE · PB · beta. ratio-solvency-market mx-auto max-w-5xl px-4 py-20 sm:px-6 md:py-28 ratio-solvency-market Solvency examines long-term survival based on debt levels; capital-market ratios link the share price to earnings, dividends and book value. Suppliers read liquidity, lenders read solvency, investors read the market. 01 Why firms borrow — and what it risks Interest is tax-deductible; dividends are not grid gap-3 md:grid-cols-2 card-warm h-full p-5 flex items-center gap-2 h-[18px] w-[18px] font-extrabold text-[#3e2c1d] mt-2 text-[.84rem] leading-relaxed text-[#2b2014] card-warm h-full p-5 flex items-center gap-2 h-[18px] w-[18px] #b3402c font-extrabold text-[#3e2c1d] mt-2 text-[.84rem] leading-relaxed text-[#2b2014] 02 The solvency ratios Debt-to-equity and interest coverage, decoded grid gap-3 md:grid-cols-2 card-warm h-full p-5 flex items-center gap-2 h-[18px] w-[18px] text-[.95rem] font-extrabold text-[#3e2c1d] mt-2 rounded-lg px-2 py-1.5 font-mono text-[.7rem] mt-2 text-[.82rem] leading-relaxed text-muted-warm card-warm h-full p-5 flex items-center gap-2 h-[18px] w-[18px] text-[.95rem] font-extrabold text-[#3e2c1d] mt-2 rounded-lg px-2 py-1.5 font-mono text-[.7rem] mt-2 text-[.82rem] leading-relaxed text-muted-warm 03 The capital-market ratios What the share price says about all of it grid gap-3 md:grid-cols-3 PE ratio Price ÷ EPS ₹300 price ÷ ₹20 EPS = 15. A high PE signals the market's optimism about future growth. Earnings yield EPS ÷ Price The PE's reciprocal — earnings as a percentage of what you pay for them. Dividend yield Dividend per share ÷ Price × 100 The percentage return coming from dividends alone. Stock return (Dividend + Price change) ÷ Opening price × 100 Buy at 100, collect ₹5 of dividend, sell at 110 → (5 + 10) ÷ 100 = a 15% return. PB ratio Price ÷ Book value per share · (Book = Equity ÷ Shares) Above 1 means the market expects returns above the required rate — expectations of future profitability. Beta Sensitivity vs the overall market Lower beta = lower volatility and risk; higher beta = bigger swings, both ways. h-full rounded-2xl border border-[#e0ece6] bg-[#fffdf9] p-4 h-5 w-5 mt-2 text-[.9rem] font-extrabold text-[#3e2c1d] mt-1 rounded-lg px-2 py-1.5 font-mono text-[.66rem] leading-snug mt-1.5 text-[.76rem] leading-snug text-muted-warm 04 Choosing investments by risk profile Same ratios, opposite shopping lists grid gap-3 md:grid-cols-2 flex h-full items-start gap-3 rounded-2xl border border-[#a9dcc4] bg-[#f2faf6] p-4 mt-0.5 h-5 w-5 shrink-0 text-[.9rem] font-extrabold mt-0.5 text-[.8rem] leading-relaxed text-[#1d4433] flex h-full items-start gap-3 rounded-2xl border border-[#e8a896] bg-[#fbeae5] p-4 mt-0.5 h-5 w-5 shrink-0 #b3402c text-[.9rem] font-extrabold text-[#b3402c] mt-0.5 text-[.8rem] leading-relaxed text-[#7c2d12] 05 Dr. Reddy's 2016 verdict Three lenses, three different headlines mt-10 grid gap-4 md:grid-cols-2 Lecture 31 · check yourself Interest coverage is 4×. How far can profit fall before interest payments are missed? 4% 25% 75% — profit can fall to a quarter and still cover 400% Coverage 4× means EBIT is 4 times the interest bill. Profit can decline by 3 of those 4 units — 75% — and interest is still covered. The cushion, not the ratio itself, is the point. Lecture 31 · check yourself Buy a share at ₹100, collect a ₹5 dividend, sell at ₹110. The stock return is… 5% — dividends are the only return 10% — the price gain 15% — (5 + 10) ÷ 100: dividend income plus capital gain 110% — the selling price Stock return = (dividend + price change) ÷ opening price × 100 = (5 + 10) ÷ 100 = 15%. Total return has two components — income and appreciation — and both count. mt-10 <SectionHead eyebrow={eyebrowOf( )} title={ Can it survive a decade — and what does the market think? } lead= /> The case for debt Debt is cheaper than equity because interest payments are tax-deductible — they reduce taxable income and lower the effective cost of borrowing. Dividends carry no such shield. The price of debt Interest is a fixed obligation regardless of performance — and non-payment can force lenders to{ } liquidate the company. Debt raises financial risk and vulnerability. Debt-to-equity Total Debt ÷ Shareholders' Equity A ratio of 0.5:1 means lenders have contributed 50 paise for every rupee of owner equity . Higher = greater risk for lenders and for the firm itself. Interest coverage EBIT ÷ Interest Expense A coverage of 4× means profit can fall 75% and interest is still paid. Higher is safer — it measures the cushion before a missed payment. {[ { t: , f: , d: , icon: TrendingUp }, { t: , f: , d: , icon: Banknote }, { t: , f: , d: , icon: Coins }, { t: , f: , d: , icon: LineChart }, { t: , f: , d: , icon: Landmark }, { t: , f: , d: , icon: Activity }, ].map((r, i) => { const Icon = r.icon; return ( {r.t} {r.f} {r.d} ); })} Risk-averse Choose higher PE and lower beta — market confidence plus lower volatility. Pay up for predictability. Risk-tolerant A lower PE may be an underpriced opportunity, and higher beta promises greater potential returns — with the increased risk that comes first. <Takeaways items={[ Debt is cheaper but riskier — interest is tax-deductible, but it is a fixed obligation that can force liquidation. , Debt-to-equity 0.5:1 = 50 paise of lender money per rupee of owner equity. , Interest coverage 4× = profit can fall 75% before a missed payment. , PE 15 (₹300/₹20) = market optimism; earnings yield is its reciprocal; PB > 1 = above-required returns expected. , Stock return = dividend + price change over the opening price — 100 / 5 / 110 = 15%. , Dr. Reddy's 2016: liquidity worse , solvency better , valuations softer — read all three lenses. , ]} />

chapters.label: Inventory & AS 2
chapters.text: Lecture 32 · Inventory & AS 2. FIFO vs weighted average · $4,140 vs $3,057. Goods Available for Sale = Opening Inventory + Purchases Goods Available for Sale = COGS + Closing Inventory COGS = Opening + Purchases − Closing Gross Margin = Revenue − COGS ∴ Higher closing inventory ⇒ lower COGS ⇒ higher margin. The valuation method is a margin decision — every time. inventory-valuation mx-auto max-w-5xl px-4 py-20 sm:px-6 md:py-28 inventory-valuation XYZ Limited sells GPS tracking systems. Identical operations, identical revenue, identical units sold — yet FIFO lands a gross margin of $4,140 and weighted average $3,057. The choice of inventory valuation method is a profit decision, which is exactly why AS 2 regulates it. 01 What counts as inventory — AS 2's scope Assets held in three distinct forms grid gap-3 md:grid-cols-3 Goods held for sale Assets acquired by traders and retailers for resale to customers. Work in progress Assets currently undergoing production or processing. Raw materials Assets consumed during the production process. card-warm h-full p-5 h-5 w-5 mt-2 text-[.92rem] font-extrabold text-[#3e2c1d] mt-1 text-[.8rem] leading-relaxed text-muted-warm 02 The measurement rule Lower of cost and net realizable value — conservatism at work grid gap-3 md:grid-cols-2 flex h-full items-start gap-3 rounded-2xl border border-[#a9dcc4] bg-[#f2faf6] p-5 mt-0.5 h-5 w-5 shrink-0 text-[.95rem] font-extrabold mt-2 space-y-1 flex items-start gap-2 text-[.8rem] leading-snug text-[#1d4433] mt-0.5 h-3.5 w-3.5 shrink-0 flex items-start gap-2 text-[.8rem] leading-snug text-[#1d4433] mt-0.5 h-3.5 w-3.5 shrink-0 #b3402c flex h-full items-start gap-3 rounded-2xl border border-[#e3c98f] bg-[#fbf4e4] p-5 mt-0.5 h-5 w-5 shrink-0 #8a5a10 text-[.95rem] font-extrabold text-[#8a5a10] mt-2 text-[.8rem] leading-relaxed text-[#5c4a22] mt-2 text-[.78rem] leading-snug text-[#5c4a22] · 03 The inventory flow Closing inventory decides COGS — and COGS decides margin Opening inventory brought forward + Purchases goods available for sale − Closing inventory the valuation decision = COGS then margin = revenue − COGS mt-3 The flow, as formulas 04 FIFO vs weighted average — live The Clear View comparison; flip the price trend 05 LIFO is prohibited Discussed in textbooks — banned by the standard warn Accounting Standard 2 explicitly prohibits LIFO 06 The three NRV rules How the lower-of-cost-and-NRV test is actually applied grid gap-3 md:grid-cols-3 01 Item by item Each inventory item is assessed independently — never written up or down in blocks. 02 Raw-material exception Raw materials are NOT written down if the finished goods made from them are expected to sell at or above cost. 03 Annual reassessment NRV is evaluated at the end of each reporting period — last year's estimate doesn't carry forward. h-full rounded-2xl border border-[#e0ece6] bg-[#fffdf9] p-4 font-mono text-[.6rem] font-black uppercase tracking-[.2em] mt-1 text-[.9rem] font-extrabold text-[#3e2c1d] mt-1 text-[.78rem] leading-snug text-muted-warm mt-10 grid gap-4 md:grid-cols-2 Lecture 32 · check yourself Clear View values closing inventory under FIFO vs weighted average. The gross margin difference is… $0 — the method cannot change the margin $1,083 — $4,140 under FIFO vs $3,057 under weighted average $27.62 — the average unit cost $7,872 — the weighted-average closing inventory FIFO: COGS $7,200 → margin $4,140. Weighted average: unit cost $27.62, closing 285 × 27.62 = $7,872, COGS $8,283 → margin $3,057. Same business, same units — $1,083 of margin turns on the method. Lecture 32 · check yourself Under AS 2, which method may a company use to value inventory? FIFO, weighted average, or LIFO — management's choice Only FIFO and weighted average; LIFO is explicitly prohibited Only LIFO during inflation Whichever produces the higher profit AS 2 permits exactly two methods — FIFO and weighted average. LIFO is named in the standard only to be prohibited. 'Whichever produces the higher profit' is not a method; it's the conservatism violation the standard exists to prevent. mt-10 <SectionHead eyebrow={eyebrowOf( )} title={ Same business, same units — different profit . } lead= /> {[ { icon: PackageSearch, t: , d: }, { icon: Factory, t: , d: }, { icon: Boxes, t: , d: }, ].map((c, i) => { const Icon = c.icon; return ( {c.t} {c.d} ); })} Cost — what went into getting it here {COST_IN.map((c) => ( {c} ))} Minus trade discounts and rebates Net realizable value — what it will fetch The estimated selling price minus all indirect selling and administrative expenses still to come. And the conservative principle underneath: anticipate no profit, but provide for all possible losses — profits are never overestimated. Never in cost: {COST_OUT.join( )}. { } LIFO (Last In, First Out) appears in textbooks and even in other jurisdictions' practice — but AS 2{ } does not permit it for inventory valuation. Only FIFO and weighted average are allowed. An exam answer valuing inventory under LIFO is wrong before the arithmetic even starts. {[ { n: , t: , d: }, { n: , t: , d: }, { n: , t: , d: }, ].map((r, i) => ( Rule {r.n} {r.t} {r.d} ))} <Takeaways items={[ Inventory = goods for sale · WIP · raw materials — measured at the lower of cost and NRV . , Cost includes purchase price (net of recoverable taxes), freight inward, direct labour, conversion & production overheads — less discounts; excludes storage, selling, admin, commissions. , COGS = Opening + Purchases − Closing ; higher closing ⇒ lower COGS ⇒ higher margin. , Only FIFO and weighted average are permitted; LIFO is prohibited under AS 2. , Clear View: FIFO $4,140 vs weighted average $3,057 — $1,083 of margin from the method alone. , NRV rules: item-by-item , the raw-material exception , and annual reassessment . , ]} />

chapters.label: PPE & depreciation
chapters.text: Lecture 33 · PPE & depreciation. The ₹57,000 build-up · straight line vs diminishing. Purchase price ₹54,000 Shipping / delivery ₹1,500 Setup / installation ₹2,500 ────────────────────────────────── Total cost ₹57,000 (In a fuller case the estimated cost of dismantling the asset at end of life joins the build-up too.) ppe-depreciation mx-auto max-w-5xl px-4 py-20 sm:px-6 md:py-28 ppe-depreciation Property, plant & equipment is not expensed on purchase day — its cost is allocated systematically across the years it serves. Depreciation is that allocation: the depreciable amount spread over useful life, by straight line or diminishing balance. 01 What qualifies as PPE Four conditions, per AS 10 grid gap-3 md:grid-cols-4 Held for the right purpose Production or supply of goods/services, rental or leasing to others, or administrative/office work. More than 12 months The asset must be expected to serve beyond one year. Identifiable benefits The future economic benefits the asset will provide can be identified. Measurable cost The cost must be objectively measurable — and the item is classified per AS 10. h-full rounded-2xl border border-[#e0ece6] bg-[#fffdf9] p-4 h-5 w-5 mt-2 text-[.86rem] font-extrabold leading-snug text-[#3e2c1d] mt-1 text-[.74rem] leading-snug text-muted-warm 02 Capital vs revenue expenditure One-line test: last longer, work better, do more? grid gap-3 md:grid-cols-2 flex h-full items-start gap-3 rounded-2xl border border-[#a9dcc4] bg-[#f2faf6] p-5 mt-0.5 h-5 w-5 shrink-0 text-[.95rem] font-extrabold mt-2 text-[.82rem] leading-relaxed text-[#1d4433] flex h-full items-start gap-3 rounded-2xl border border-[#e8a896] bg-[#fbeae5] p-5 mt-0.5 h-5 w-5 shrink-0 #b3402c text-[.95rem] font-extrabold text-[#b3402c] mt-2 text-[.82rem] leading-relaxed text-[#7c2d12] mt-3 insight The one-line test 03 Building the cost Everything needed to get the asset ready to work The printing press — cost build-up 04 The four terms Learn these four and every depreciation question opens grid gap-3 md:grid-cols-4 Depreciable amount Cost − residual value: 57,000 − 10,000 = ₹47,000. The pool to be allocated. Residual value The expected disposal price at the end — ₹10,000 after five years. Useful life The period the company expects to use the asset — 5 years. Carrying amount Cost − accumulated depreciation: the net book value on the balance sheet at any point. h-full rounded-2xl border border-[#e0ece6] bg-[#fffdf9] p-4 font-mono text-[.6rem] font-black uppercase tracking-[.2em] mt-1 text-[.88rem] font-extrabold leading-snug text-[#3e2c1d] mt-1 text-[.74rem] leading-snug text-muted-warm mt-3 why The definition to quote 05 The race — straight line vs diminishing balance Flip between the methods and watch the timing move 06 Disposal — selling before the end Selling price vs carrying amount decides gain or loss grid gap-3 md:grid-cols-2 rounded-2xl border p-5 #f2faf6 text-[.7rem] font-black uppercase tracking-[.14em] mt-2 text-[.85rem] leading-relaxed text-[#1d4433] rounded-2xl border border-[#e8a896] bg-[#fbeae5] p-5 text-[.7rem] font-black uppercase tracking-[.14em] text-[#b3402c] mt-2 text-[.85rem] leading-relaxed text-[#7c2d12] mt-10 grid gap-4 md:grid-cols-2 Lecture 33 · check yourself A printing press costs ₹57,000 with a ₹10,000 residual and a 5-year life. Straight-line depreciation per year is… ₹11,400 — ₹57,000 ÷ 5 ₹9,400 — (₹57,000 − ₹10,000) ÷ 5 ₹47,000 — the whole depreciable amount in year 1 ₹10,000 — the residual value Straight line spreads the DEPRECIABLE amount, not the cost: (57,000 − 10,000) ÷ 5 = ₹9,400/year. Forgetting the residual (option A) is the classic error — the asset must still be worth ₹10,000 at the end. Lecture 33 · check yourself At 40% diminishing balance, year-2 depreciation on the ₹57,000 press is… ₹22,800 — same as year 1 ₹13,680 — 40% of the ₹34,200 opening carrying amount ₹9,400 — methods must match after year 1 ₹4,925 — 40% of ₹12,312 Year 1: 40% × 57,000 = 22,800 → carrying 34,200. Year 2: 40% × 34,200 = 13,680. Each year's charge is 40% of the OPENING carrying amount — the charge shrinks as the book value falls. mt-10 <SectionHead eyebrow={eyebrowOf( )} title={ The asset pays its bill every year . } lead= /> {[ { t: , d: }, { t: , d: }, { t: , d: }, { t: , d: }, ].map((c, i) => ( {c.t} {c.d} ))} Capital — becomes an asset New machinery; upgrades that extend existing life; major improvements that enhance { } functionality — adding a supercharger to a vehicle. These capitalize onto the balance sheet. Revenue — goes to the P&L Routine maintenance and repairs — the six-monthly machine servicing ; ordinary repairs that neither extend life nor improve quality; costs that merely keep machinery running. Does the spending make the asset last longer, work better, or do more ? Then it is capital expenditure. Does it merely maintain current functionality? Revenue expenditure. That single sentence sorts nearly every case the exam will pose. { } {[ { t: , d: }, { t: , d: }, { t: , d: }, { t: , d: }, ].map((c, i) => ( 0{i + 1} {c.t} {c.d} ))} Depreciation is the systematic allocation of the depreciable amount over the useful life of the asset. Not a valuation of the machine — an allocation of its cost. Gain on disposal Carrying amount ₹29,200 , sold for ₹31,000 → selling price exceeds carrying amount →{ } +₹1,800 gain . Loss on disposal The same press sold for ₹27,100 → below the ₹29,200 carrying amount →{ } −₹2,100 loss . <Takeaways items={[ PPE: production/supply, rental, or admin use; >12 months ; identifiable benefits; measurable cost (AS 10). , Capital = last longer / work better / do more ; revenue = merely maintains (supercharger vs servicing). , Cost build-up: 54,000 + 1,500 + 2,500 = ₹57,000 ; depreciable amount 57,000 − 10,000 = ₹47,000 . , Straight line ₹9,400/yr (47,600 → 38,200 → 28,800 → 19,400 → 10,000); diminishing 40%: 22,800 / 13,680 / 8,208 , capped at the residual. , Total lifetime depreciation is identical under both methods — only the timing differs. , Disposal: 29,200 → 31,000 = +₹1,800 gain ; → 27,100 = −₹2,100 loss . , ]} />

chapters.label: Intangibles
chapters.text: Lecture 33 · Intangibles. AS 26 · the 10-year presumption · the ₹8,000/yr patent. Patent cost ₹48,000 Legal life 12 years Expected useful life 6 years ← the SHORTER one governs Annual amortization ₹48,000 ÷ 6 = ₹8,000 per year (An uncapped life of 12 years would also collide with the 10-year presumption — it would need documented justification, and it would still lose to the shorter expected life of 6 years.) intangible-amortization mx-auto max-w-5xl px-4 py-20 sm:px-6 md:py-28 intangible-amortization Patents, copyrights, trademarks and goodwill are non-physical assets — and their cost is amortized under AS 26 with the same formula depreciation uses. The rules just get sharper about time. 01 The three rules of AS 26 Allocation, presumption, and the shorter life grid gap-3 md:grid-cols-3 01 Systematic allocation Allocate the depreciable amount over the best estimate of useful life — starting when the asset is AVAILABLE FOR USE, not when payment is made. 02 The 10-year presumption Useful life is presumed NOT to exceed 10 years — rebuttable only with a documented justification for longer use. 03 Shorter of two lives Always amortize over the shorter of the LEGAL life (set by law) and the ECONOMIC life (how long the firm will actually benefit). h-full rounded-2xl border border-[#e0ece6] bg-[#fffdf9] p-5 h-5 w-5 mt-2 block font-mono text-[.6rem] font-black uppercase tracking-[.2em] mt-1 text-[.92rem] font-extrabold text-[#3e2c1d] mt-1 text-[.78rem] leading-relaxed text-muted-warm 02 The patent, worked ₹48,000 · legal 12 years · expected 6 years Amortization — the same formula depreciation uses 03 Why the timing rule matters Available for use — not paid for grid gap-3 md:grid-cols-2 card-warm h-full p-5 font-extrabold text-[#3e2c1d] mt-2 text-[.84rem] leading-relaxed text-[#2b2014] card-warm h-full p-5 font-extrabold text-[#3e2c1d] mt-2 text-[.84rem] leading-relaxed text-[#2b2014] mt-10 grid gap-4 md:grid-cols-2 Lecture 33 · check yourself A patent cost ₹48,000; its legal life is 12 years but the firm expects to benefit for 6. Annual amortization is… ₹4,000 — ₹48,000 ÷ 12 legal years ₹8,000 — the shorter expected life governs ₹10,000 — the maximum AS 26 allows per year ₹6,000 — averaging the two lives AS 26: amortize over the SHORTER of legal and economic life — 6 years here — giving 48,000 ÷ 6 = ₹8,000/yr. The 12-year legal life never gets a vote when the economic benefit ends sooner. Lecture 33 · check yourself Under AS 26, when does amortization of an intangible begin? When the supplier is paid When the asset is available for use At the financial year-end When the asset is sold Systematic allocation starts from when the asset is available for use — not the payment date. The 10-year presumption is the second rule; the shorter-of-two-lives rule is the third. mt-10 <SectionHead eyebrow={eyebrowOf( )} title={ No physical form, same discipline . } lead= /> {[ { n: , t: , d: , icon: CalendarClock, }, { n: , t: , d: , icon: FileWarning, }, { n: , t: , d: , icon: Scale, }, ].map((r, i) => { const Icon = r.icon; return ( Rule {r.n} {r.t} {r.d} ); })} { } Amortization ≠ depreciation of goods Amortization is simply depreciation for intangibles : (cost − residual value) ÷ useful life, under AS 26. What changes is the evidence around the life estimate — the law may grant 12 years of patent protection, but if the technology will be obsolete in 6, 6 years is the honest number . Start the clock at availability Allocation begins when the asset is available for use — not at the payment date. A licence bought in March but usable from January amortizes from January; payment timing is a cash-flow fact, not a benefit fact. <Takeaways items={[ Intangibles: patents, copyrights, trademarks, goodwill — no physical form , real economic benefits. , Amortization = AS 26's depreciation : (cost − residual) ÷ useful life. , Rule 1: allocate from available for use , not payment date. , Rule 2: the 10-year rebuttable presumption — longer needs documented justification. , Rule 3: shorter of legal and economic life — the ₹48,000 patent over 6 years = ₹8,000/yr . , ]} />

chapters.label: Techniques
chapters.text: Lecture 34 · Techniques. Horizontal · trend · vertical · ratio · four standards. Base year: sales 100 → indexed 100 Year 4: sales 1,400 → 1,400 ÷ 1,000 × 100 = 140 (+40%) Year 4: profit 150 → 150 ÷ 100 × 100 = 150 (+50%) Profit is growing FASTER than sales — margin is expanding. A single-year view never shows that; multi-year trends reveal whether management is controlling costs and improving efficiency. analysis-techniques mx-auto max-w-5xl px-4 py-20 sm:px-6 md:py-28 analysis-techniques ₹100 crores of profit means nothing on its own — it becomes information only against a base: the rule of thumb, the company's own past, management's internal targets, or the industry's peers. Then four techniques turn comparison into computation. 01 Four standards of comparison — and how each fails Lecture 28 introduced them; Lecture 34 shows the failure modes grid gap-3 md:grid-cols-2 Rule of thumb The 2:1 current ratio is 'healthy'. Simple and useful across firms — but blind to quality: it ignores inventory turnover and receivables aging, so a 2.2:1 firm with dead stock can look better than a 1.6:1 firm that turns stock fast. Past performance Trend projection against history. Kodak: peak sales $16bn (1996), $2.5bn profit (1999) — and bankruptcy in 2012. Regulation, technology and policy changes (depreciation, inventory valuation) break comparability, and one-time gains distort. Growing while the industry grows faster is the illusion of growth. Internal standards Management's own benchmarks: target ROA/ROI, sales growth, market share, budgets for profit centres, predetermined product costs. The operational-control lens — designed for monitoring, not for outsiders. Industry standards A 7% gross margin looks weak — until the industry's 12% turns out to include firms with different mixes: HUL spans soaps, detergents, toothpaste and food, so P&G, ITC and Colgate overlap only partially. And policies differ — FIFO vs weighted average, different asset-life estimates — even within one industry. card-warm h-full p-5 flex items-center gap-2 h-4.5 w-4.5 h-[18px] w-[18px] text-[.95rem] font-extrabold text-[#3e2c1d] mt-2 text-[.82rem] leading-relaxed text-muted-warm 02 Technique 1 — horizontal (CY − PY) ÷ PY × 100 — with Dr. Reddy's, worked 03 Technique 2 — trend Base year = 100; index everything after it Trend analysis — the lecture's own numbers 04 Technique 3 — vertical (common-size) Every line as a % of revenue — or of total assets grid gap-3 md:grid-cols-2 card-warm h-full p-5 font-extrabold text-[#3e2c1d] mt-2 text-[.84rem] leading-relaxed text-[#2b2014] card-warm h-full p-5 font-extrabold text-[#3e2c1d] mt-2 text-[.84rem] leading-relaxed text-[#2b2014] 05 Technique 4 — ratio The relationship itself — and the base decides the verdict overflow-hidden rounded-2xl border border-[#c7e5d6] bg-[#fffdf9] flex flex-wrap items-center gap-2 border-b border-[#e4f1ea] bg-[#f4faf7] px-4 py-3 h-4 w-4 font-mono text-[.64rem] font-black uppercase tracking-[.2em] grid gap-px bg-[#e4f1ea] sm:grid-cols-2 bg-white p-4 text-center text-[.66rem] font-black uppercase tracking-[.16em] text-[#8a6b45] mt-1 font-mono text-[1.15rem] font-black mt-1 text-[.72rem] text-muted-warm bg-white p-4 text-center text-[.66rem] font-black uppercase tracking-[.16em] text-[#8a6b45] mt-1 font-mono text-[1.15rem] font-black #b3402c mt-1 text-[.72rem] text-muted-warm border-t border-[#e4f1ea] bg-white px-4 py-3 text-[.82rem] leading-relaxed text-[#2b2014] mt-10 grid gap-4 md:grid-cols-2 Lecture 34 · check yourself Trend analysis: sales rise from a 1,000 base to 1,400 while profit rises from a 100 base to 150. What does this reveal? Sales are growing faster than profit — worry Profit is growing faster than sales — margin expansion Nothing — the bases differ so the indices cannot compare Both grew exactly 40% Sales index 140 (+40%), profit index 150 (+50%). Profit outpacing sales means costs are being controlled and margins are widening — the trend, not any single year, carries the insight. Lecture 34 · check yourself Dr. Reddy's: revenue +4.49%, expenses +3.49%, PBT −7.74%. The single reconciling item is… A change in the depreciation method A $461 million exceptional forex loss in the Venezuela operations A collapse in unit sales A tax-rate hike Operations were strong — revenue outgrew expenses. The PBT fall is the exceptional, non-recurring $461m forex loss. Horizontal analysis exists to expose exactly this kind of divergence. mt-10 <SectionHead eyebrow={eyebrowOf( )} title={ A single number is neither good nor bad . } lead= /> {[ { t: , d: , icon: Target, }, { t: , d: , icon: TrendingUp, }, { t: , d: , icon: Briefcase, }, { t: , d: , icon: Factory, }, ].map((s, i) => { const Icon = s.icon; return ( {s.t} {s.d} ); })} { } The mechanics Income statement: every line ÷ total revenue . Balance sheet: every line ÷ total assets . Formula: (line item ÷ base figure) × 100. What 13.47% means If profit is 13.47% of revenue, then ₹13.47 of every ₹100 of sales becomes profit — and a two-person firm can stand next to a billion-rupee corporation on the same page. That is why it is called common-size . Identical ₹10 lakh profits — two companies Company A · ₹50 lakh sales 20% margin ₹20 kept per ₹100 of sales Company B · ₹200 lakh sales 5% margin ₹5 kept per ₹100 of sales Same ₹10 lakh — Company A is significantly more profitable per rupee of sales . The ratio, not the absolute number, carries the judgment. <Takeaways items={[ A single number is neither good nor bad — meaning arrives only through comparison. , Four standards: rule of thumb, past performance (Kodak's trap), internal, industry — each with a known failure mode. , Horizontal: (CY − PY) ÷ PY × 100 — Reddy's +4.49% revenue vs −7.74% PBT on a $461m forex loss. , Trend: base year = 100 — sales 140 vs profit 150 index = margin expansion. , Vertical/common-size: every line as % of revenue or total assets — 13.47% = ₹13.47 per ₹100. , Ratio: the same ₹10 lakh is 20% of ₹50 lakh sales but 5% of ₹200 lakh. , ]} />

chapters.label: DuPont & exam
chapters.text: Lecture 34 · DuPont & exam. Margin × turnover · the exam brief · homework. 2015: 15.00% margin × 0.87 turnover = 13.05% ROA 2016: 13.71% margin × 0.81 turnover = 11.11% ROA Margin fell — the foreign-exchange losses Turnover fell — assets grew faster than revenue Performance deteriorated on BOTH fronts: operational and asset-utilization. A single ROA number would have hidden which lever moved; the decomposition names both. dupont-exam mx-auto max-w-5xl px-4 py-20 sm:px-6 md:py-28 dupont-exam DuPont breaks ROA into its two drivers — margin and turnover — so 'profitability fell' becomes 'margin fell AND assets slowed'. Then the final lecture hands over the exam brief: numericals emphasised, simple calculator only, concise answers. 01 The DuPont decomposition Two presets land on 20%; two land on Dr. Reddy's decline 02 Dr. Reddy's decomposition, 2015 → 2016 Both drivers deteriorated — that is the finding The DuPont walk, verbatim figures 03 Nalesh and the banker A ₹25-lakh FMCG loan, answered in statements Nalesh asks ₹25 lakh for his FMCG distribution The bank responds common-size · comparative · trend Plus three lenses liquidity · profitability · solvency The decision will profit continue? can debt be serviced? mt-3 story What the banker actually reads 04 The exam brief Read this twice before you prepare mt-10 grid gap-4 md:grid-cols-2 Lecture 34 · check yourself DuPont 2016: margin 13.71% × turnover 0.81 = ? 13.05% — that was 2015 11.11% — and both drivers fell from 2015 13.49% — the reported ROA 0.87 — the 2015 turnover 13.71% × 0.81 = 11.11%. The margin fell (forex losses) and turnover fell (assets grew faster than revenue) — deterioration on both fronts, which is exactly what DuPont is built to expose. Any calculator you own A financial calculator — it handles annuities A scientific calculator — it handles logs A SIMPLE calculator only — scientific and financial calculators are barred The exam brief is explicit: simple calculator only — no scientific or financial calculators — and concise answers, because lengthy responses indicate lack of clarity. mt-10 <SectionHead eyebrow={eyebrowOf( )} title={ Decompose the return — then sit the exam . } lead= /> { } Statements alone are raw data; analysis turns them into evidence. The banker reads trends — common-size, comparative and trend statements — to judge whether the profit pattern will continue and whether the borrower can service the debt . The stove and strainer do work (functions); the ingredients themselves are the data. Lecture 1 · working definitions An algorithm is… Any programming language Organised steps that convert data into the desired output A chart of the company A type of flowchart By definition: organised steps that convert data into the desired output. Languages and flowcharts are only ways to write the algorithm down. Lecture 1 · definition mt-6 Pen-paper drill Define data, variable, algorithm and function in one line each — no peeking at the cards above. Data is the what; variables are the where; the algorithm is the how; functions are the reusable inside. Write the tea algorithm as 6 numbered steps, then label each step INPUT, OUTPUT or PROCESS. Adding water/milk/tea/sugar are inputs; straining and serving are outputs; boiling and simmering are processing. List the 4 working definitions from memory. Repeat tomorrow until all four come out in order. D-V-A-F: Data, Variables, Algorithm, Function. mt-6 grid justify-items-start gap-3 chip h-3.5 w-3.5 <SectionHead eyebrow={eyebrowOf( )} title={ An algorithm is just a recipe a machine can follow } lead= /> } Ingredients {[ , , , ].map((i) => ( {i} ))} } Equipment Gas / induction stove · strainer do actual work on the data Saucepan · teacups hold the data while steps run } Steps {[ , , , , , , ].map((s, i) => ( {i + 1} {s} ))} Try the recipe with the milk poured first, or the sugar skipped entirely — the{ } sequence flexes with preference , but the outcome stays the same: a cup of tea. That is the quiet surprise of Lecture 1 — an algorithm is not a sacred order, it is organised steps that work toward an output . Which is exactly why they turn up everywhere: in the kitchen, at the ATM, inside every app you opened today. A payroll run, a loan approval, an inventory reorder — each one is an algorithm. Data goes in (hours worked, credit score, stock level), organised steps run in between, and a decision comes out. Once you see the shape{ } business process = data + algorithm , you can redesign any of them.
