Rounded rectangle Diamond Trapezoid Arrow The rounded rectangle is the START / END terminal — the lecture’s fifth symbol. Diamonds decide, trapezoids move data in and out, arrows carry the flow. Lecture 1 · symbol kit Which symbol would you use for 'INPUT the length and width'? Rectangle Diamond Parallelogram Oval Input and output steps use the parallelogram — the lecture’s trapezoid, the slanted rectangle. The rectangle is for processing, the diamond for decisions, the rounded rectangle for start/end. Lecture 1 · symbol kit mt-4 Flowchart drills Draw the tea flowchart from memory — all 10 nodes, correct symbols. Parallelograms: add water, add leaves, add milk & sugar, serve. Rectangles: boil, boil 1 min, simmer, strain. Mark each step as I/O or processing. Which single step becomes a decision if the taster is picky? Simmer — split it into “Sufficiently brewed?” with a loop back. A colleague documents a refund process using only rectangles. Which maturity stage is that, and what would you add first? Simple — processing only. Add trapezoids to separate the input (refund request) from the output (money returned), then a diamond for the approval check. <SectionHead eyebrow={eyebrowOf( )} title={ Drawing algorithms — the five symbols } lead= /> {[ { cx: 80, name: , use: , d: , fill: , tf: , inner: }, { cx: 240, name: , use: , d: pRect(240, 82, 124, 56), fill: , tf: , inner: }, { cx: 400, name: , use: , d: pPara(400, 82, 138, 56, 20), fill: , tf: , inner: }, { cx: 566, name: , use: , d: pDiamond(566, 110, 148, 84), fill: , tf: , inner: }, ].map((s, i) => ( {s.inner} {s.name} {s.use} ))} Arrows FLOW Lecture 1 · symbol kit One naming note: this course draws the trapezoid as a parallelogram — same slanted shape, same input/output job. Different textbooks pick different names; the meanings above are the lecture’s. And one law the kit hides in plain sight: arrows never branch by themselves — only a diamond may split the flow. A drawing that forks without a diamond is not a flowchart; it is a wish. Read it back symbol by symbol and the grammar explains itself. START { } and END sit in rounded rectangles — the only two of their kind. Every add step (water, leaves, milk & sugar) and the final serve move data into or out of the pot, so they get the trapezoid . Every{ } boil , simmer and strain transforms what is already inside, so they stay rectangles . Ten nodes, nine arrows, zero branches — the arrows simply carry the flow downward, one direction, no arguments. Input, processing and output each live in their own symbol: that is what makes this a refined { } flowchart. Lecture 1 · decision loop The rose edge loops back — “No, keep simmering” — until the tea is sufficiently brewed. The flow revisits its own steps: the mark of a complex flowchart. A diamond asks a yes/no question. Yes and No each open a branch — and a branch that loops backwards gives you a{ } loop : repeat until the answer flips. Branching + looping is the entire control vocabulary of every business rule ever written. Trace it Under-brewed pot: the flow passes the diamond — is the tea sufficiently brewed? — three times before Strain; the loop edge (rose) fired twice. The ATM machine — branching in action. atm atm grad-text One real machine, two decisions, three possible endings — a successful withdrawal and two polite refusals. Trace it once and every approval workflow you will ever meet — loans, refunds, KYC — becomes obvious. 1 The numbered algorithm Eight steps; steps 6 and 7 each hide a two-way branch. max-w-3xl text-[.95rem] leading-relaxed text-[#cbb392] grid gap-4 sm:grid-cols-2 card-warm flex h-full gap-3 p-4 flex h-8 w-8 shrink-0 items-center justify-center rounded-full bg-gradient-to-br from-[#f59e0b] to-[#c2410c] text-[.8rem] font-extrabold text-white font-bold text-[#f5e6cd] mt-1 text-[.84rem] leading-relaxed text-[#cbb392] mt-2 flex flex-wrap gap-2 rounded-full px-2.5 py-1 text-[.72rem] font-bold olive rgba(124,154,62,.18) #c4d9a0 1px solid rgba(124,154,62,.4) rgba(190,74,74,.18) #eba3a3 1px solid rgba(190,74,74,.4) 2 The same algorithm as a flowchart Yes edges in olive, No edges in rose — and watch both No edges join. card-warm p-5 md:p-7 mt-3 text-center text-[.78rem] text-[#cbb392] mt-5 why Branches + joins = every business process 3 Two observations the lecture insists on They read like footnotes; they are the whole point of the example. grid gap-4 md:grid-cols-2 card-warm h-full p-5 chip h-3.5 w-3.5 mt-3 font-extrabold leading-snug text-[#f5e6cd] mt-2 text-[.86rem] leading-relaxed text-[#cbb392] card-warm h-full p-5 chip h-3.5 w-3.5 mt-3 font-extrabold leading-snug text-[#f5e6cd] mt-2 text-[.86rem] leading-relaxed text-[#cbb392] font-mono text-[.78rem] mt-5 insight The vocabulary, all on duty mt-6 grid gap-4 md:grid-cols-2 In the ATM flowchart, the two No branches both lead to… Request PIN again Release cash End Input amount Both failure checks route to the same END oval — the rose lane is a join. Real ATMs add retries around this skeleton, but the lecture version ends on any failure. Lecture 1 · ATM example During one customer’s run, how many branches of each decision actually execute? Both — every branch runs once Exactly one — the outcome picks the path None — decisions are skipped It alternates between customers A decision resolves to one outcome per run: the flow takes that branch and never visits the other. The chart shows possibilities; an execution shows one path. Lecture 1 · ATM example mt-4 Branch drills Trace what happens when the PIN is wrong: list every node the flow visits, in order. Start → Check card → Request PIN → Input PIN → Pin OK? → NO lane → End. Five nodes, never reaching amount. Write the 6a/6b branch pattern for a UPI payment (balance check + limit check). 6a: within limit → check balance; 6b: over limit → decline. Mirror the ATM diamonds. “Release cash” is a function. Write 4 steps its own algorithm must contain. Count the notes → verify denominations → update the ledger → confirm pickup and close the session. <SectionHead dark eyebrow={eyebrowOf( )} title={ The ATM machine — branching in action } lead= /> The ATM is Lecture 1’s business application: cash dispensing, stripped to its skeleton. Notice the rhythm before you read a single step — input, input, decision, input, decision, function, end . Machines that handle money are mostly polite questions with hard stops: fail any check and the session ends immediately, no exceptions, no negotiation. Keep this skeleton — you will redraw it for loan approvals, KYC gates and refund flows for the rest of the course. {ATM_STEPS.map((s, i) => ( {s.n} {s.t} {s.d ? {s.d} : null} {s.branches ? ( {s.branches.map((b) => ( {b.tag} · {b.text} ))} ) : null} ))} Both rose lanes join at END — a failure anywhere still reaches a clean ending. That shared exit is what makes the machine safe to automate. A loan application: check credit score (branch), verify income (branch), then{ } join into one approval decision. A refund request, a KYC check, an insurance claim — same skeleton: inputs, checks, branches, a join, one end. If you can draw the ATM, you can draw your company. Lecture 1 · one run, one path Not all paths execute in a single run The flowchart shows every route the machine could take — but a decision is a fork, and each run picks exactly one branch. The lucky customer never visits either rose No-lane; the unlucky one never sees “release cash”. Every branch is always{ } possible ; on any given run, most are never executed . Lecture 1 · a function inside “Release cash” is a function of its own One plain box hides a private algorithm: count the notes, verify denominations, update the ledger, confirm pickup. Complex operations get boxed away as{ } functions — subgroups of organised steps, identical wherever they appear — so the main flow stays readable. You will meet the same idea as{ } AVERAGE two chapters from now. Run the labels back through the machine: reading the card, requesting the PIN and the amount are inputs — trapezoids. Verifying the PIN and checking the balance are decisions — diamonds. Dispensing the notes is a{ } function — a pre-defined process with an algorithm of its own. One everyday machine; every Lecture 1 term working at once.

chapters.label: Average, step-by-step
chapters.text: Lecture 02 · Average, step-by-step. Memory boxes, data types & FIRST CLASS. average average grad-text Five marks, one average. The school answer is a number; the algorithmic answer is a machine-followable process — and the difference is exactly what this course is about. 1 The school way Arithmetic gets the answer — but it forgets the method. card-warm p-6 text-center font-mono text-lg font-bold text-[#3e2c1d] md:text-2xl grad-text mt-5 Add the marks 60 + 65 + 70 + 55 + 60 = 310 h-5 w-5 #c2410c Divide by the number of subjects 310 ÷ 5 = 62 h-5 w-5 #7c9a3e 2 The algorithmic way — memory boxes Step through the pseudocode and watch each variable appear, receive data and compute. 3 Data types matter Every variable is declared with a pre-determined datatype. card-warm overflow-x-auto p-1.5 warm-table inline-flex items-center gap-2 font-bold text-[#a0410a] h-4 w-4 text-[#5d4a35] mt-3 text-[.85rem] leading-relaxed text-muted-warm 4 Level up: FIRST CLASS One IF statement turns the average into a decision. grid items-start gap-5 lg:grid-cols-2 first_class.pseudo 62.0 AVG is a FLOAT, so the machine prints 62.0 — and because 62.0 IS MORE THAN 60, the IF fires. card-warm flex h-full flex-col justify-center gap-5 p-5 flex flex-wrap justify-center gap-x-3 gap-y-4 SUM 310 AVG 62.0 flex flex-col items-center justify-end gap-1.5 font-mono text-[.62rem] font-bold uppercase tracking-widest text-[#8a6b45] anim-pop inline-flex items-center gap-2 rounded-xl px-4 py-2.5 font-mono text-[.85rem] font-extrabold #eef4dd #44621d 1px solid #cfe0ae h-4 w-4 text-center text-[.8rem] leading-relaxed text-muted-warm mt-6 grid gap-4 md:grid-cols-2 CGPA = 8.74. Best primitive type? Integer Float Boolean Character 8.74 has a decimal part — CGPA values are floats (that is exactly why AVG was DEFINE-d AS FLOAT in the lab). Lecture 1 · datatypes AVG is defined as INTEGER but SUM/5 = 62.5. What happens conceptually? It stays 62.5 — nothing changes The decimal part is dropped — it becomes 62 The program always crashes It becomes the text “62.5” An integer box cannot hold a decimal part — conceptually it is truncated to 62. This is why the lecture declares AVG AS FLOAT before dividing. Lecture 1 · datatypes mt-6 <SectionHead eyebrow={eyebrowOf( )} title={ Average marks — arithmetic vs algorithm } lead= /> Average = (60 + 65 + 70 + 55 + 60) / 5 = 310 / 5 = 62 <StepsFlow steps={[ { label: , sub: , icon: }, { label: , sub: , icon: }, ]} /> Type What it holds Business examples {DTYPES.map((t) => ( {t.name} {t.holds} {t.ex} ))} Note: modern languages can infer the type from the first input — assign 8.74 to a fresh variable and it quietly becomes a float. Older languages force you to declare it up front, as our pseudocode does. IF fires FIRST CLASS Same five marks as the lab above — but SUM is reused, AVG is a float, and the output is now a verdict, not just a number. <Takeaways items={[ An algorithm is a series of steps to complete a task — chai, payroll or an ATM withdrawal. , It can be represented as a flowchart (five symbols — four shapes plus the arrows that join them) or as pseudocode . , Algorithms get more complex as details are added — each decision adds a branch. , They are finally implemented in languages like C/C++, Java and Python — but the thinking comes first. , Variables can have pre-determined datatypes (integer, float, boolean, character); modern languages can infer them. , Functions simplify algorithms by carrying out common tasks — shown in flowcharts as pre-defined process boxes. , ]} />

chapters.label: Algorithm vs code
chapters.text: Lecture 03 · Algorithm vs code. Logic vs implementation · machines can't 'look okay'. algvscode algvscode grad-text An algorithm is a set of organized, step-by-step instructions converting input data into desired output. Code is just one language’s implementation of it. The logic is the asset — and it must be precise, because computers cannot assume or infer. 1 “Add water” is four instructions for a machine Intuitive processes become complex when written step-by-step — prerequisites (equipment needed) must be defined before the process itself. text-[.95rem] leading-relaxed text-[#2b2014] the four sub-steps a person infers silently are exactly the four a machine must be told — that gap is the whole discipline. What happens next? — refining one vague step into four real ones The recipe says: ‘Add water’. A human nods; a machine stalls. No quantity, no source, no container, no action order. flex flex-wrap items-center gap-3 instruction ‘Add water’ broken machine can act? no broken Unpack 1: FIND the water — where is it stored? Every implicit prerequisite becomes an explicit step. flex flex-wrap items-center gap-3 step 1 find the water twin instruction ‘Add water’ + 1 Unpack 2–3: LOCATE the container, FILL it. Equipment prerequisites surface: which container? how much? flex flex-wrap items-center gap-3 steps 2–3 locate · fill twin Unpack 4: POUR — now the machine can execute every token. Four measurable actions replaced one subjective phrase. That is algorithm quality improving. flex flex-wrap items-center gap-3 steps 4 explicit twin machine can act? yes twin 2 Algorithm vs code — three distinctions Algorithm = what to do; code = how to implement. Legacy one-off programs vs cloud-reused parameterised solutions. Pseudocode bridges the two. mt-4 grid gap-3 md:grid-cols-3 Algorithm vs language The algorithm is independent of language choice; the same one may be easier or harder to implement in different languages. Quality is language-independent. One-time vs reusable Legacy: custom programs written for individual companies. Modern: cloud-based solutions reuse the same code for multiple organizations — parameterization lets one codebase serve diverse needs. Pseudocode vs code Pseudocode uses English-like language; programming code uses language-specific syntax. Pseudocode is the intermediate step that eases conversion to actual code. card-warm h-full p-4 font-extrabold text-[#3e2c1d] mt-2 text-[.82rem] leading-relaxed text-[#2b2014] mt-6 insight Subjective machines — the design challenge mt-4 warn Misconceptions the live session retired mt-6 grid gap-4 md:grid-cols-2 Why is algorithm quality language-independent? It compiles the same everywhere Quality lives in the logic, not the syntax All languages share keywords Pseudocode is a language The algorithm focuses on what to do; code focuses on how to implement. The same algorithm may be easier or harder in different languages — but its quality is judged on the logic. Lecture 3 · algorithm vs code Modern cloud solutions replace legacy custom programs mainly through… Faster servers Parameterization — one codebase serves many organizations Hiring more developers Rewriting in Python Parameterization enables a single codebase to serve diverse needs — the modern approach reuses the same code across users/organizations instead of one-off custom programs. Lecture 3 · distinctions <SectionHead eyebrow={eyebrowOf( )} title={ Algorithm vs code — and the machine that cannot guess } lead= /> Teaching machines — robots or algorithms — demands precision that everyday language never carries. The tea exercise shows it: defining prerequisites first, then adding details progressively improves algorithm quality. All algorithms are simplifications of real-world processes that grow more exact with every detail added. <AtbStepper title= steps={[ { label: , detail: , frame: ( ), }, { label: , detail: , frame: ( ), }, { label: , detail: , frame: ( ), }, { label: , detail: , frame: ( ), }, ]} /> {[ { t: , d: }, { t: , d: }, { t: , d: }, ].map((c, i) => ( {c.t} {c.d} ))} “Gentle boil” and “looks okay” are fine for people and useless for machines: computers require objective, measurable criteria for decision-making. Human interpretation and subjective judgment remain areas where AI still struggles compared to human intelligence. Computers cannot be trained with new algorithms at first — they operate through pre-existing ones · precise descriptions do not guarantee perfect results if the precision itself is ambiguously defined · algorithms and coding go hand-in-hand but are conceptually distinct · functions are reusable components of algorithms, not replacements for them · Boolean is preferred over integer for true/false — memory efficiency and error prevention · flow diagrams use sequential diamonds for multiple conditions; a single diamond allows only yes/no branching.

chapters.label: Types & the BA bridge
chapters.text: Lecture 03 · Types & the BA bridge. Data types · validation · SRS · real-time calls. babridge babridge grad-text Choosing a data type is a business decision — and when the machine’s checks pass but the value is still wrong, a human judgement (and often a business analyst) has to close the gap. 1 Why data types exist Define what a variable can store · optimize memory usage · prevent errors by restricting invalid inputs. Classical languages require predefined types; modern languages like Python can infer them. card-warm mt-4 overflow-x-auto p-0 w-full text-left text-[.86rem] bg-[#fbf3e3] px-4 py-2.5 font-extrabold text-[#3e2c1d] px-4 py-2.5 font-extrabold text-[#3e2c1d] px-4 py-2.5 font-extrabold text-[#3e2c1d] border-t border-[#f3e2c8] bg-[#fffaf1] px-4 py-2.5 font-bold text-[#3e2c1d] px-4 py-2.5 text-[#2b2014] px-4 py-2.5 text-[#5b4a33] mt-3 text-[.9rem] leading-relaxed text-[#2b2014] 2 Validation has two layers System-level checks validate type and range (marks between 0–100). The human/managerial layer catches logical errors — the system accepts 63 as valid, but the employee may have meant 65. What happens next? — a mark of 63 enters the system Entry: the clerk types 63 into the marks field. The declared type is integer; the field expects 0–100. active ghost ghost ghost ghost marks System check: is it an integer? Is it within 0–100? Both pass. System-level validation only sees type and range — it cannot read intent. flex flex-wrap items-center gap-3 type = integer pass twin 0 ≤ 63 ≤ 100 pass twin system verdict valid twin Human check: the student’s paper says 65. A logical error — valid data, wrong value. No system check could catch it. flex flex-wrap items-center gap-3 entered broken intended twin gap human judgement active Correction entered; the bridge between the two layers is the process, not the code. This is exactly where business analysts and domain experts earn their place. flex flex-wrap items-center gap-3 final value twin caught by managerial review active 3 Real-time or not — the business decides UPI transfers confirm instantly but backend settlement runs periodically (every two hours); daily sales summaries run at midnight, not continuously. Maintenance windows host heavy computations. the user sees an instant confirmation while the settlement quietly runs every two hours — responsiveness for people, batching for machines, each tuned by business requirements. mt-6 grid gap-4 md:grid-cols-2 A customer ID contains letters and digits (e.g. B26-SME-001). Its correct data type is… Integer Float Character / text Boolean Mixed letter–number identifiers must be stored as text — arithmetic on them is meaningless and integer storage would corrupt them. Lecture 3 · data types Why is Boolean preferred over integer for true/false values? It prints nicer Memory efficiency and error prevention It is faster to type Python requires it The live session’s stated reasons: a Boolean can only hold two values, so it saves memory and makes invalid states unrepresentable — error prevention. Lecture 3 · misconceptions mt-4 Bridge work A retailer wants daily totals but instant stock alerts. Which functions run real-time, which run at midnight — and who decides? Alerts: real-time (business need). Daily sales summary: fixed interval (midnight). The business requirements determine processing frequency — not the developer’s preference. Write the two validation layers for a marks field in one sentence each. System: integer within 0–100. Human/managerial: does the entered value match the source document (63 vs 65)? <SectionHead eyebrow={eyebrowOf( )} title={ Data types, validation & the BA bridge } lead= /> Data type Purpose Example {TYPE_TABLE.map(([t, p, e]) => ( {t} {p} {e} ))} Selection needs business domain understanding , determined through consultation with end-users and domain experts. The classic trap: a customer ID that mixes letters and numbers must be stored as{ } text, not a pure number . <AtbStepper title= steps={[ { label: , detail: , frame: , }, { label: , detail: , frame: ( ), }, { label: , detail: , frame: ( ), }, { label: , detail: , frame: ( ), }, ]} />

chapters.label: Finiteness
chapters.text: Lecture 04 · Finiteness. Countable steps · the store counter that never ends. finiteness finiteness grad-text Property 1 of the five core technical characteristics: an algorithm must terminate after a countable, finite number of steps — without looping indefinitely. 1 The valid twin — counting a classroom Start at the first desk, count each student exactly once, move desk by desk, stop at the last student and display the total. text-[.95rem] leading-relaxed text-[#2b2014] What happens next? — the classroom count, traced Start at the first student. Count = 1 — exactly once. Each student is counted once; the counter is the data. active ghost ghost ghost ghost desk 1 desk 2 desk 3 desk 4 desk 5 Move to the next desk. Count = 2, then 3, 4… The loop body repeats — but each repetition is one more countable step. done done done active ghost ✓ ✓ ✓ desk 4 desk 5 Decision: is this the last student? No → keep counting. The diamond asks the question every pass; the answer is knowable because the room is finite. done done done done active ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ desk 5 Yes — display the total and STOP. 5 steps for 5 students. Terminated after a countable, finite number of steps. Finiteness holds. flex flex-wrap items-center gap-3 done done done done done total active state ENDED active 2 The broken twin — the retail store counter Check if a customer has entered; if no, check again; if yes, count and return to step 1. No defined endpoint — an infinite loop. text-[.95rem] leading-relaxed text-[#2b2014] the working loop has an exit diamond and a display step; the broken one only ever re-checks — its dashed path circles forever until you bolt on the midnight reset. mt-6 grid gap-4 md:grid-cols-2 A stock monitor that ‘checks whether a customer has entered, and if no, checks again’ violates which property? Generality Finiteness Determinism Well-defined inputs It never ends — there is no defined endpoint, so the step count is unbounded. Finiteness demands termination after a countable, finite number of steps. Lecture 4 · finiteness The lecture’s official repair for the store counter is… Delete the counter Add a reset condition (reset to zero at midnight) Count faster Count only paying customers Adding ‘reset counter to zero at midnight’ bounds the loop within each time period, making the algorithm finite and the collected data meaningful. Lecture 4 · finiteness mt-4 <SectionHead eyebrow={eyebrowOf( )} title={ Finiteness — the algorithm must end } lead= /> The steps are countable and the endpoint is defined: whether the room holds 40 students or an auditorium holds 600 , the count finishes. Finiteness does not mean “few steps” — it means the steps are countable and the algorithm stops . <AtbStepper title= steps={[ { label: , detail: , frame: , }, { label: , detail: , frame: , }, { label: , detail: , frame: , }, { label: , detail: , frame: ( ), }, ]} /> The system continuously checks for incoming customers and there is no condition under which it stops on its own — it violates finiteness and, running forever, can never hand you a meaningful total. The official fix from the lecture: add a reset condition — “reset the counter to zero at midnight” — so the algorithm becomes finite within each period and the day’s data becomes meaningful. <Takeaways items={[ Finiteness = the algorithm ends after a countable, finite number of steps , without looping indefinitely. , Valid twin: the classroom count — stop at the last student, display the total. , Broken twin: the store counter that re-checks forever — repaired by a reset condition (midnight). , An algorithm that never ends also compromises effectiveness — the properties interlock. , ]} />

chapters.label: Definiteness
chapters.text: Lecture 04 · Definiteness. Exact measures · the AGI connection. definiteness definiteness grad-text Property 2: each step must be clearly defined with no ambiguity. “Some”, “a little” and “a while” are subjective — machines cannot guess them. 1 The valid twin — the average of marks Input five marks, compute (M1+M2+M3+M4+M5) ÷ 5, display, stop. Every step has precisely one meaning. text-[.95rem] leading-relaxed text-[#2b2014] 2 The broken twin — the ambiguous tea “Take some tea leaves, add a little milk, boil for a while, add sugar if needed.” Four steps, four ambiguities. text-[.95rem] leading-relaxed text-[#2b2014] the exact formula funnels into one number — 62 — while every subjective phrase in the tea recipe fans out into as many outcomes as there are cooks. What happens next? — two cooks follow the same ambiguous recipe “Take some tea leaves.” Cook A reads one spoon; Cook B reads three. The word has no quantity — interpretation is already diverging. flex flex-wrap gap-6 1 spoon Cook A · ‘some’ 3 spoons Cook B · ‘some’ pivot “Add a little milk.” A pours 40 ml; B pours 100 ml. Same instruction, different data — indefiniteness compounds. flex flex-wrap items-center gap-3 Cook A milk 40 ml Cook B milk 100 ml active recipe said ‘a little’ broken “Boil for a while.” A brews 3 minutes; B brews 9. Time has no number either — every subjective word widens the gap. flex flex-wrap items-center gap-3 Cook A boil 3 min Cook B boil 9 min active Two cups, one recipe — the outputs disagree. A machine following this ‘algorithm’ could not even say which cup is correct. Definiteness is broken. flex flex-wrap items-center gap-3 cup A weak, milky cup B strong, stewed active agreement none broken mt-6 insight The AGI connection mt-6 grid gap-4 md:grid-cols-2 “Add sugar if needed” violates… Generality Definiteness Feasibility Finiteness “If needed” is not precisely defined — two people (or machines) would act differently. That is a failure of definiteness (unambiguity). Lecture 4 · definiteness Why is “250 ml of milk” a definiteness repair while “a little milk” is not? It is shorter It has exactly one interpretation It uses metric units Milk is a variable A quantity with a unit admits a single reading — every executor (human or machine) pours the same 250 ml. ‘A little’ invites as many readings as there are readers. Lecture 4 · definiteness <SectionHead eyebrow={eyebrowOf( )} title={ Definiteness — exactly one interpretation } lead= /> Numerical operations, exact thresholds, an exact display. Two different people executing the steps — or the same machine twice — land on the same result. That is definiteness: no room for multiple interpretations . “Some”, “little” and “a while” are subjective interpretations — different people produce different results, and first-time learners cannot follow the recipe without outside knowledge. Good recipes and good algorithms specify exact measurements: “250 ml of milk” instead of “a little milk”. Machines and computers cannot make subjective interpretations — they require precise, quantified instructions. <AtbStepper title= steps={[ { label: , detail: , frame: ( ), }, { label: , detail: , frame: ( ), }, { label: , detail: , frame: ( ), }, { label: , detail: , frame: ( ), }, ]} /> The challenge of creating artificial general intelligence stems partly from this property. Humans easily interpret ambiguous instructions like “come near me”; machines require explicit quantitative specifications. Current AI systems work well with specific, definite tasks but struggle with ambiguous, general-purpose instructions — definiteness is exactly where the difficulty lives.

chapters.label: Inputs & outputs
chapters.text: Lecture 04 · Inputs & outputs. Rectangle area · the loan that always answers. inputs-outputs inputs-outputs grad-text grad-text Properties 3 and 4: external data requirements must be explicitly specified, and the algorithm must produce at least one clear expected result — even when the conditions are not met. 1 Well-defined inputs — the rectangle area Input: exactly two values, length L and width W. Compute Area = L × W. Display. Stop. text-[.95rem] leading-relaxed text-[#2b2014] 2 Well-defined outputs — the loan that always answers Criteria: income > 50,000 AND credit score > 600. Output: “Loan Approved” OR “Loan Rejected” — always a clear, definitive decision. text-[.95rem] leading-relaxed text-[#2b2014] both branches terminate in a named, quotable output — Approved or Rejected — so even rejection is a well-defined result; ‘Processing Complete’ would leave the applicant with nothing to act on. What happens next? — two applicants through the same loan algorithm Applicant A: income 62,000, credit 640. Both criteria met. Same deterministic criteria from Lecture 5: fixed thresholds, no judgement calls. flex flex-wrap items-center gap-3 income credit income > 50,000 true twin credit > 600 true twin Output: “Loan Approved” — a clear, quotable decision. The well-defined output contract: at least one clear expected result. flex flex-wrap items-center gap-3 output Loan Approved twin applicant knows yes twin Applicant B: income 44,000, credit 710. Income fails. One false criterion is enough — the algorithm still produces an output. flex flex-wrap items-center gap-3 income credit income > 50,000 false broken credit > 600 true twin Output: “Loan Rejected” — still a well-defined answer. Rejection is not silence. ‘Processing Complete’ would have been the broken twin here. flex flex-wrap items-center gap-3 output Loan Rejected broken applicant knows yes twin vague twin ‘Processing Complete’ broken mt-6 grid gap-4 md:grid-cols-2 A loan system that ends by displaying ‘Processing Complete’ violates… Finiteness Well-defined outputs Language independence Generality The user cannot know whether the loan was approved or rejected — there is no clear expected result. A well-defined output means a definitive decision in every branch. Lecture 4 · well-defined outputs ‘Input the required value, calculate the area’ fails which property? Well-defined inputs Determinism Effectiveness Finiteness ‘The required value’ does not say which values or how many — the external data requirements are not explicitly specified. The rectangle twin names exactly L and W. Lecture 4 · well-defined inputs <SectionHead eyebrow={eyebrowOf( )} title={ Well-defined inputs &{ } outputs } lead= /> The inputs are specific — exactly two values are required, and the step names them. The broken twin says “input the required value… calculate the area” : which values? how many? which formula? Both the input specification and the step itself are ambiguous, so the algorithm cannot even begin. The user knows the decision regardless of outcome . The broken twin displays “Processing Complete” after applying the criteria — the applicant never learns whether the loan was approved or rejected, so neither the input nor the output is well-defined. The lecture’s real-world parallel: good customer service — an email that says “we’re working on it, will respond within 48 hours” — is a well-defined output even when the complete solution is not ready. The algorithm should always communicate a clear status or result. <AtbStepper title= steps={[ { label: , detail: , frame: ( ), }, { label: , detail: , frame: ( ), }, { label: , detail: , frame: ( ), }, { label: , detail: , frame: ( ), }, ]} />

chapters.label: Effectiveness
chapters.text: Lecture 04 · Effectiveness. The 50-unit reorder line · properties interlock. effectiveness effectiveness grad-text Property 5: the algorithm must solve the problem in a practical, useful manner — considering time, resources and business objectives. Correctness alone is not effectiveness. 1 The valid twin — the inventory reordering system Input current stock; safety stock threshold = 50 units; purchase order quantity = 200 units; if stock < 50, create a PO for 200, otherwise maintain. text-[.95rem] leading-relaxed text-[#2b2014] What happens next? — stock falls toward the reorder line Week 1: stock 240 units. Above 50 → maintain, no order. The condition stock < 50 is false — the algorithm does nothing, correctly. done done done done ghost wk 1 wk 2 wk 3 wk 4 wk 5 Weeks 2–4: 190 → 140 → 95. Still above the line. Each week is one read of current stock — the only input the algorithm needs. done done done active ghost ✓ ✓ ✓ wk 4 wk 5 Week 5: stock 48 < 50 → create the purchase order for 200 units. The threshold is explicit, the quantity is explicit — nothing is left to judgement. flex flex-wrap items-center gap-3 done done done done active ✓ ✓ ✓ ✓ wk 5 48 < 50 true active PO qty twin Stock restored to 248. Production continuity + cost control. Both business objectives hold — that is what effectiveness means here. flex flex-wrap items-center gap-3 stock after PO twin production risk none twin overstock none twin the olive curve only acts at the exact 50-unit line and restores exactly 200 units — the vague twin’s ‘looks low’ has no line to cross and no quantity to order. 2 The broken twin — ‘order more whenever stock looks low’ “Low” is undefined; “more items” has no quantity. One manager orders 200, another orders 1,000 — inconsistent and costly. text-[.95rem] leading-relaxed text-[#2b2014] 3 The properties interlock — and the practice pairs Infinite loops violate finiteness AND effectiveness; missing well-defined outputs usually means unclear inputs; violating definiteness makes well-defined outputs impossible. mt-4 grid gap-4 md:grid-cols-2 card-warm p-5 flex items-center gap-2 font-extrabold text-[#3e2c1d] h-4 w-4 text-[#c2410c] mt-2 text-[.85rem] leading-relaxed text-[#2b2014] mt-2 text-[.85rem] leading-relaxed text-[#44621d] card-warm p-5 flex items-center gap-2 font-extrabold text-[#3e2c1d] h-4 w-4 text-[#c2410c] mt-2 text-[.85rem] leading-relaxed text-[#2b2014] mt-2 text-[.85rem] leading-relaxed text-[#44621d] mt-6 grid gap-4 md:grid-cols-2 An algorithm solving the problem in 3 hours is ineffective for real-time loan approval because effectiveness includes… Language choice Time and resource practicality The number of lines The output format Effectiveness = solving the problem usefully within time and resource constraints. 3 hours fails a real-time approval regardless of correctness. Lecture 4 · effectiveness ‘Return to Step 2’ after evaluating eligibility breaks finiteness. What is the secondary casualty? Language independence Well-defined output (it never concludes) Feasibility Generality The lecture lists it explicitly: the loop never reaches a conclusion, so no well-defined output is ever produced. The properties interlock. Lecture 4 · exercises mt-4 <SectionHead eyebrow={eyebrowOf( )} title={ Effectiveness — useful , not just correct } lead= /> Effectiveness here is a balance : production continuity (never risk running out) against cost management (never overstock). One threshold, one quantity, one doable step — a manager can execute it and a machine can run it. <AtbStepper title= steps={[ { label: , detail: , frame: , }, { label: , detail: , frame: , }, { label: , detail: , frame: ( ), }, { label: , detail: , frame: ( ), }, ]} /> The result is either production risk (too little, too late) or excessive inventory cost (too much, too early). And effectiveness has a time and resource dimension too: an algorithm that solves loan approval in 3 hours is ineffective for real-time approvals; one that demands excessive computing resources is ineffective on limited devices. Effectiveness encompasses not just correctness but practicality . Practical exercise 1 — the flawed loop Step 1: input applicant details → Step 2: evaluate eligibility → Step 3: return to Step 2 . Violated: finiteness (the loop never ends). Secondary: well-defined output — it never reaches a conclusion. Practical exercise 2 — the vague discount Input purchase amount → “if the purchase amount is large, give a large discount” → display bill, stop. Violated: definiteness — “large” is undefined for both the purchase and the discount, so different staff apply different criteria. <Takeaways items={[ The five core technical properties: finiteness, definiteness, well-defined inputs, well-defined outputs, effectiveness . , Every property is easiest to remember by its broken twin — and the twin is shown neutral, never red. , Ambiguity and vagueness are the enemies of algorithms in computational contexts. , Real-world algorithms must be theoretically sound and practically useful — the two halves of effectiveness. , ]} />

chapters.label: Execution properties
chapters.text: Lecture 05 · Execution properties. Loan vs visa · cloud & ML · the Rahul bonus. props2 props2 grad-text Language independence, determinism, feasibility and generality decide whether an algorithm can be properly implemented and generalized in the real world. 1 Four execution & design characteristics These sit on top of the core technical five — an algorithm can be ‘correct’ and still fail here. grid gap-4 md:grid-cols-2 card-warm h-full p-5 flex items-center gap-2.5 flex h-9 w-9 items-center justify-center rounded-xl #f5c889 h-4 w-4 #7c4a12 font-extrabold leading-tight text-[#3e2c1d] mt-2.5 text-[.85rem] leading-relaxed text-[#2b2014] mt-3 grid gap-2 flex items-start gap-2 rounded-lg px-2.5 py-1.5 #eef4dd mt-0.5 h-3.5 w-3.5 shrink-0 text-[#5d7a2e] text-[.78rem] leading-snug text-[#44621d] flex items-start gap-2 rounded-lg px-2.5 py-1.5 #f0ede5 mt-0.5 h-3.5 w-3.5 shrink-0 text-[#8a8578] text-[.78rem] leading-snug text-[#5d6670] cloud and machine-learning algorithms existed decades before they were feasible — feasibility is a moving line drawn by internet speeds, costs, computing power and data availability. What happens next? — determinism, run twice Run 1: income 62,000, credit 720 → the loan algorithm evaluates. Fixed criteria: income > 50,000 AND credit score > 700. flex flex-wrap items-center gap-3 run income > 50,000 true twin credit > 700 true twin output Approved twin Run 2: the exact same inputs → the exact same output. Determinism: the criteria are fixed, so re-running cannot change the verdict. flex flex-wrap items-center gap-3 run inputs identical output Approved twin matches run 1 yes twin The visa twin, run 1: officer A reads ‘trustworthy’ → granted. Subjective judgement — no fixed threshold exists to re-check. flex flex-wrap items-center gap-3 run criterion ‘feels trustworthy’ broken output Granted The visa twin, run 2: same file, officer B → rejected. Same input, different output — indeterminate. Algorithms must be deterministic to be reliably implementable. flex flex-wrap items-center gap-3 run criterion ‘feels trustworthy’ broken output Rejected broken matches run 1 no — not an algorithm broken mt-6 insight The two review questions, answered mt-6 grid gap-4 md:grid-cols-2 A discount algorithm randomly chooses between 5% and 20% for every customer. Which property fails? Language independence Determinism Feasibility Generality Random selection means the same purchase amount can produce different discounts each run — the same input no longer guarantees the same output. Lecture 5 · review questions ‘Determine the customer’s true intention, then provide a solution’ fails which property? Determinism Generality Feasibility Finiteness Reading true intentions is not strictly executable by a computing system without extreme measures (AI with facial recognition) — not feasible for a standard complaint system. Lecture 5 · review questions <SectionHead eyebrow={eyebrowOf( )} title={ The execution family — four more properties } lead= /> {EXEC_PROPS.map((p, i) => ( {p.name} {p.rule} {p.yes} {p.no} ))} <AtbStepper title= steps={[ { label: , detail: , frame: ( ), }, { label: , detail: , frame: ( ), }, { label: , detail: , frame: ( ), }, { label: , detail: , frame: ( ), }, ]} /> Random discount (5–20%) for all customers → determinism fails: the same purchase may get a different discount each time; randomness may be company policy but it violates algorithmic principles. chapters.text: Lecture 07 · Linked lists. Flexible chains of songs — nodes, pointers & shuffles. linkedlists linkedlists grad-text The second major linear data structure after arrays. Concept check After deleting Song 2 by rewiring Song1.next → Song 3, Song 2 itself… is erased from memory at once is still in memory but no longer part of the list moves to the end of the list becomes the new head Deletion is only a redirect of the previous node's pointer — nothing is wiped, nothing shifts. Concept check When a playlist is shuffled, what actually moves? The song files, into a new packed block Nothing physical — only the pointer connections change order The head node, to a random song The nodes are physically re-sorted by name Reshuffling rewrites the pointer connections only: every node stays at its memory address, and the visiting path (Head → … → Null) defines the new playback order. chapters.label: Arrays vs lists
chapters.text: Lecture 08 · Arrays vs lists. The Venn that settles the choice. venn8 venn8 grad-text Both structures underpin everything from stacks to graphs. The live session drew the choice as one picture: a small shared core, two opposite personalities. 1 The flagship Venn One shared core, two opposite personalities the shared core is small and structural — linear, ordered, foundational — while the personalities clash around it: the array buys speed with rigidity, the list buys flexibility with traversal. Venn diagram comparing arrays and linked lists: they share being linear, ordered and foundational; arrays alone are fixed-size, contiguous, index-accessed and shift on insert or delete; linked lists alone are dynamic, scattered nodes behind a head pointer, accessed by pointer hops with cheap re-wiring Arrays Fixed size defined at creation — resizing copies the world Contiguous memory one sequential block of locations O(1) direct access the index IS the address Shift to insert/delete middle changes push neighbours around both Linear elements arranged one after another Ordered elements every item has a position in the sequence Foundations stacks, queues, trees & graphs are built on these two Linked lists Dynamic size grows and shrinks — no preset length Scattered nodes + head data anywhere; the head pointer starts the walk Pointer-hop access no index — follow links node by node Cheap re-wiring insert/delete = redirect a pointer, shift nothing Same family, different memory story. The array buys speed with rigidity — fixed size, contiguous, instant indexing. The list buys flexibility with traversal — dynamic size, scattered nodes, pointer hops. The live session's verdict: arrays when the size is known and access is frequent; lists when the size is unknown and the structure changes constantly. 2 Which one, when The ten-second decision — plus the playlist grid gap-4 md:grid-cols-3 Known size + frequent access → array Thirty days of sales: the count is fixed and any day is read directly by its index. Unknown size + frequent changes → linked list Add, remove and reorder constantly without ever reallocating the world. The foundation duty → both Stacks, queues, trees and graphs are all implemented on arrays or linked lists. card-warm p-4 flex items-center gap-2 h-4.5 w-4.5 shrink-0 #b45309 text-[.86rem] font-extrabold leading-snug text-[#3e2c1d] mt-1.5 inline-block rounded-lg bg-[#f6e3c8] px-2 py-0.5 text-[.74rem] font-extrabold text-[#8a4508] mt-2 text-[.82rem] leading-relaxed text-[#5d4a33] mt-4 text-[.9rem] leading-relaxed text-muted-warm mt-8 grid gap-4 lg:grid-cols-2 A visa officer can rule differently on two identical files. A subjective interview breaks it — the loan check with quantitative criteria is its deterministic twin. Memory considerations — where the undo history actually lives Lecture 9 · memory considerations • Static stacks (Excel, Photoshop): the stack is cleared when the file is saved — saved work needs no undo history. • Dynamic stacks: limited by the device's physical memory (RAM) — they grow only as far as the hardware allows. • Exhaust that memory and the app crashes — a dynamic stack's only ceiling is the machine itself. • Saving often keeps stacks small — each save wipes the unsaved-changes pile before it can grow toward the limit. chapters.text: Lecture 10 · Queues. FIFO — first come, first served. queues queues grad-text A queue is a linear structure with two doors: entries at the rear, exits at the front. Fairness by arrival order — the structure behind every waiting line in software. 1 The popcorn line Interval time at the movies story Waiting at the movie interval mt-3 flex flex-wrap gap-2 chip h-3.5 w-3.5 chip h-3.5 w-3.5 chip h-3.5 w-3.5 2 Front and rear Enqueue, Dequeue, Peek, Size — press the buttons mt-5 card-warm p-6 flex flex-wrap items-center gap-3 text-lg font-bold chip mt-4 grid gap-4 sm:grid-cols-2 NQ on an empty queue The very first element occupies BOTH front and rear — one value, two pointers. A and B leave in arrival order — C never moved, yet it becomes the front. Find the queue hiding in a printer, a call center, and a ticket window. In each, what is 'enqueue' and what is 'dequeue'? What happened? the main queue restarted from zero the interrupted sub-queue restarted — the main queue kept its progress the whole video was re-downloaded the circular queue wrapped around Queue of queues: the main playback queue preserves segment progress, but the sub-queue of frames inside the interrupted segment restarts — so playback resumes a few seconds early. mt-8 font-mono-warm font-bold font-mono-warm font-bold <SectionHead dark eyebrow={eyebrowOf( )} title={ Four queues for four situations } lead= /> 1 Linear queue The plain version: insert at the rear, remove from the front . Its limitation is memory wastage — in an array implementation, once rear hits the end you cannot insert, even if front spaces have been freed by earlier deletions. Lecture 11 · pointer detail front points to the first location where an element is still stored — not to array slot 0. 2 Circular queue The last position connects back to the first — the queue becomes a ring. It reuses the spaces freed by deletions , fixing the linear queue's waste. The rear keeps wrapping into vacated cells , so the ring can serve insertions and deletions indefinitely . Classically implemented via a linked list — and beyond the slides: arrays can do it too, by wrapping indices with modulo . traffic lights multiplayer games circular playlists CPU round-robin scheduling 3 Priority queue Served by priority, not arrival . Equal priorities serve FIFO. The lecture's example: the queue holds (A,8) (T,6) (B,3) ; a new (S,7) arrives and slots before (T,6) — arrival order be damned. CPU task scheduling hospital emergency room airport traffic control railway disaster management Tatkal quota The lecture's triage, spelled out: accident cases beat recurring headaches · low-fuel long-hauls land before short-hauls · Rajdhani & Shatabdi get green-corridor signals · system tasks run before user apps · rescue goes first to those in immediate danger. 4 Doubly ended queue (Deque) Insert and delete from BOTH ends — so one deque can act as a{ } queue AND a stack at once : front-only use is FIFO, end-only use is LIFO. Each segment is itself a{ } SUB-QUEUE of thousands of tiny frames / packets . The{ } graphics card rapidly plays the frames inside the current segment — and that is why the video stays smooth while the outer queue quietly refills. chapters.text: Lecture 12 · Trees. Hierarchy: roots, parents & leaves. trees trees grad-text Arrays, lists, stacks and queues are linear: the path through them is predetermined. Trees are the first nonlinear structure — multiple possible paths, hierarchical relationships. Every org chart, folder structure and family album is one — drawn upside down, root at the top, leaves at the bottom. 1 From family album to data structure A flat list is not enough when the data itself is shaped like a family story The album that would not sit still card-warm p-5 md:p-7 mb-3 flex flex-wrap items-center gap-2 chip h-3.5 w-3.5 chip mt-4 grid gap-2 root the grandfather — the first, topmost element of the tree parent → child Son A, Son B and Daughter are children of the grandfather — and parents of their own children below leaf D1, S1 and S2 — plus Son B, who has no children; a tree is really nested sub-trees, the way a branch of a real tree is a whole tree in miniature 4 Where you already met trees Five hierarchies you use without calling them data structures mb-4 flex flex-wrap items-center gap-2 chip h-3.5 w-3.5 grid gap-4 sm:grid-cols-2 lg:grid-cols-3 card-warm lift flex h-full flex-col gap-3 p-5 flex items-center gap-3 flex h-10 w-10 shrink-0 items-center justify-center rounded-xl linear-gradient(135deg,#fde8cf,#fbcf9f) #8a3d10 h-5 w-5 text-[.95rem] font-bold text-[#3e2c1d] flex flex-wrap items-center gap-1.5 h-3 w-3 text-[#c2410c] rounded-lg border border-[#ecd9bd] bg-[#fffaf1] px-2 py-1 text-[.72rem] font-semibold text-[#7c4a12] mt-auto text-[.76rem] leading-relaxed text-[#8a6a48] mt-10 grid gap-5 lg:grid-cols-2 The first element of a tree, drawn at the top, is the… leaf root edge subtree The root is the one node with no parent — everything else hangs below it. Parents (by definition) have at least one. lg:col-span-2 Lecture 12 · depth vs height Every node carries its own depth; the tree as a whole carries a single… height edge count parent map level order Depth is per node — edges from that node UP to the root, with the root at 0. But you also want the{ } hierarchy : grandparents → parents → you → siblings. That branching shape is a tree : one element at the top (the{ } root ), others hanging below it, level after level. Real trees grow up; data trees are drawn upside down — root at the top, growing downward. chapters.label: Traversals
chapters.text: Lecture 12 · Traversals. Pre · in · post · level order. traversals traversals grad-text A tree is useless if you cannot walk it. A traversal visits every node exactly once — and the order you choose changes the answer you get. Left-before-right holds in all of them. <SectionHead dark eyebrow={eyebrowOf( )} title={ Reading a tree four ways } lead= /> Lecture 12 · the one rule that never changes Left before right. Always. Every traversal — depth-first or breadth-first — visits the{ } left subtree before the right subtree . Flip that order and you get a different, wrong sequence. Only the root moves; the left-first rule never does. Lecture 12 · naming rule The root's position names the traversal Root first → pre-order · root in the middle → in-order ·{ } root last → post-order. (In-order reads cleanly when nodes have at most two children — one of the lecture's fine-print notes.) Lecture 12 · breadth-first · queue-based Reads the tree like text Level order finishes every node at the current depth before going a single step deeper — top-to-bottom, left-to-right, staying on each level until the level is done. It runs on a queue — the mechanism Lecture 17 calls BFS. Lecture 13 · the stack-vs-queue Venn · Quiz One briefing. recap13 recap13 grad-text The live session put the last two linear structures side by side: a stack with one open end and a queue with two. Same family, opposite personalities — and between them they run undo, printing, scheduling and buffering. mb-2 story Lecture 13 · the second consolidation point — and the Quiz One briefing 1 The flagship Venn — stack vs queue Shared plumbing, opposite doors Venn diagram comparing stacks and queues: they share being linear, constrained, built on arrays or linked lists, prone to overflow and underflow, and logically ordered over flat memory; stacks alone are LIFO with one open end for push, pop, peek and size, powering undo and function calls; queues alone are FIFO with two open ends, enqueue at the rear and dequeue at the front, powering printing and scheduling Stack LIFO last in, first out One open end everything happens at the top push · pop · peek · size add, remove, glance, count Undo & Ctrl+Z the last change is the first reversed Function calls the call stack remembers where to return both Linear structures elements kept in sequence Constrained access insertion & removal only at designated ends Built on arrays or linked lists not primitive types — implemented, with rules Overflow & underflow add to full / remove from empty Logical, not physical flat memory below; chapters.label: BST & AVL
chapters.text: Lecture 14 · BST & AVL. Ordered children · the |h(left)−h(right)| ≤ 1 rule. bstavl bstavl grad-text A binary search tree adds ordering to shape: values matter, left is always less than the parent and right always greater — recursively. Then the AVL tree defends the shape: the height difference between left and right subtrees may never exceed one. 1 The ordering property — values matter now Left subtree values are always less than the parent node value; right subtree values are always greater. The property holds recursively for all subtrees. the minimum is found by traversing left continuously from the root until a leaf; the maximum by traversing right continuously — dictionary-style search in tree form. 2 Where BSTs work — and the skew trap Dictionary searches, database indexing, student ID lookups with systematic templates — any scenario needing frequent search. But data inserted in sorted order (increasing or decreasing) makes the tree highly unbalanced: it behaves like a linked list and needs sequential traversal, defeating the efficiency advantage. What happens next? — the skew trap, sorted input Insert 10 into an empty BST — it becomes the root. A healthy start: any value could land on either side. 10 twin Insert 20 — greater than 10 → right child. Still balanced enough. But the input is rising. 10 20 idle active root right child Insert 30, 40, 50 — every value walks right, always. Each new node chains off the previous right child. 10 20 30 40 50 ghost ghost ghost ghost active → → → → right chain The tree IS a linked list now — search for 50 costs 5 hops, not ⌈log₂ 5⌉ = 3. This defeats the BST’s whole advantage. The AVL tree exists to stop exactly this. flex flex-wrap items-center gap-3 shape right-skewed chain broken search cost O(n) — sequential broken healthy BST would be O(log n) twin 3 The AVL rule A self-balancing BST where, for ANY node, |height(left subtree) − height(right subtree)| ≤ 1. Rotation — conceptually like restructuring a hanging string-and-ball system — redistributes nodes during insertion without violating BST properties. mt-4 grid gap-4 md:grid-cols-2 For every node of an AVL tree, which condition must hold? |h(left) − h(right)| ≤ 1 |h(left) − h(right)| ≤ 2 left ≥ parent Every leaf at the same depth The balancing rule, exactly: the height difference between left and right subtrees may not exceed one for any node. Rotations restore it during insertion. Lecture 14 · AVL trees Inserting sorted data into a plain BST produces… A perfectly balanced tree A heap A highly unbalanced tree that behaves like a linked list A complete binary tree Sorted (increasing or decreasing) input chains every node to one side — sequential traversal, no branching advantage. AVL rotations are the fix. chapters.label: Heaps
chapters.text: Lecture 14 · Heaps. Complete trees · the parent-child ordering that powers priority queues. heaps heaps grad-text A heap keeps the complete binary tree shape and orders only the parent-child relationship: max heap parents are greater (root = maximum), min heap parents are smaller (root = minimum). Insertions reorder VALUES — the structure never changes. 1 Two heaps, one shape Max heap: parent value always greater than child values — the root contains the maximum. Min heap: parent always less — the root holds the minimum. No left-right ordering requirement: only the parent-child relationship matters. the shape is identical on both sides — complete, last level filled left to right — only the value ordering flips. There is no left-vs-right rule anywhere in a heap. 2 Insertion reorders values, never the structure During insertion, values are rearranged to maintain the heap property; the structure remains a complete binary tree after each insertion — values are reordered (not repositioned structurally) to satisfy the parent-child constraint. What happens next? — inserting 95 into the max heap The new value 95 must land so the tree stays COMPLETE — next slot, left to right, at the last level. Structure first: the shape rule is non-negotiable. 90 70 80 30 20 40 95 idle idle idle idle idle idle active root new slot 95 > parent 40 → the VALUES swap to restore ‘parent ≥ child’. Values are reordered, not repositioned structurally. 90 70 80 30 20 95 40 idle idle idle idle idle active idle swapped up 95 > 80 → swaps again. Now 95 reaches… the root. The climb continues until its parent is larger — or it becomes the root. 95 70 90 30 20 40 80 twin idle idle idle idle idle idle new root Heap property restored — still a complete binary tree, still parent ≥ child everywhere. Max heap: higher priority numbers processed first (root = highest priority). 95 70 90 30 20 40 80 done done done done done done done 3 Priority queues — the primary application Max heap: higher priority elements processed first (higher numbers get higher priority). Min heap: lower priority numbers first (priority 1 before priority 2). Medical example: emergency patients attended before routine cases. System processes take precedence over user-level applications. card-warm mt-4 overflow-x-auto p-0 w-full min-w-[640px] text-left text-[.86rem] bg-[#fbf3e3] px-4 py-2.5 font-extrabold text-[#3e2c1d] px-4 py-2.5 font-extrabold text-[#3e2c1d] px-4 py-2.5 font-extrabold text-[#3e2c1d] px-4 py-2.5 font-extrabold text-[#3e2c1d] border-t border-[#f3e2c8] bg-[#fffaf1] px-4 py-2.5 font-bold text-[#7c4a12] px-4 py-2.5 text-[#2b2014] px-4 py-2.5 text-[#2b2014] px-4 py-2.5 text-[#5b4a33] mt-6 grid gap-4 md:grid-cols-2 A hospital queue serves priority 1 before priority 2. chapters.label: Graphs
chapters.text: Lecture 15 · Graphs. G = (V, E) — relationships. V = {A, B, C, P, Q, R, S, X, Y} E = {(C,S), (A,P), (A,Q), (B,R), (S,P), (Q,R), (S,X), (P,X), (Q,Y), (R,Y), (X,Y)} # 11 edges degree(P) = 3 # P connects to A, S and X degrees: C=1, A=2, B=1 · S=3, P=3, Q=3, R=3, X=3, Y=3 Σ degrees = 22 = 2 × |E| # every edge has two ends graphs graphs grad-text Friendship, roads, bank transfers: real relationships refuse to live under a single parent. Stack vs queue traversal. def dfs(graph, start): stack = [start] while stack: node = stack.pop() # take the TOP if node not in visited: mark node visited for nb in graph[node]: if nb not visited: stack.push(nb) def bfs(graph, start): queue = [start] while queue: node = queue.dequeue() # take the FRONT if node not in visited: mark node visited for nb in graph[node]: if nb not visited: queue.enqueue(nb) dfsbfs dfsbfs grad-text Same nine vertices and eleven edges as Lecture 15's graph. Tiny input change → a completely different digest. <SectionHead eyebrow={eyebrowOf( )} title={ Hashing — fixed-length fingerprints } lead= /> Recall the function box : input → function → output. A{ } hash function is a function with one iron rule: the output is{ } always the same fixed length — that output is the digest . Standard functions flex: square(x) grows with the number, uppercase(s) grows with the string — ordinary outputs vary in length with the input. Hash functions never do: the output is a fixed-length digest (a.k.a. message digest ), typically alphanumeric — five characters or five million, same size out. before — the normal table Roll No Name B26SME001 Amar Sharma M26ME002 Akbar Khan P25ELE0003 Anothony Gonzalves Sea

Big O · best/avg/worst · DS costs. complexity complexity grad-text Search is the heartbeat of the internet — every web search, product recommendation and train booking is a search, and users expect the answer instantly. How many seconds does the algorithm take on my laptop? If the input grows, in what proportion does the time requirement grow? How many lines of code does the algorithm need? How much memory does one run consume? Big O describes the ORDER OF MAGNITUDE of work growth with input size — never wall-clock seconds, which depend on the machine. It is the manager's ruler: compare algorithms by how their time scales, from 100 records to 10 lakh. Concept check An O(n²) routine runs on an input of 5. How much effort? 5 10 25 32 Quadratic means effort = input²: input 2 → effort 4; input 5 → effort 25. The work grows dramatically — and that is why O(n²) sits on the 'avoid unless necessary' rung of the business ladder. Concept check Why is searching a balanced binary search tree O(log n)? Because the tree secretly stores a sorted array Because each level halves the remaining candidates — left subtree smaller, right subtree larger Because trees are always small in practice Because the search uses a queue to sweep levels The BST property (left < parent < right) lets every comparison discard one whole branch — the problem subdivides into one relevant sub-problem, halving at every level. Warning: an UNBALANCED BST loses the halving and degrades toward O(n), behaving like a linked list. Concept check Search inside a stack costs O(n) because… stack el

Perform a linear search forward from that point until the term is found. flex items-start gap-3 mt-0.5 flex h-6 w-6 shrink-0 items-center justify-center rounded-full bg-gradient-to-br from-[#f59e0b] to-[#c2410c] text-[.7rem] font-bold text-white mt-4 text-[.9rem] leading-relaxed text-[#6f5438] 4 Exponential search Jumps that double — then binary inside the block card-warm p-6 md:p-8 chip h-3.5 w-3.5 mt-3 max-w-4xl text-[.93rem] leading-relaxed text-[#2b2014] mt-4 grid gap-3 md:grid-cols-2 rounded-2xl p-4 rgba(217,119,6,.10) text-[.78rem] font-extrabold uppercase tracking-[.14em] #92600a mt-1.5 text-[.88rem] leading-relaxed text-[#2b2014] rounded-2xl p-4 rgba(124,154,62,.12) text-[.78rem] font-extrabold uppercase tracking-[.14em] #4c6b1f mt-1.5 text-[.88rem] leading-relaxed text-[#2b2014] mt-4 text-[.9rem] leading-relaxed text-[#6f5438] mt-5 Concept check The real difference between jump search and exponential search? Exponential uses fixed jumps; jump search uses growing jumps Exponential doubles its jumps and binary-searches inside the block; jump search uses fixed √n jumps with linear search inside Exponential needs no sorting; jump search does They are the same algorithm under two names Two dials differ: jump SIZE (fixed √n vs doubling 1, 2, 4, 8, 16…) and the IN-BLOCK method (linear vs binary). Both need sorted data; the doubling-plus-binary combination is what lifts exponential search to O(log n) — and makes it ideal for rapidly growing databases. 5 Hash-based search Compute the address — no comparisons, no sorting card-warm p-6 md:p-8 chip h-3.5 w-3.5 mt-3 max-w-4xl text-[.93rem] leading-relaxed text-[#2b2014] font-mono-warm font-bold text-[#a0410a] mt-5 rounded-2xl p-4 #fffaf1 1px dashed #e5c79d mt-4 grid gap-3 sm:grid-cols-3 Average · O(1) A fixed number of steps regardless of database size — the fastest when the hash distributes data evenly. #4c6b1f rgba(124,154,62,.14) Worst · O(n) When everything collides into the same index — one long chain to walk end to end. #8c2f2f rgba(190,74,74,.12) Balanced chains · O(log n) If the chains are organized as balanced trees, even collisions stay logarithmic. #92600a rgba(217,119,6,.12) rounded-2xl p-4 text-[.85rem] font-extrabold mt-1.5 text-[.84rem] leading-relaxed text-[#2b2014] mt-4 text-[.9rem] leading-relaxed text-[#6f5438] mt-5 Concept check Hash search averages O(1). When does it collapse to O(n)? When the data is unsorted When every key collides into the same index — one chain holds everything When the table is smaller than the data When keys are negative numbers The average case is a fixed number of steps because the hash jumps straight to the index. The worst case is collision-intensive: ALL data points to the same index, so lookup degenerates into walking one long chain — O(n). Balanced-tree chains rescue it to O(log n); even distribution prevents it. 6 The search race Same array, same target — three very different bills mt-5 Concept check Your data is unsorted — and sorting it is not an option. Which strategies still work? Binary and jump search Exponential search only Linear and hash-based search Binary and hash-based search Binary, jump and exponential all REQUIRE sorted data — halving, bounding and block-stepping collapse without order. Linear search works on anything, and hash-based search never needed order in the first place: it computes the address instead of comparing values. 7 Which one, when The lecture's five use cases — and the four selection factors card-warm overflow-hidden px-4 pt-4 md:px-6 md:pt-6 chip h-3.5 w-3.5 overflow-x-auto p-4 md:p-6 warm-table min-w-[720px] Find a guest in today's hotel check-in register Linear search No inherent order — unstructured data; one-by-one is all you can do Find a product in a catalog sorted by categories Jump search Non-numeric category order — fixed √n jumps over blocks work better Find a student record using roll number in a database Ha

At the front — it floated left In its final position at the end Still at index 0 In the middle of the list Each pass sinks the largest unsorted value all the way to the end: 10 won all five comparisons of pass 1 and locked into the last slot — which is why pass 2 needs only four comparisons. Lecture 25 · complexity The exact comparison count is n(n−1)/2 = ½n² − ½n. Why do we report O(n²)? Because swaps count double Because Big O discards lower-order terms and constants Because passes are counted twice Because n(n−1)/2 simplifies to n² exactly Two Big O rules: the −½n term is negligible next to n² (drop lower orders), and the ½ constant is dropped too. ½n² − ½n collapses to O(n²) — quadratic growth. mt-5 Pen-and-paper drills — bubble sort Trace Pass 2 of [10, 5, 8, 4, 3, 2] by hand: list every comparison, every swap, and the final array with two settled values. Select · swap · one swap per pass · O(n²). selectionsort selectionsort grad-text Selection sort picks one element per pass — the minimum of everything still unsorted — and swaps it into its final position. One element finalised per pass, exactly one swap per pass. 1 The core loop Assume the first unsorted slot holds the minimum. Compare with everything to its right; when something smaller appears, mark it. Adjacent pairs are compared and swapped wherever the left is larger The minimum of the unsorted portion is found and swapped with the first unsorted slot Each element is inserted into its correct position among the sorted ones The list is split in half and the halves are merged Selection = SELECT one element per pass: assume the first unsorted slot is the minimum, sweep the rest, then perform exactly one swap. Adjacent-compare-and-swap is bubble sort; insert-into-the-sorted-portion is insertion sort. Lecture 26 · selection sort Sorting [10, 5, 8, 4, 3, 2]: what does the array look like after Pass 2? [2, 5, 8, 4, 3, 10] [2, 3, 8, 4, 5, 10] [2, 3, 4, 5, 8, 10] [5, 10, 8, 4, 3, 2] Pass 1 swaps the global minimum 2 with 10 → [2, 5, 8, 4, 3, 10]. Pass 2 finds the minimum of positions 2–6 (the 3) and swaps it with 5 → [2, 3, 8, 4, 5, 10]. Two slots finalised, four comparisons' worth of scanning still ahead. Lecture 26 · worked example mt-4 Trace it on paper Run maximum selection sort on [4, 9, 1, 7]. Show the array after every pass and count the swaps. Pass 1: max 9 → end. Pass 2: max 7 → second-from-end. Two swaps, done. Selection sort performs at most n−1 swaps for n elements. Why can bubble sort need far more for the same list? Bubble hops an element right by one position at a time — up to n−1 hops for a single element in one pass. mt-4 <SectionHead eyebrow={eyebrowOf( )} title={ Select it, swap it home } lead= /> {[ { pass: , find: , do: , after: }, { pass: , find: , do: , after: }, { pass: , find: , do: , after: }, { pass: , find: , do: , after: }, ].map((r, i) => ( {r.pass} {r.find} {r.do} {r.after} ))} Final result — the array is sorted after n−1 passes. {SEL_VARIANTS.map((v, i) => ( {v.name} {v.tag} {v.line} ))} Passes drop to half — but every pass still has to compare from both ends toward the middle, so the{ } total number of comparisons stays the same . O(n²) is O(n²), whichever direction you sweep. Aspect Bubble sort Selection sort Complexity O(n²) O(n²) — all variants Swaps per pass up to n−1 — an element can hop many times exactly ONE — after the minimum is found Guaranteed after a pass largest unsorted element bubbles to the end smallest unsorted element selected to the front Verdict simplest possible idea more swap-efficient — still impractical at scale Alphabetical data works identically — compare letters lexicographically (A < B < C … < Z), select the earliest, swap it home. <Takeaways items={[ Selection sort = select one element per pass , place it in its correct position through swapping. , Exactly one swap per pass — the swap-efficient sibling of bubble sort. , Minimum, maximum and bidirectional variants all keep O(n²) time complexity . , Great for education and small datasets ; avoid it for larger lists despite the tidy swap count. , ]} />

chapters.label: Insertion sort
chapters.text: Lecture 27 · Insertion sort. Keys · movements · nearly-sorted wins. insertionsort insertionsort grad-text Bubble and selection swap; insertion moves. Pick the next key, shove everything larger one slot to the right, drop the key into the gap. The left portion is always sorted — the algorithm only ever extends it. 1 The five steps Start from the second item — the first element is assumed sorted. card-warm p-5 grid gap-2.5 md:grid-cols-5 Take the second item as the KEY; compare it with the items on its left Move every element LARGER than the key one position to the right Keep comparing until something smaller appears — or the list begins INSERT the key at the vacant position Repeat for each subsequent element until the whole list is sorted rounded-2xl border border-[#f3e2c8] bg-[#fffaf1] p-4 font-mono text-[.66rem] font-extrabold text-[#c2410c] mt-1.5 text-[.78rem] leading-relaxed text-[#2b2014] 2 The machine [10, 5, 8, 4, 3, 2] — watch each key lift, its larger neighbours slide right, and it drop into place. 3 The lecture walkthrough Same array, all five passes, movements counted. card-warm p-5 grid gap-2.5 Pass 1 5 10 moves right [5, 10, 8, 4, 3, 2] Pass 2 8 10 moves right [5, 8, 10, 4, 3, 2] Pass 3 4 10, 8, 5 move right [4, 5, 8, 10, 3, 2] Pass 4 3 all larger elements move right [3, 4, 5, 8, 10, 2] Pass 5 2 everything moves right [2, 3, 4, 5, 8, 10] grid grid-cols-[auto_auto_1fr_1fr] items-center gap-x-3 gap-y-1 rounded-xl border border-[#f3e2c8] bg-[#fffaf1] px-3 py-2 font-mono text-[.68rem] font-extrabold text-[#c2410c] text-[.78rem] font-extrabold text-[#3e2c1d] text-[.8rem] text-[#2b2014] font-mono text-[.8rem] font-bold text-[#5d7a2e] 4 Three variants, same O(n²) Direction changes the choreography — never the complexity class. grid gap-4 md:grid-cols-3 Minimum insertion sort Classical: minimum elements land at the beginning; larger elements move right; starts from the front. Maximum insertion sort Maximum elements land at the end; smaller elements move left; starts from the second item from the end — the mirror image. Bi-directional insertion sort Both ends at once: minimum and maximum found in a single pass, placed at their respective correct positions. card-warm h-full p-5 font-extrabold text-[#f5e6cd] mt-2 text-[.84rem] leading-relaxed text-[#e9d7bf] 5 Where insertion sort actually wins O(n²) rules out large random lists — but four scenarios make it the right tool. grid gap-3 sm:grid-cols-2 card-warm flex h-full items-start gap-3 p-5 flex h-9 w-9 shrink-0 items-center justify-center rounded-xl rgba(124,154,62,.2) h-4 w-4 text-[#dcebc2] text-[.88rem] font-extrabold text-[#f5e6cd] mt-1 text-[.8rem] leading-relaxed text-[#cbb392] mt-5 grid gap-4 md:grid-cols-2 warn The disadvantage insight The name is the algorithm mt-6 grid gap-4 md:grid-cols-2 Sorting [10, 5, 8, 4, 3, 2] by insertion: what does Pass 3 produce? [5, 8, 10, 4, 3, 2] [4, 5, 8, 10, 3, 2] [3, 4, 5, 8, 10, 2] [5, 10, 8, 4, 3, 2] Pass 3 takes key = 4: every element larger than 4 (10, 8, 5) moves one position right, and 4 is inserted at the front of the sorted portion → [4, 5, 8, 10, 3, 2]. Lecture 27 · walkthrough A sorted roster receives one new student. Which sort fits best — and why? Bubble sort — it handles any order Insertion sort — a nearly-sorted list needs only a short leftward comparison for the new key Selection sort — one swap per pass Any O(n²) sort works equally well here This is insertion sort's signature use case: inserting new elements into already-sorted lists. The new key compares leftward only until it finds its slot — the rest of the list is never touched. Bubble would churn the whole array; selection would re-scan everything. Lecture 27 · use cases mt-4 mt-4 Trace it on paper Run minimum insertion sort on [7, 3, 9, 1]. List the array after each pass and count total movements. Pass 1: key 3, 7 moves right. Pass 2: key 9 stays. Pass 3: key 1 — 9, 7, 3 all move right. Why is insertion sort 'significantly useful for inserting new elements into already sorted lists' while bubble sort is not? Insertion touches only the leftward path of one key; bubble sweeps every adjacent pair of the whole list each pass. <SectionHead dark eyebrow={eyebrowOf( )} title={ Movement, not swapping } lead= /> {[ , , , , , ].map((s, i) => ( STEP {i + 1} {s} ))} {[ { pass: , key: , move: , after: }, { pass: , key: , move: , after: }, { pass: , key: , move: , after: }, { pass: , key: , move: , after: }, { pass: , key: , move: , after: }, ].map((r, i) => ( {r.pass} key {r.key} {r.move} {r.after} ))} {[ { name: , line: }, { name: , line: }, { name: , line: }, ].map((v, i) => ( {v.name} {v.line} ))} {INS_USECASES.map((u, i) => ( {u.title} {u.line} ))} Inefficient for large, randomly ordered lists — O(n²) means comparisons and movements grow by the square (list of 4 → 9 operations, 5 → 16, 6 → 25…). Multiple comparisons and movements per unsorted element. Insertion sort takes an element and inserts it into its proper place within the sorted portion. Small lists: efficient. Nearly-sorted lists: excellent. Sorted lists receiving new arrivals: unbeatable. <Takeaways dark items={[ Insertion sort moves elements to create space — it does not swap them. , Every variant — minimum, maximum, bi-directional — stays O(n²) . , It shines on small, partially sorted, or dynamically growing lists. , New-item insertion into a sorted list is its home turf — no full re-sort needed. , ]} />

Halving beats scanning at any business scale. Lecture 28 · final recap Inserting into the MIDDLE of a linked list is O(1) — but inserting while SEARCHING for the spot is O(n). Why the gap? But reaching the insertion point means walking node by node — that traversal dominates, so search-insert is O(n). No shifting happens: that's arrays.
