chapters.label: Heterogeneity
chapters.groupLabel: Part II · Expectation Gap, Loyalty & STP
chapters.text: Principles of Marketing · Lecture 11 Zoom in and the market splits 100 Netflix users look identical from a distance. Zoom in and six content tribes appear. That zoom — from a homogeneous blob to meaningful segments — is where STP begins. Market heterogeneity The reality that creates the need for segmentation Consumers differ in meaningful ways that affect their purchase and consumption decisions. A market appears homogeneous from a distance but reveals significant diversity when examined closely. Consumers differ in who they are, what they want, why they buy, and how they buy — and different consumer groups value different product attributes. Understanding this diversity is what lets marketers identify meaningful differences worth addressing. Defining segmentation Meaningful groups — not just any groups Segmentation is the process of finding meaningful groups within a market whose members are similar enough to be marketed to differently . The key distinction: segmentation is not simply dividing consumers into groups — divisions must be meaningful and usable to create differentiated marketing strategies, and the differences must be actionable and relevant for marketing purposes. Within vs between Members within a segment share similar characteristics, needs, and desires; segments are distinctly different from each other — so different that each justifies its own marketing strategy, messaging, and product positioning. The face serum market Four segments, four formulations Without segmentation, a generic "daily serum for all skin types" may be acceptable to many but relevant to few . With segmentation, companies create targeted solutions — and each segment requires different product formulations, ingredient focus, and messaging strategies. chapters.label: Bases of segmentation
chapters.groupLabel: Part II · Expectation Gap, Loyalty & STP
chapters.text: Principles of Marketing · Lecture 11 Three classic bases Where you are (Zudio's city-by-city racks), who you are (Pulsar's 'Definitely Male', L'Oréal's age ladder), and how you think (Nike's four tribes) — the geographic, demographic and psychographic bases of segmentation. The bases lab Three windows into the same market Netflix's messaging map Same platform, six segment scripts 100 students watching Netflix appear homogeneous from a distance; zooming in reveals six distinct content preference segments — and each requires different marketing messaging: K-drama fans get emotional messaging ; true crime fans get mystery, twists and investigation focus ; sitcom fans get newer-episodes, feel-good, familiar-content messaging . Common questions, straight answers The three questions every segmenter asks What creates the need for segmentation? Market heterogeneity — the fundamental reality that consumers are different from one another. Why isn't age (18–25) automatically useful? Age alone is insufficient. Within an age group, consumers have vastly different needs and preferences — 18–25 year-old Netflix users have completely different content tastes. Age works only combined with other variables: gender, benefits sought, psychographic profiles. Can two firms segment the same market differently? Yes, absolutely. Different organizations can segment identical markets using different criteria — the strategy depends on company objectives, resources, and positioning goals. Why segmentation matters — and when it didn't Strategic importance + the mass-era exception Targeted product development addressing specific needs Relevant marketing communications Justifies differentiated strategies across segments Improves marketing efficiency and ROI Competitive advantage through relevance, not just acceptance card-warm p-4 text-[.84rem] font-semibold #3a4a48 Historical context — the Pond's era In the mass production eras ( 1980s–1990s ), one-size-fits-all products were viable — think Pond's cold cream . With increasing competition and product variety, segmentation became essential; modern markets require targeted approaches to succeed. [ Geographic: Zudio sells winter layers in Delhi, monsoon-weight clothing in Mumbai, streetwear in Bangalore. , Demographic: Pulsar's "Definitely Male" owns 17–24 males; L'Oréal runs 20+/30+/40+ variants on a 70–80% shared base with age-matched ambassadors. , Psychographic: Nike serves Fitness Focused, Sport Aspirers, Style & Status Seekers, and the Sustainability Conscious — inside 15 major psychographic segments. , Age alone fails — it must be linked to benefits and aspirations; two firms can legitimately segment the same market differently. , Mass eras made one-size-fits-all viable (Pond's); competition made segmentation essential. , ] /> const [tab, setTab] = useState<"geo" | "demo" | "psy">("geo"); const [age, setAge] = useState(21); const band: LorealBand = age < 30 ? chapters.label: Behavior & benefits
chapters.groupLabel: Part II · Expectation Gap, Loyalty & STP
chapters.text: Principles of Marketing · Lecture 12 How they act, what they seek Behavioral segmentation reads what consumers do — usage rate, mode, frequency, pack size, promotional sensitivity. Benefit segmentation reads what they want. Surf Excel turned 25% penetration into 75% by doing both. The five behavioral metrics Dividing consumers by how they act and consume Usage rate How frequently and intensively consumers use a product — heavy users who wash clothes frequently need products offering more washes and value for money. Mode of usage How consumers use the product — machine-wash users prefer convenience and need better stain removal, making liquid detergents ideal for them. Frequency of purchase How often consumers buy — distinct from usage rate; helps identify occasional users who may prefer smaller pack sizes. Pack size Occasional users prefer small sachets, while heavy users benefit from larger, value-oriented bulk packs. Promotional sensitivity Responsiveness to offers and discounts — value seekers actively switch brands based on promotional incentives and special offers. Surf Excel: four behaviors, four products 25% → 75% market penetration By segmenting their market behaviorally, Surf Excel created different products for each segment , significantly increasing market penetration. Without this segmentation, only 25% of potential consumers would purchase ; behavioral segmentation enables the company to effectively target up to 75% of the market . Colgate: benefit-based segmentation The final method — what consumers seek from products The benefit-based principle Within each segment, consumers are similar; between segments, distinctly different. That lets organizations communicate specific product benefits to targeted audiences, address diverse consumer needs within the same product category, and expand market coverage by serving multiple benefit-seeking segments. Exercise: segmenting a fitness app Four segments emerge from one user base card-warm lift p-5 flex items-center gap-1.5 font-extrabold h-4 w-4 mt-1 text-[.72rem] font-extrabold uppercase tracking-[.1em] mt-2 text-[.84rem] font-semibold leading-relaxed #3a4a48 mt-1 text-[.8rem] leading-relaxed Why segmentation matters — and where it leads Organizing chaos, feeding STP Organizing chaos Converting a large, complex consumer base into meaningful, manageable groups. Simplifying strategy Enabling marketers to cater specifically to each segment's unique requirements. Reducing complexity Transforming a 10-lakh consumer base into smaller, focused segments with specific characteristics. card-warm p-5 font-extrabold mt-1.5 text-[.84rem] leading-relaxed #3a4a48 Segmentation is not merely a classification tool — it is the marketer's systematic approach to organizing and managing market heterogeneity. Without it, organizations risk appealing to no one effectively , wasting resources on misaligned products, and missing significant market opportunities. chapters.label: Tupo
chapters.groupLabel: Part II · Expectation Gap, Loyalty & STP
chapters.text: Principles of Marketing · Lecture 13 Tupo and the 3–15 gap nobody served Segmentation and targeting in the real world: a personal-care brand for growing children — too old for baby products, too young for adult products — and the parents who still control the wallet. A market with only two shelves Homogeneous division, heterogeneous reality Market segmentation divides a homogeneous market into heterogeneous groups with similar characteristics. Traditional personal care was divided into just two categories — baby products (0–2 years) and adult & family products (16+ years) . Tupo identified and filled the previously overlooked gap in between: children aged 3–15 who were “too old for baby products but too young for adult products.” Segmentation, then dual targeting Demographic + psychographic; preference-makers + purchasers Demographic Age 3–15 years (growing children) · life stage: early childhood through adolescence Psychographic Age-appropriate product beliefs · natural & organic preference · gentle, non-harsh formulations that prevent skin irritation and infections The key insight — quoted “Children are old enough to have preferences, but young enough that parents still control the wallet and strongly care about their safety.” Children become the preference-makers ; parents remain the purchasers — safety and well-being outrank price. Behaviour shifts the decision pattern Children advocate; parents fund • Children now have distinct preferences rather than simply using parental products. • They actively advocate for specific brands — the lecture's example: daughters requesting Tupo shampoo with shikakai . • Parents value age-appropriate formulations over cost savings. Lessons & the company it keeps What the case teaches — and who else plays this game Cetaphil Bioderma Plum Juicy Chemistry Mama Earth chip Brands employing similar niche-segmentation strategies — each identified an underserved segment and created a specialised product category. Real-world marketing lessons Live through the problem to identify genuine market gaps · understand evolving preferences and generational differences · create authentic value propositions from genuine needs · balance consumer preference with purchasing-power dynamics · and charge premium prices when clear value differentiation exists. Lecture 13 · concept check Tupo charges ₹450 for a 300ML shampoo against a market standard of ₹150. The lecture justifies this premium by… mass-production economies of scale age-appropriate formulation and ingredient quality parents value for safety heavy discounting to build trial spending more on celebrity advertising alone Premium positioning is justified by age-appropriate formulation and ingredient quality — parents demonstrated willingness to pay premium prices for child health and safety. /> [ A gap between two served shelves — 0–2 and 16+ — left 3–15 unserved ; niches hide in plain sight. , Segment on two lenses : demographic (age, life stage) and psychographic (age-appropriate, natural, gentle). , Target twice : children choose, parents pay — dual targeting of preference-makers and purchasers. , Position on dadi-nani trust (turmeric, hibiscus, amla, shikakai) rather than the “organic” label. , ₹150 → ₹450 for 300ML: clear differentiation lets you price premium — and expand (face wash, makeup, Farah Khan). , ] /> const [revealed, setRevealed] = useState(false); return ( The age map — find the hole Lecture 13 · segmentation in the wild Age axis from 0 to 20 with baby products for 0 to 2, adult and family products for 16 plus, and the 3 to 15 gap glowing once revealed 40 150 600 150 8 middle 12 800 0–2 · baby 8 middle 12 800 16+ · adult & family 10 middle 14 800 3–15 · the gap Tupo claimed middle 11.5 700 “too old for baby products but too young for adult products” middle 11.5 700 nobody's products — a market served by no one 0 2 3 15 16 20 150 158 #5f7472 1.6 172 middle 10.5 700 #5f7472 middle 10.5 700 age → ghost teal Show the market before Tupo Before Tupo teal gold Reveal the 3 to 15 gap Reveal the 3–15 gap Tupo identified and filled a previously overlooked gap for children aged 3–15 — a heterogeneous market divided into just two categories until then. chapters.label: SAFE targeting
chapters.groupLabel: Part II · Expectation Gap, Loyalty & STP
chapters.text: Principles of Marketing · Lecture 14 Targeting and the SAFE framework Segmentation hands you many groups; limited budgets and resources force a choice. Targeting evaluates the segments and decides which to focus upon — because if everyone is your priority, then nobody is your priority. The constraint that creates targeting You cannot market to all segments equally Targeting is the process of evaluating market segments and deciding which segment or segments the organisation will focus upon. Organisations have limited budgets and resources, which makes it impossible to market to all identified segments equally — hence the lecture's fundamental principle: “if everyone is your priority, then nobody is your priority.” Four gates before you commit Size · Accessibility · Fitment · Economics Two dangerous assumptions The traps hiding inside 'obvious' choices The largest-segment assumption The largest market segment is not automatically the best target. Volume matters, but so do value and profit margin — a smaller, more profitable segment may generate greater revenue than a larger one with lower willingness to pay or higher competition. The fastest-growing assumption The fastest-growing segment may not align with the organisation's product fit or capabilities. Growth rate alone should not decide — brand capability and product–segment alignment matter equally. The framework in the wild Netflix, Spotify and the sneaker company Netflix A crime-thriller launch with a limited promotional budget of 10 crores concentrates on the “true crime” segment rather than spreading equally across all six consumer segments — focus maximises return on investment Spotify Students were not the largest segment in Europe & India, yet Premium for Students at a subsidised price delivered higher overall revenue — large volume × price elasticity Sneaker company Four segments (sneakerheads, first-time runners, marathon runners, comfort walkers) scanned with SAFE for one new product line → first-time runners: high market size, medium competition, high brand capability, medium willingness to pay Lecture 14 · concept check In the sneaker-company SAFE scan, which segment is the optimal target for the single new running-shoe line? Sneakerheads First-time runners Marathon runners Comfort walkers First-time runners win with high market size, medium competition, high brand capability and medium willingness to pay — superior to the other options. [ Targeting = evaluating and choosing — limited budgets make “everyone” impossible. , SAFE : Size, Accessibility, Fitment, Economics — all four gates must open. , Largest ≠ best (volume vs value & margin ); fastest-growing ≠ best (growth vs fit & capability ). , Netflix puts a 10-crore budget on true crime ; Spotify wins big with students via volume and price elasticity. , If everyone is your priority, nobody is your priority . , ] /> const = useStepPlayer(5, 2800); const statuses = [ "Gate 1 · Size — assess demand inside each segment; it must be large enough to justify the investment and generate revenue.", "Gate 2 · Accessibility — reach and serviceability. chapters.label: Positioning's 3 questions
chapters.groupLabel: Part II · Expectation Gap, Loyalty & STP
chapters.text: Principles of Marketing · Lecture 14 Positioning: the three questions Positioning designs an offering and its image so it occupies a distinctive and valued place in the target consumer's mind relative to competitors. How do we differentiate ourselves in the minds of our target audience? The mind already has shelves Mental associations are manufactured Positioning creates immediate mental associations . Dettol is safety and germ protection; adrenaline and action brands are thrill and adventure; Coca-Cola dominates the cola category; Bisleri is the first brand that comes to mind for mineral water. None of this is accidental — each association results from a deliberate positioning strategy. Three fundamental questions Every positioning strategy must answer them — Sensodyne does Why the three questions work Answering who / what / why lets Sensodyne occupy a distinct space focused specifically on sensitivity relief — differentiation from broader competitors like Colgate or Close-Up, without abandoning the toothpaste category. The complete STP framework Three moves, one integrated strategy [ label: "Segmentation", sub: "divide the heterogeneous market into homogeneous groups", icon: , label: "Targeting", sub: "prioritise by size, accessibility, fitment, economics", icon: , label: "Positioning", sub: "create a distinctive image that resonates and differentiates", icon: , ] The cost of skipping it Appealing to everyone results in diluted messaging and wasted resources. STP keeps new product launches and campaigns strategically focused. [ Positioning = a distinctive and valued place in the target consumer's mind, relative to competitors. , Associations — Dettol = safety, Coca-Cola = cola, Bisleri = water — are built, not born . , Three questions: Who is the target, what category are we in, why choose us? , Sensodyne: sensitive-teeth consumers · toothpaste category · specialised sensitivity relief & protection. , STP is one integrated strategy — skip a step and the messaging dilutes . , ] /> const [flipped, setFlipped] = useState ([false, false, false]); return ( Mental associations — flip to check not accidental; deliberately built button Flip the ${c.brand} card to reveal its mental association h-44 w-full cursor-pointer relative h-full w-full easeInOut preserve-3d card-warm lift absolute inset-0 flex flex-col items-center justify-center gap-2 rounded-2xl p-4 hidden h-8 w-8 #0f766e text-lg font-extrabold text-[#1f2b2b] text-[.72rem] font-bold uppercase tracking-[.14em] text-[#5f7472] absolute inset-0 flex flex-col items-center justify-center gap-2 rounded-2xl p-4 text-center hidden rotateY(180deg) linear-gradient(165deg,#171f1e 0%,#1f2b2b 100%) 1px solid rgba(227,194,107,.25) text-[.7rem] font-bold uppercase tracking-[.16em] #e3c26b text-[.95rem] font-extrabold leading-snug #e9f2ee Positioning creates immediate mental associations when consumers encounter a brand — adrenaline/action brands own thrill and adventure. chapters.text: Principles of Marketing · Lecture 15 The Accor map : many positions, one parent Positioning creates a distinct space in consumers' minds — beyond product features, into perception and psychology. Perceptual maps show how one group serves many segments at once. Why positioning earns its own lecture Mental space · dual time · competitive advantage Mental space Positioning is not only what you do with a product — equally important is what you do to the minds of consumers. Coca-Cola and Bisleri created brand perceptions beyond just being beverages Dual-time perspective Effective positioning puts “one foot in the present and one foot in the future” — anticipating market changes and consumer needs Competitive advantage Positioning correctly to multiple segments simultaneously increases revenue and profitability without one segment negatively influencing the parent company's brand image Accor's three-tier map Ibis · Novotel & Mercure · Pullman & Sofitel Legend The parallel at home ITC runs the same play ITC — five stars above, boutique below Similarly, ITC maintains five-star properties while launching boutique hotel chains to reach price-sensitive consumers — preserving the luxury brand image while capturing segments that would never book the flagship. Multi-segment positioning without brand dilution. chapters.label: Frames · POPs · PODs
chapters.groupLabel: Part II · Expectation Gap, Loyalty & STP
chapters.text: Principles of Marketing · Lecture 15 Frames of reference, POPs & PODs Positioning strategy, step by step: first choose the arena you compete in — natural and extended — then defend the points of parity and build the points of differentiation. Step 1 — the frame of reference Natural competitors vs extended substitutes Natural frame Direct competitors offering similar products — for cooking oil: Safola, Dhara, Fortune Extended frame Indirect competitors that may substitute your product — olive oil, pure ghee, mustard oil, as health consciousness increases The Gypsy King lesson An empty natural frame is not a strategy Key takeaway — the long game Understanding both natural and extended frames of reference is essential for long-term positioning success rather than short-lived market dominance. Step 2 — POPs and PODs Parity earns you a seat; differentiation wins the game POPs Attributes shared with competitors — the bare minimum standards required to be competitive. Uber, Ola and Meru all provide cab services; without POPs a brand loses competitive credibility and consumer trust PODs Unique attributes that distinguish your brand — Uber and Ola run outsourced driver models with personal vehicles, while Meru owns its fleet Lecture 15 · concept check If Lysol removed germ-killing — a POP shared with traditional phenyl — the lecture predicts that… its lime fragrance would carry the brand consumers would revert to Gainda Phenyl nothing would change — PODs are enough removing POPs strengthens positioning Removing a POP significantly weakens competitive positioning: consumers would revert to Gainda Phenyl. POPs must be maintained while building PODs. chapters.label: POD → POP evolution
chapters.groupLabel: Part II · Expectation Gap, Loyalty & STP
chapters.text: Principles of Marketing · Lecture 16 The POD → POP treadmill Points of parity are the minimum requirements to compete; points of differentiation are the reasons to choose. The catch: differentiation decays into parity the moment competitors copy it. POP and POD, defined Category entry ticket vs reason to choose Point of parity Attributes shared by competing brands in the same category — industry-standard features and the minimum requirements to be considered. All disinfectants must kill germs; without POP a brand cannot be competitive Point of differentiation Unique attributes that distinguish one brand from competitors — reasons to choose one over another, creating competitive advantage Lysol vs Genda-Final: better fragrance, plastic bottle, superior packaging Oral-B blue indicator bristles that fade to white when it's time to replace the toothbrush Gillette Mark 3 three-blade design vs two-blade competitors — originally a POD Watch a POD die Three blades → parity → five blades Strategic implications What the treadmill demands Flexibility Operate at multiple levels simultaneously with different product lines Brand portfolio Large organisations may own multiple distinct brands for different segments — L'Oréal and Body Shop Market research Niche and individual-level success requires deep consumer insights into specific needs Positioning Effective STP needs clear understanding of competitors, frame of reference and meaningful differentiation The one-line summary Continuous innovation is necessary to maintain a POD and prevent commoditisation — balance cost efficiency with customisation, because the appropriate strategy depends on resources, market conditions and consumer preferences. [ POP = industry-standard attributes required to compete (all disinfectants kill germs). , POD = unique attributes that create preference (Oral-B's fading bristles, Lysol's fragrance & packaging). , Copied PODs become POPs: three blades → parity → five-blade Fusion as the new POD. , Run multiple levels and brands at once — flexibility is part of the design (L'Oréal / Body Shop). , Innovate continuously or be commoditised . , ] /> const = useStepPlayer(5, 2400); const gillette = step < 1 ? 2 : step < 3 ? 3 : 5; const competitors = step < 2 ? 2 : 3; const notes = [ "The baseline: two-blade razors are the category norm — the POP every competitor must match to be considered.", "Gillette Mark 3 arrives with three blades against two-blade competitors — a genuine POD.", "Competitors copy. chapters.label: The three circles
chapters.groupLabel: Part II · Expectation Gap, Loyalty & STP
chapters.text: Principles of Marketing · Lecture 17 The three circles of positioning POPs and PODs, located on a map: consumer desires × competitor features × your organisation's features. Where the circles overlap decides what you must have, what wins, and what is wasted. Why the model exists Two elements, balanced POPs represent features and benefits common across all competing brands — basic consumer expectations and category requirements (a toothbrush maintaining oral hygiene; an antiseptic having antiseptic properties). PODs are unique features or benefits competitors do not offer — valued by consumers, genuinely different, and able to fulfil desires in ways competitors cannot. Establish parity to compete; create differentiation to win. The map itself Light the zones PODs expire The Dettol motion-sensor lesson Motion-sensor hand wash — a POD that didn't travel Dettol's motion-sensor hand-wash dispenser was initially a POD — but it became expensive and impractical for home use due to the high frequency of use, never achieved universal adoption, and remained primarily in commercial establishments . PODs have a finite lifespan; once competitors copy a differentiation, it automatically becomes a POP. The two-step strategy, revisited Frame first, then differentiation [ label: "Determine frame of reference", sub: "natural + extended competitors → the required POPs", icon: , label: "Identify points of differentiation", sub: "find gaps between competitor offerings and consumer desires", icon: , ] Critical success factors for a POD Five tests before you ship • Valued by consumers — addresses a genuine need or desire. • Defensible — ideally built on sustainable advantages: technology, patents, brand equity. • Addresses a market opportunity — a gap between what competitors offer and what consumers want. • Not easily replicated — if easily copied, it becomes a POP. • Clearly communicated — the target audience must understand and appreciate the differentiation. Lecture 17 · concept check In the three-circles model, a POD lives… at the triple intersection of all three circles where consumer desires meet your features, excluding competitors where you and competitors overlap without consumer desire outside all three circles POP is the triple intersection; POD is consumer desire ∩ your features excluding competitors; the you∩competitor overlap without desire is the invalid zone. [ POPs ensure viability in the category; PODs create preference and justify premium pricing or share gains. , POP = triple intersection ; POD = desires ∩ you, minus competitors . , The you∩competitor overlap without desire is the invalid zone — effort nobody asked for. , PODs have a finite lifespan — Dettol's motion-sensor dispenser stayed commercial for a reason. , Great positioning fulfils consumer desires in ways competitors cannot . , ] /> const [zone, setZone] = useState (null); const labels: Record , string> = POP — the triple intersection: where consumer need overlaps both your offering and competitors'. The category entry ticket. POD — consumer desire ∩ your features, excluding competitors: the unique value proposition. Invalid positioning — features you and competitors both offer that consumers don't desire. Effort with no value. ; return ( The three-circles locator desires × competitors × you Three overlapping circles: consumer desires, competitor features and your features. chapters.label: Why people buy
chapters.text: Principles of Marketing · Lecture 18 Why do people buy ? The fundamental question of consumer behaviour: purchases driven by needs, desires, impulses and emotional states — in minds that are never empty. Every purchase closes a gap Reach · restore · maintain · protect Consumers purchase to reach, restore, maintain, or protect a desired state — the gap between their current state and where they wish to be. And marketing never lands on a blank page: it engages with existing memories, experiences, expectations, desires, identities, biases and goals. Minds are never empty. Stimulus and imagination Consumers respond to imagined consumption almost as strongly as to actual product information. Visual representations and storytelling create experiences that make products feel real and desirable. Three case studies — the story beyond the product Swiggy mangoes · TRIA · Forest Essentials Swiggy mangoes Water droplets, fresh appearance — sensory appeal through visual representation. Consumers feel they are looking at real mangoes: imagined consumption that sells an experience and freshness, not just a product. TRIA hair treatment Targets people experiencing hair loss or thinning; before-and-after narratives attempt to reduce the distance between actual self and desired self , connecting with self-esteem. Relevance varies by audience — it matters only to those with the problem. Forest Essentials serum ₹5,500–7,000 for 30ml. Statistics — 100%, 97%, 94% — build credibility; luxury minimalistic upmarket packaging; visual appeal plus scientific claims create desirability. Sample size: 36. Story over product The insight that ties the cases together • Marketing creates narratives and storylines, not just product features. • The emotional narrative helps consumers achieve their desired state more than the product itself. • Consumers frequently use the appearance of evidence — how data is presented — rather than the actual quality of evidence. • Successful marketing combines product benefits with storytelling that addresses aspirations and self-esteem. [ People buy to reach, restore, maintain or protect a desired state. , Marketing works on minds that are never empty — memories, biases, identities, goals already live there. , Imagined consumption is nearly as strong as the real thing — Swiggy's droplets sell freshness . , TRIA sells the distance between actual self and desired self — relevance varies by audience. , ₹5,500–7,000 serum: 100% · 97% · 94% stats on a sample of 36 — appearance of evidence beats quality of evidence. , ] /> const [verb, setVerb] = useState (null); const v = verb === null ? null : VERBS[verb]; return ( The desired-state machine reach · restore · maintain · protect desired state current state absolute top-1/2 h-9 w-9 -translate-y-1/2 rounded-full linear-gradient(135deg,rgba(15,118,110,.82),#0f766e) 3px solid #fff 0 4px 12px rgba(15,118,110,.35) ${v.from * 100}% ${v.to * 100}% maintain easeInOut maintain protect absolute left-[82%] top-[-14px] -translate-x-1/2 rounded-lg px-2 py-0.5 text-[.62rem] font-extrabold #0f766e #f4fbf9 teal ghost Animate the ${b.k} motivation Clear the machine Clear Buy to ${v.k.toUpperCase()} a desired state — ${v.d}. The purchase is about the gap between the current state and where the consumer wishes to be. Purchases are driven by needs, desires, impulses and emotional states — and context matters (the same consumer buys coffee differently at different times of day). Pick a verb. ); const = useStepPlayer(2, 2600); return ( Forest Essentials — the evidence machine ₹5,500–7,000 for 30ml 100% 97% 94% text-[.78rem] font-bold text-[#5f7472] mt-1 h-7 rounded-lg #eef0ea h-7 rounded-lg linear-gradient(135deg,#e3c26b,#a97d2c) ${s.v}% fine mt-4 rounded-xl px-4 py-3 #f7ecec 1px dashed #dcc3c9 text-[.9rem] font-extrabold text-[#9f3d54] mt-1 text-[.85rem] leading-relaxed text-[#2b2014] the stats the fine print ); const VERBS = [ reach cross the gap from where you are to where you wish to be , restore return to a desired state you once held , maintain hold the desired state steady , protect guard the desired state from slipping , ] as const;

chapters.label: Eras & nudges
chapters.text: Principles of Marketing · Lecture 18 Rational → irrational → nudged How the study of the consumer evolved: classical economics trusted the rational buyer, Kahneman and Tversky broke the assumption, and Thaler's nudges now design the choice environment itself. The evolution, era by era Play through seventy years Evidence for irrationality The breakfast menu experiment Idly, biryani, desserts — in the morning Presented with food menu options in the morning, people choose varied items — idly, biryani, desserts — despite it being early morning. Rational behaviour would suggest everyone picks light breakfast options; the varied choices reflect individual experiences, memories, beliefs and preferences . Heuristics at work — Nutella's Amazon listing 800 ratings 4.5 stars ₹311 discount free delivery cash back offers stock availability chip Mental shortcuts that help consumers move from one decision stage to the next — and choose right options efficiently. The nudge toolkit Choice architecture in the wild European trash disposal Adding an interactive ramp near trash cans transformed waste disposal into a fun activity — proper disposal behaviour increased. Staircase placement Positioning stairs before elevators encourages physical activity; design influences behaviour positively. Bestseller labels Marking products as bestsellers creates choice architecture without demeaning other products — guiding selection toward popular options. Product recommendations Suggesting products based on consumption patterns guides consumers toward suitable choices. card-warm lift p-5 flex items-center gap-2 font-extrabold text-[#1f2b2b] h-4 w-4 #a97d2c mt-1.5 text-[.86rem] leading-relaxed text-[#2b2014] Heuristics vs nudges — the distinction Shortcuts in the mind vs design of the environment Heuristics Mental shortcuts that help compare options — ratings, prices, discounts Nudges Environmental design that guides behavior toward naturally better choices without direct persuasion Lecture 18 · concept check A 'bestseller' label on a menu is best described as… a heuristic, because it is a mental shortcut a nudge, because it redesigns the choice environment without restricting choice a discount, because it changes the price irrational behaviour with no logical basis Nudges are environmental design — choice architecture that guides behavior toward naturally better choices without direct persuasion. Heuristics are the mental shortcuts inside the consumer. [ Classical era (1950s–60s): rational, predictable consumers who buy only what they need. , Cognitive revolution (1970s–90s): Kahneman & Tversky , “Judgment under Uncertainty” — consumers are irrational. , Contemporary era: Thaler's nudges — the mother-elephant philosophy of gentle environmental design. , Heuristics are mental shortcuts (800 ratings · 4.5 stars · ₹311 discount); nudges are designed environments . , Ethical marketing nudges consumers toward decisions beneficial to both parties . , ] /> const = useStepPlayer(3, 3400); const EraIcon = ERAS[step].icon; return ( Three eras of the consumer rational → irrational → nudged ${(step / 2) * 100}% absolute top-1/2 flex h-9 w-9 -translate-x-1/2 -translate-y-1/2 items-center justify-center rounded-full text-[.72rem] font-extrabold transition-all duration-300 ${(i / 2) * 100}% linear-gradient(135deg,rgba(15,118,110,.82),#0f766e) #ffffff #f4fbf9 #5f7472 2px solid #0f766e #d5e6e1 w-1/3 text-center last:text-right first:text-left wait · classical era cognitive revolution contemporary era ); const ERAS = [ Classical era 1950s–60s Dominated by classical economics: consumers are rational beings making predictable choices. People buy only what they need; demand and supply balance naturally; behaviour is easy to forecast. , Cognitive revolution 1970s–90s The key shift: consumers are irrational, not rational decision-makers. Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky's “Judgment under Uncertainty” showed decisions can be irrational with no logical basis — behaviour cannot be predicted with certainty. , Contemporary era present Nudge theory, introduced by Professor Richard Thaler: create a choice environment that guides consumers toward decisions good for them ethically and socially — without restricting freedom of choice. Like a mother elephant nudging her baby back on track. , ];

chapters.label: The five stages
chapters.text: Principles of Marketing · Lecture 19 The five stages of buying Problem recognition → information search → evaluation of alternatives → purchase decision → post-purchase behavior — the theoretical framework every marketer learns first. Walk the stages Play, or step through manually Heuristics speed every stage up Mental shortcuts without extensive analysis Ratings & reviews High ratings — like 4.5 stars — provide assurance of product quality. Brand name Established brands like JBL or Samsung serve as quality indicators. Price discounts Percentage off or reduced prices influence purchase decisions. Scarcity “Only 6 rooms left” creates urgency to purchase immediately. Free delivery Adds perceived value to the offering. Warranty & returns Warranty and return policies reduce perceived risk. Visual elements Product images and property photos influence decision-making. H&M's nudge Items labelled “Few pieces left” create urgency to buy before stock-outs. card-warm lift p-4 text-[.84rem] font-extrabold text-[#1f2b2b] mt-1 text-[.8rem] leading-relaxed text-[#2b2014] Lecture 19 · concept check Weighted scoring — assigning importance to attributes like memory, graphics and price — belongs to which stage? Problem recognition Information search Evaluation of alternatives Post-purchase behavior Evaluation of alternatives compares options within the consideration set, often weighting attributes; the final choice is the best overall value. [ Problem recognition is the trigger — a gap between desired and existing state. , Search happens across Amazon, Swiggy Instamart, stores, social media, peers, experts . , Evaluation = a consideration set + weighted scoring on key attributes. , Purchase is the transaction point , accelerated by heuristics. , Post-purchase feelings (satisfaction ↔ regret) decide retention and loyalty — often overlooked, always essential. , ] /> const = useStepPlayer(5, 2600); const Icon = STAGES[step].icon; return ( 🧭 The five-stage step player the textbook spine of a decision rounded-xl px-3 py-3 text-center transition-all duration-300 linear-gradient(135deg,rgba(15,118,110,.82),#0f766e) #edf6f4 #ffffff 1px solid ${active ? "#0f766e" : "#dce8e4"} mx-auto h-5 w-5 #e3c26b #0f766e mt-1.5 text-[.76rem] font-extrabold leading-tight #f4fbf9 #1f2b2b wait Stage · Stage 5 closes the loop — post-purchase satisfaction feeds retention and loyalty, and sets up the next problem recognition. The theory assumes a linear, sequential process — consumers follow all five stages in order. (Reality is messier; see the next chapter.) ); const STAGES = [ Problem recognition A need or gap between desired and existing state is identified — as simple as feeling hungry, as complex as needing new electronics. The triggering point for all subsequent purchasing decisions. , Information search Consumers actively seek information about potential solutions across channels: websites (Amazon, Swiggy Instamart), physical stores, social media, peer recommendations, expert reviews. The extent of search varies with product importance and involvement. , Evaluation of alternatives Comparison within a consideration set. Key attributes are identified (memory, graphics, price for laptops) and a weighted scoring method is often used — the final choice goes to the best overall value. , Purchase decision The consumer commits to buying — the actual transaction point, often influenced by heuristics and mental shortcuts that expedite the decision. , Post-purchase behavior Feelings after purchase range from satisfaction and confidence to regret and dissatisfaction. Critical for customer retention and brand loyalty — often overlooked in theoretical models but essential in practice. , ];

chapters.label: The messy middle
chapters.text: Principles of Marketing · Lecture 19 The messy middle Linear vs non-linear: real decisions skip stages, backtrack, and loop between exploration and evaluation — an infinity that only closes when the gap between desired and existing state is satisfied. Theory vs reality The same five stages, two very different shapes The loop, live Exploration and evaluation trade places What makes the middle messy Involvement and time High-involvement products Cars, laptops, properties — all five stages methodically; extensive evaluation; multiple sources; test drives, physical visits, detailed comparisons. Low-involvement products Everyday items, routine purchases — stages compressed or skipped; reduced evaluation; habit or convenience; heuristics play a more significant role. Time constraints Limited time encourages skipping or compressing stages; speed over thorough evaluation; heuristics become more critical in expedited decisions. chapters.label: Journey variations
chapters.text: Principles of Marketing · Lecture 20 Journey variations Schiffman and Professor Jain define consumer behavior; the stimulus–choice frame and the five-stage model give it a skeleton — and then real buyers skip, reverse and loop right through it. Consumer behavior is a multidisciplinary field — psychology, marketing, anthropology, behavioral economics and neurology — that explains why, when, how and where purchases are made. It covers not just the purchase decision itself but the emotions, psychology and behaviors that accompany it. Schiffman Consumer behavior is the study of consumers' choices during searching, evaluating, purchasing, and using products and services that satisfy their needs. Professor Jain Consumer behavior is the study of people and activities associated with purchases — how products are chosen, distributed, and used, considering the emotions, psychology, and behaviors these processes create. Stimulus → choice the whole phenomenon in between is the field STIMULUS — any external element that grabs attention momentarily: advertisements, celebrities, colour combinations. CHOICE — the consumer's preference and decision to purchase a product, brand or service. understanding what stimulus triggered a purchase — and how it influenced the mind — is the heart of the field The five-stage model, summarized the theoretical spine every journey is measured against [ icon: , label: "Need recognition", sub: "gap between current & desired state — internal or external trigger" , icon: , label: "Information search", sub: "online, stores, platforms, recommendations" , icon: , label: "Evaluation of alternatives", sub: "specs, price, availability, discounts, benefits" , icon: , label: "Purchase decision", sub: "the transaction" , icon: , label: "Post-purchase", sub: "satisfaction → regret — it decides loyalty" , ] /> …and then reality happens run the five real-world shapes of the same journey gold stage skipping Impulse: jump straight from stimulus to purchase — a 70%-off item bought with no prior need or planning. Direct purchases: a parent's clear instruction ("buy ketchup") skips the first three stages entirely. gold stage reversal After evaluation, new information can send the consumer back to search . Post-purchase experiences or external feedback may even revisit need recognition — questioning whether the purchase was necessary at all. gold circular patterns The journey is not always a forward progression — it can loop , with consumers revisiting earlier stages based on new information, changing circumstances, or unexpected feedback from others. [ Consumer decision-making theoretically follows a linear path but often deviates in practice. , Consumers may skip stages, reverse directions, or loop back based on new information and circumstances. , Both the framework and its real-world variations matter — that is what makes the behavior influencable. , Post-purchase behavior is as important as the pre-purchase process in shaping future decisions and brand loyalty. , Discounts, time constraints, recommendations and availability decide which stages get prioritized or skipped . , ] /> const [mode, setMode] = useState ("linear"); const script = J_SCRIPTS[mode]; const p = useStepPlayer(script.length, 1700); const cur = script[p.i]; const visited = script.slice(0, p.i + 1).map((s) => s.node); const pick = (m: JMode) => ; return ( The journey-path machine one model · five real-world shapes Journey mode linear impulse direct reverse loop Set journey mode to ${m} impulse Skip · impulse (70% off) direct Skip · direct (ketchup) Five-stage journey diagram running in ${mode} mode: ${cur.log} 72 #3f615c 2 impulse M 42 ${J_Y - 26} C 150 ${J_Y - 92}, 430 ${J_Y - 92}, 535 ${J_Y - 26} none 2.5 7 6 direct M 42 ${J_Y + 26} C 150 ${J_Y + 96}, 430 ${J_Y + 96}, 535 ${J_Y + 26} none 2.5 7 6 reverse M 400 ${J_Y - 24} C 370 ${J_Y - 64}, 295 ${J_Y - 64}, 265 ${J_Y - 24} none #f0b6a4 2.5 6 5 loop M 265 ${J_Y + 24} C 295 ${J_Y + 66}, 370 ${J_Y + 66}, 400 ${J_Y + 24} none 2.5 6 5 8 middle 11 800 stimulus 20 #155e57 #122e2b #3f615c 2 middle 13 800 #d8f3ec #7ea49d middle 11 700 #cfe9e2 #7ea49d 12 spring middle 10.5 700 the entire phenomenon between the stimulus and the choice is consumer behavior Journey machine Mode: · step / — ); const J_Y = 82; type JMode = "linear" | "impulse" | "direct" | "reverse" | "loop"; const J_SCRIPTS: Record = A stimulus grabs attention — an ad, a celebrity, a colour combination. Need recognition — a gap opens between the current and the desired state. Internal (the product is running out) or external (an ad, a recommendation). Information search — online research, retail stores, multiple platforms, recommendations. Evaluation of alternatives — specifications, pricing, availability, discounts, benefits. Purchase decision — the final choice and the transaction. Post-purchase — satisfaction and happiness, or dissatisfaction, regret, guilt. It shapes loyalty. Impulse: a heavily discounted tag — 70% off — shouts from the shelf. Straight to purchase. No prior need, no planning — need recognition, search and evaluation are all bypassed. Post-purchase still arrives — a bargain glow, or a small twinge of guilt. Direct purchase: a clear instruction — \u201Cplease buy ketchup.\u201D The first three stages are skipped entirely; the consumer proceeds directly to purchase. Post-purchase — was it the right ketchup? Feedback still loops back. Need recognition — the journey starts normally. Information search — options gathered. Evaluation — comparing specifications, price, discounts\u2026 Stage reversal — new information sends the journey BACK to search to explore additional options. Back to evaluation, with a better-informed consideration set. Purchase decision. Post-purchase can reverse too: external feedback may revisit need recognition itself — \u201Cwas this even necessary?\u201D A stimulus starts the journey\u2026 Need recognition. Search. Evaluation. Circular pattern — new information, changing circumstances or unexpected feedback pulls the consumer back to an earlier stage. Evaluate again — the loop can repeat any number of times. Purchase decision — the loop finally exits. Post-purchase — and the whole journey feeds the next one. ;

chapters.label: Autopsy of a purchase
chapters.text: Principles of Marketing · Lecture 20 Autopsy of a purchase A classroom exercise takes one real, ordinary purchase and dissects it stage by stage — revealing the actual path a consumer walks, and the exact nudge that closes the deal. The autopsy of purchase is a practical application of everything above: analyze a recent purchase and surface the stages you actually went through — including the ones theory says should be there but weren't. The specimen on the table: Moroccan oil shampoo . Lay the stages on the table trigger → search → alternatives → the closing nudge → purchase → post-purchase Why the autopsy matters The textbook says every stage runs in order. The autopsy found search across Nyka, Amazon and retail stores , four serious alternatives — L'Oreal, Kerastase, Nat Habit, Flam — and then a single 15% discount settling the whole evaluation. Real journeys are shorter than models, and one heuristic can carry the final weight. The stage that outlives the receipt Post-purchase here was satisfaction and confidence in nourishing hair — happiness and positive feelings. That emotional residue is not the end of the journey; it is the trigger waiting for the next repurchase , which lets the consumer skip exploration entirely next time. [ An autopsy maps the actual stages of a real purchase — not the theoretical checklist. , Search spanned platforms and stores ; evaluation produced four alternatives with similar benefits. , The final decision factor was a 15% discount on Nyka — one heuristic, one closed deal. , Post-purchase satisfaction feeds the next journey — as important as everything before the receipt. , ] const p = useStepPlayer(AUTOPSY.length, 1900); const cur = AUTOPSY[p.i]; return ( The autopsy table — step through it Moroccan oil shampoo · classroom exercise Autopsy of a purchase, step ${p.i + 1} of ${AUTOPSY.length}: ${cur.t} — ${cur.tag} 70 58 690 58 5 6 58 17 #155e57 #122e2b #3f615c 62.5 middle 12 800 #d8f3ec #7ea49d 94 middle 10.5 700 #cfe9e2 #7ea49d 20 5 #a97d2c 1 spring 4 4 Autopsy machine wait Step of · Autopsy status — step / : · ); const AUTOPSY = [ Trigger Need recognition Internal need — the existing shampoo was running out. The gap opened on its own; no advertisement required. , Search Information search Multiple platforms checked — Nyka, Amazon, retail stores — comparing price, expiry dates and availability. , Alternatives Evaluation of alternatives L'Oreal, Kerastase, Nat Habit and Flam — brands offering similar benefits, all in the consideration set. , Final factor the nudge that closed it A 15% discount on Nyka made the final difference in choosing the product. , Purchase Purchase decision The transaction completes — the Moroccan oil shampoo is bought, the discount having tipped the evaluation. , Post-purchase Post-purchase behavior Satisfaction and confidence in nourishing hair — happiness and positive feelings that quietly book the next purchase. , ];

chapters.label: Touchpoints & framework
chapters.text: Principles of Marketing · Lecture 21 Touchpoints & the integrated framework The journey is non-linear; involvement sets its depth; marketing acts far beyond the point of sale — and underneath it all runs a six-part cycle from unfulfilled need to tension reduction. low involvement Pizza at 11:30 PM — triggered by immediate need or a notification. Minimal search or evaluation; a quick decision without extensive comparison; driven by convenience and impulse. high involvement Laptop purchase — extensive search and evaluation; specifications, brands, configurations and price ranges; detailed comparison with assigned weightage; significant emotional response post-purchase. No generalized pattern applies Decision-making is highly subjective and varies from individual to individual — the same person sails through a pizza order and spends weeks inside the messy middle for a laptop. Marketing lives at every touchpoint not just at the point of sale gold trigger Discounts, celebrity endorsements, events — influence at the trigger phase itself. gold search Discovering product popularity or best sellers while exploring options. gold evaluation Product quality comparisons — the evaluation stage is a marketing surface too. gold post-purchase Reviews, ratings, recall — and past positive experiences become future triggers, letting consumers skip exploration and go straight to purchase. The integrated consumer behavior framework unfulfilled need → fear/tension → drive → behavior → consumption → goal fulfillment & tension reduction Individual variability The drive → behavior transition depends on individual perceptions, personality traits, ability to learn, and personal attitudes. The messy middle Once triggered, consumers enter an infinity zone of continuous exploration and evaluation — comparing across Amazon, Flipkart and physical stores, filling carts and wish lists — until a strong enough stimulus converts it into an actual purchase. [ Decision-making is a continuous, non-linear process of exploration and evaluation. , The journey differs sharply by involvement level — pizza at 11:30 PM vs a laptop. , Marketing influences multiple touchpoints across the entire journey , not just at purchase. , Behavior is fundamentally driven by the need to reduce tension from unfulfilled needs, wants or desires . , Outcomes are individually specific — explaining them requires perception, personality, learning and attitudes . , ] /> const p = useStepPlayer(CYCLE.length, 1700); const cur = CYCLE[p.i]; return ( The framework-cycle machine unfulfilled need → tension reduced Integrated consumer behavior framework, stage ${p.i + 1} of 6: ${cur.t} — ${cur.d} 6 7 middle 12 800 tension ↓ middle 10 700 at goal fulfillment 24 #155e57 #122e2b #3f615c middle 12 800 #d8f3ec #7ea49d spring middle 10.5 800 unfulfilled need middle 10.5 800 goal fulfillment & tension reduction Framework cycle wait Stage of 6 mt-3 flex flex-wrap gap-2 Cycle status — stage /6: ); const CYCLE = [ Unfulfilled need A gap between the current state and the desired state — the lecture's example: hunger. It can be a need, a want or a desire. , Fear / tension The psychological discomfort the unmet need creates. Tension is the engine of everything that follows. , Drive An internal trigger — the motivation to act, produced to reduce the tension. , Behavior Individual-specific actions. One hungry person cooks; another orders delivery; another visits a restaurant, eats what's available at home, or asks family to prepare food. , Consumption The actual use of the product or service the behavior produced. , Goal fulfillment The need is satisfied — tension reduces. The cycle closes and can begin again with the next unfulfilled need. , ]; const CYCLE_POS = [-90, -30, 30, 90, 150, 210].map((a) => );

chapters.label: Three theories
chapters.text: Principles of Marketing · Lecture 23 Three theories of motivation Freud, Maslow and Herzberg answer the same question — why do we do what we do? — from three directions: the subconscious, the hierarchy of needs, and the two factors of satisfaction. These theories explain what initiates the five-stage decision-making process — need recognition, search, evaluation, purchase, post-purchase. All three remain fundamentally relevant; consumers may not climb the ladder linearly and might skip stages, but knowing which theory is operating helps predict and influence behavior. Freudian theory — the iceberg behavior is guided by subconscious, not conscious, motivations ID Basic instincts and immediate desires — wanting that samosa right now. Ego Rationality and reality — eating only the cover of the samosa, balancing desire with health. Super Ego Morality and what is considered correct — refusing the samosa for health reasons. Application Consumer decisions are motivated by which of the three dominates — instinct, reality, or moral consideration. Only 10% of decision-making comes from the conscious mind; 90% originates from the subconscious and pre-conscious. Maslow's hierarchy — the pyramid behavior is driven by the lowest unmet need The hungry-person test A hungry person would prioritize buying food over purchasing luxury items — the lowest unmet level runs the show. Life journey: students secure physiological and safety needs through education; young professionals build security through employment; mid-career, social and esteem needs dominate; later in life, the pursuit turns to self-actualization and personal meaning. Herzberg's two-factor theory hygiene prevents dissatisfaction; motivating factors create satisfaction The Free Chai Rule Free chai at work will not make employees love their jobs — but removing it creates discontent . Salary, working conditions and basic amenities are expected : they prevent dissatisfaction without inspiring motivation. True motivation comes from meaningful work, recognition, and opportunities for growth. [ Freud: 90% of decision-making is subconscious — ID (instinct), Ego (reality), Super Ego (morality). , Maslow: physiological → safety → social → esteem → self-actualization; the lowest unmet need leads. , Herzberg: hygiene factors prevent dissatisfaction; motivating factors create satisfaction — fix both, inspire with the second. , All three remain relevant; consumers may skip stages and rarely climb in a straight line. , These theories are the ignition system for the five-stage decision process. , ] /> return ( Freud's iceberg: 10% conscious above the waterline, 90% subconscious below — pre-conscious near the surface, unconscious in the depths 0 0 0 1 0 104 560 104 10 8 12 800 Conscious — thoughts and beliefs you are fully aware of 22 800 10% 22 800 90% 12 800 Subconscious & pre-conscious — where most decisions originate 214 140 470 140 5 5 10.5 700 pre-conscious — memories recalled when triggered 214 222 470 222 5 5 10.5 700 unconscious — deep desires, accessible through dreams ); const p = useStepPlayer(MASLOW.length, 1700); const cur = MASLOW[p.i]; return ( Maslow's pyramid — climb it the lowest unmet need drives behavior Maslow's five-level pyramid, level ${5 - p.i} highlighted: ${cur.t} — ${cur.d} 0 0 1 1 url(#mp-act) rgba(15,118,110,.34) rgba(233,242,238,.10) #3f615c pointer middle 9.5 800 SELF-ACTUALIZATION middle 9.5 800 ESTEEM middle 9.5 800 SOCIAL middle 9.5 800 SAFETY middle 9.5 800 PHYSIOLOGICAL click a level, or let the climber run Maslow pyramid wait Level of 5 · climbing from the base Life journey: Pyramid status — level /5: . Consumers do not progress until the current level is satisfied. ); const [hyg, setHyg] = useState(true); const [mot, setMot] = useState(false); const dissat = hyg ? 18 : 92; const sat = mot ? 88 : 12; return ( The two-factor dials hygiene prevents · motivating propels Hygiene factors — job dissatisfiers Salary & compensation · working conditions · company policies · supervisor relationships ${dissat}% spring Dissatisfaction meter Toggle hygiene factors hygiene present hygiene removed polite Present → dissatisfaction is prevented. Motivating factors — job satisfiers Achievement & accomplishment · recognition & appreciation · responsibility · growth & development ${sat}% spring Satisfaction meter Toggle motivating factors motivators present motivators absent polite Present → genuine satisfaction and motivation appear. This is the only dial that inspires. Absent → not dissatisfaction — just neutrality. Nothing to be unhappy about, nothing to be excited by. Later in life, the climb turns to personal meaning. , Esteem needs Self-esteem, recognition, social status and respect. chapters.label: Perception & brands
chapters.text: Principles of Marketing · Lecture 24 Perception & the brand flip Perception is the lens through which consumers view products and brands — and it is not built on objective reality. Marketers shape it with cues, illusions and brand associations. Perception is the process of how individuals see and interpret the world around them. It is not based solely on objective reality — it is heavily influenced by the external cues and stimuli marketers provide. How marketers influence perception illusions prove the flip is possible — cues decide what you see The classic illusions The lecture uses two famous ambiguous images — the young lady / elderly lady and the duck / rabbit . Same image, two readings: adding elements — like carrots in the rabbit-duck exercise — dramatically shifts how consumers perceive the object. The marketer's cue kit • Adding visual elements — packaging design, colours, imagery • Introducing price points and discounts • Creating brand associations through endorsements and advertising • Attaching meaning and messaging to physical products The brand flip the same model, three brands, three completely different expectations [ Perception is selective, subjective, constructive and abstract — never a neutral camera. , Illusions (young lady / elderly lady, duck–rabbit) prove that cues decide what is seen . , Nykaa flips the same model to makeup and skincare; Fab India to clothing and accessories; Label Life to fashion and lifestyle. , The brand name alone re-categorizes the ad — that is the power of brand perception in decision-making. , ] /> const [cue, setCue] = useState<"duck" | "rabbit">("duck"); const rabbit = cue === "rabbit"; return ( Cue check — duck, or rabbit? Marketers do exactly this: packaging, colours, imagery, price cues. The duck–rabbit exercise: same lines, different perception. Adding elements (like carrots) dramatically shifts how the object is read. ); const [idx, setIdx] = useState(0); const cur = BRAND_FLIP[idx]; return ( The brand-flip switcher same model · three different expectations The identical model, shown for ${cur.brand}: the ad never changes — only the brand name does middle 10 700 the model — identical in all three ads 14 10 8 Choose the brand Show the ad branded as ${b.brand} wait The viewer now expects to see: Same model, same pose — the brand name alone re-categorizes the entire ad. chapters.label: The almonds experiment
chapters.text: Principles of Marketing · Lecture 24 The almonds experiment Four packs of essentially the same almonds. The class prefers one — until the prices are revealed. Then meet perceptual product categories: the shelf trick that ends pure price wars. Product categories vs perceptual product categories how consumers file products by default — and how marketers want them filed By default, consumers store information as broad product categories — "toothpaste", "cars", "ketchup". The marketing goal is to create perceptual product categories built on specific needs and benefits. That lets marketers cater to different needs, reduce direct price competition, increase overall market sales, and build loyalty on benefits rather than product type. Toothpaste Sensitive teeth (Sensodyne) · overall protection (Colgate Total) · freshness (Close-Up) · whitening (Colgate Visible White) — four perceptual categories, one basic category. Cars Hatchbacks, sedans, trucks, ambulances, fire trucks — same basic category, very different perceived jobs. Ketchup Fresh tomato, premium, chef special — the condiment aisle, split into meanings. The Horlicks case one brand, five perceptual categories — each a life stage Growth Plus children's growth & development Light health-conscious, reduced sugar Jr. children aged 8–14 Mother's pregnant women's nutrition Women's 30+ age-specific needs for women 30+ card-warm h-full p-4 text-[.95rem] font-extrabold mt-1 text-[.8rem] leading-relaxed text-[#5f7472] [ Consumers chose Option D (~9/10) for perceived benefits — California almonds, gluten-free, high fiber, antioxidants, reusable zip-lock — not better almonds. , The price reveal (₹1,000 / ₹800 / ₹550 / ₹2,700) reshuffled preferences toward C and B — but premium buyers stayed with D. , Price is a perceptual cue : expensive reads as better quality. , Perceptual product categories (Sensodyne = sensitivity, Colgate Total = 24-7 protection, Close-Up = freshness, Visible White = whitening) end pure price competition — and Horlicks multiplied itself into five life-stage variants. , ] /> const [priced, setPriced] = useState(false); const [pick, setPick] = useState (null); const reset = () => ; return ( The almonds experiment same almonds · four meanings Marketing rarely changes the physical product — it changes the meaning attached to it. chapters.label: Sensory thresholds
chapters.text: Principles of Marketing · Lecture 25 Sensory thresholds & the four stages Perception is what people think in their minds — subjective and changeable. It starts at the senses: absolute, subliminal and differential thresholds decide what gets in; four stages decide what it becomes. "First impression is the last impression" — first impressions significantly shape consumer perception. Marketers can mold it strategically by understanding how the brain processes information, and perception's inherent biases can be leveraged for marketing advantage. flex items-start gap-3 rounded-xl px-3.5 py-2.5 transition-colors duration-200 #fffaf1 1px solid rgba(227,194,107,.45) mt-0.5 shrink-0 text-[.86rem] leading-relaxed text-[#241a0f] mr-2 font-mono text-[.72rem] font-bold uppercase tracking-wider From stimulus to purchase intent exposure → attention → interpretation → organization → outcome [ Perception is subjective and can change over time — and it can be strategically molded. , Absolute threshold : the minimum stimulus that captures attention (the lit candle in a dark room). , Subliminal perception : multi-sensory ads — pouring liquid, ice cubes — create emotional connection. , Differential threshold : the just-noticeable difference, grain by grain of rice. , Exposure → attention → interpretation → organization — and the outcome is a purchase or the intent to purchase . , ] /> const p = useStepPlayer(PSTAGES.length, 1600); const cur = PSTAGES[p.i]; const xs = [95, 265, 435, 605, 715]; return ( The four-stage flow machine exposure → attention → interpretation → organization → outcome Perception formation, stage ${p.i + 1} of 5: ${cur.t} — ${cur.d} 56 56 #3f615c 2 56 #7c5a1e #155e57 #122e2b #3f615c 61 middle 12.5 800 #d8f3ec #7ea49d ₹? 102 middle 10.5 700 #cfe9e2 #7ea49d Organization Organi- Organization 116 middle 10.5 700 #cfe9e2 #7ea49d spring middle 10.5 700 sensory receptors register the stimulus — then four stages build the perception Perception stages wait Outcome Stage ${p.i + 1} of 4 Stage machine — step /5: . Final outcome: purchase or intent to purchase. ); const PSTAGES = [ Exposure Encountering the advertisement or product — the stimulus first reaches the senses. , Attention Focusing on specific elements — most of the exposure is filtered out right here. , Interpretation Making sense of what is perceived — meaning is assigned, biased by experience. , Organization Structuring the perception in the mind — Gestalt principles do much of this work. , Outcome A purchase, or the intent to purchase — perception has done its job. , ];

chapters.label: The Gestalt lab
chapters.text: Principles of Marketing · Lecture 25 The Gestalt lab The brain does not process images like a camera — it organizes elements into patterns and predicts from past experience. Five principles, five live demos, and the marketing that rides on each. The Gestalt principle: humans organize visual elements into meaningful patterns rather than processing them separately. The brain predicts what it expects to see from past experience — and when predictions don't match reality, it finds the closest matching interpretation. Aesthetic, organized interfaces (like Pinterest) work precisely because of this: navigation becomes easy to understand. [ Figure & ground — distinguish object from background to create the focal point (iPod, Sensodyne). , Continuity — guide viewers through sequences and natural decision flows (road arrows, Cars24). , Grouping & similarity — organize related information for easier comprehension (uniforms, menus). , Proximity — create logical relationships and facilitate comparison (notice boards, price displays). , Closure — engage consumers by letting them mentally complete incomplete information . , ] /> const [tab, setTab] = useState(0); const cur = GESTALT_TABS[tab]; return ( The Gestalt lab — five live demos the brain organizes; it doesn't photograph Gestalt principles button tab Gestalt principle: ${g.t} rounded-xl px-3.5 py-2 text-[.8rem] font-bold shadow-sm transition-transform duration-200 hover:-translate-y-0.5 #f0faf7 #fffdf9 1px solid ${CREAM_BORDER} wait Principle of 5 · In marketing gold Gestalt lab — demo /5: . The brain organizes visual objects into coherent patterns and predicts what it expects to see. );

chapters.label: Attitude & the buckets
chapters.text: Principles of Marketing · Lecture 26 Attitude & the two buckets Attitude is the bridge between perception and decision — Attitude = f(Object, Attributes). And brands that connect attributes to human traits escape the transactional bucket entirely. Motivation drives individuals to act on needs and desires; perception is how consumers interpret and categorize products — which differs from objective reality. Consumers naturally file products into broad categories ("cars", "toothpaste"), but organizations win by shaping the perceptual categories: Sensodyne = sensitivity relief, Colgate Total = 24/7 protection, Close-Up = fresh breath — and Horlicks splitting into variants for children, adults and diabetics. Attitude as the bridge perception ⇄ attitude, formed from past + fresh experiences Perception Attitude Attitude = f(Object, Attributes) A favorable or unfavorable response toward something. The relationship is bidirectional — perception leads to attitude, and attitude influences perception. Formation depends on past experiences and fresh experiences . The decision is never based solely on the product itself, but on the product's attributes as perceived by the consumer . Humanizing brands — the two buckets Epicurus, 340–270 BC: almost everything is transactional. Almost. Case study — why father-daughter in a tire ad? Because a tire is the most utilitarian product imaginable — so the ad humanizes it. Daughters feel protected and safe with their fathers; that emotional connection (safety, protection) maps to tire quality — a quality tire provides vehicle stability and safety. The tire becomes associated with protecting loved ones , not just a transactional purchase — the brand lands in the love bucket , and loyalty follows. [ Attitude = f(Object, Attributes) — bidirectional with perception, built from past + fresh experiences. , Attributes are the marketer's flexible lever — the Borges tea won on 2× antioxidants, 4× vitamin C, oleuropin, zero caffeine. , Epicurus: everything is transactional except parent → child — the only true love-bucket relationship. , Humanized brands shift the relationship from transactional to relational — the tire ad's father-daughter safety story is the template. , ] /> const rows = [ Antioxidants 2× , Vitamin C 4× , ]; return ( The attribute war — Borges Olive Leaf Infusion Tea vs green tea flex items-baseline justify-between text-[.84rem] font-bold text-[.84rem] font-extrabold mt-1 h-3 overflow-hidden rounded-full #e8e2d2 h-full rounded-full ${r.w}% oleuropin — helps regulate blood pressure zero caffeine zero added flavors These attributes were perception-driven — organizations have far more flexibility manipulating attributes than the core product itself, and that is what positioned Borges as superior. ); const [placed, setPlaced] = useState >( ); const [log, setLog] = useState("Click a relationship — it lands in the bucket Epicurus filed it under (340–270 BC)."); const reset = () => Cleared. Click a relationship to file it again. ; const file = (it: (typeof BUCKET_ITEMS)[number]) => ${it.label} → ${it.bucket === "love" ? "LOVE bucket" : "utilitarian bucket"}. ${it.why} ; const utilItems = BUCKET_ITEMS.filter((it) => placed[it.id] === "util"); const loveItems = BUCKET_ITEMS.filter((it) => placed[it.id] === "love"); return ( The bucket sorter Epicurus · 340–270 BC File "${it.label}" into its bucket text-[.82rem] font-bold Utilitarian / transactional bucket You give something, I give something in return. rounded-lg border px-2.5 py-1 text-[.74rem] font-bold #fff text-[.76rem] font-bold text-[#9aa5a0] Love bucket Pure affection — no expectation of return. rounded-lg px-2.5 py-1 text-[.74rem] font-bold #f0faf7 text-[.76rem] font-bold text-[#9aa5a0] Reset the bucket sorter Reset );

chapters.label: Retention vs acquisition
chapters.text: Principles of Marketing · Lecture 26 Retention vs acquisition Acquisition is expensive and the market is overcrowded; churn keeps draining the funnel. Retention costs roughly a seventh to a tenth as much — the ROI case is not subtle. The takeaway that outlives the spreadsheet Organizations succeed by understanding that consumers don't purchase products — they purchase solutions to their needs and emotional satisfaction . Recognize perceptual product categories, leverage attributes, humanize the brand — and retention follows. [ CAC is high in an overcrowded market — attention is the scarce resource. , Retention costs about 1/7th to 1/10th of acquisition — the cheapest growth lever available. , Churn — customers leaving for competitors — is the major organizational challenge. , Focus on retention: better ROI than constant acquisition . , Consumers purchase solutions and emotional satisfaction, not products . , ] const [ratio, setRatio] = useState<7 | 10>(7); return ( The cost-comparison machine acquire 1 vs retain 1 Acquire a new customer — CAC 10 units 100% High investment — especially in an overcrowded market where every competitor is bidding for attention. Retain an existing one 1 unit — 1/ th of CAC ${100 / ratio}% spring Retention costs approximately one-seventh to one-tenth of acquisition costs. Show retention at one-seventh of CAC 1/7th Show retention at one-tenth of CAC 1/10th Churn — the leak in the bucket Customer churn : consumers leave for competitors despite every rupee of acquisition effort spent on them. Every churned customer must be re-acquired — at 7–10× the cost of simply keeping them. Focus on retention and the ROI beats constant acquisition — the same effort compounds instead of leaking. Comparison — acquire: 10 units · retain: unit s (1/ th of CAC). Switch the dial to see the bar move; either way, retention wins. );

chapters.label: The ABC model
chapters.text: Principles of Marketing · Lecture 27 The ABC model of brand humanization Attribute → Benefit → Characteristic: physical features, the advantages they buy, and the human values they carry. CEAT, Asian Paints and a pug show how brands stop selling products and start selling meaning. Walk the chain two brands, the same three steps from spec sheet to human value Love bucket vs utilitarian bucket why the humanized approach compounds loyalty utilitarian — transactional • Focuses on product quality, performance, value for money • Every competitor can offer similar features • Easily replaceable — subject to consumer churn love bucket — relational • Incorporates emotional and human elements • Creates deeper consumer connections • Positive word-of-mouth and favorable attitudes • Reduces churn — loyalty beyond functional benefits Anthropomorphism — the Hutch pug Humanizing a brand — anthropomorphism — means relating human-like traits to products and using living elements (humans, animals) to create emotional connection. The Hutch pug advertisement outperformed many celebrity-endorsed campaigns: the dog followed the boy everywhere, and the network "followed you too" — no superstar required. The full sequence where humanization plugs into consumer behavior [ icon: , label: "Motivation", sub: "the drive that initiates the purchase decision" , icon: , label: "Perception", sub: "interpretation of product attributes and features" , icon: , label: "Attitude", sub: "favorable / unfavorable — f(object, attributes)" , icon: , label: "Decision", sub: "the final choice, influenced by attitude toward the brand" , ] /> [ A → B → C : attributes (tire grooves, paint colors) → benefits (anti-skid traction, personalized spaces) → characteristics (safety, belongingness, self-expression). , CEAT : groove tech → anti-skid → a father protecting his family → the love bucket. , Asian Paints : "Har Ghar Kuch Kehta Hai" — belongingness, self-expression, memories, identity; relatable families, not celebrities. , Anthropomorphism works: Hutch's pug beat celebrity campaigns. , Humanization influences motivation → perception → attitude → decision — and builds long-term preference. , ] /> const [caseIdx, setCaseIdx] = useState(0); const p = useStepPlayer(3, 1700); const cur = ABC_CASES[caseIdx].nodes[p.i]; return ( The A → B → C chain machine Run the ABC chain for ${c.brand} ${ABC_CASES[caseIdx].brand} ABC chain, step ${p.i + 1} of 3: ${cur.t} — ${cur.d} 66 66 #3f615c 2.5 30 128 72 16 #155e57 #122e2b #3f615c 50% 50% 60 middle 11 800 #7ea49d ABC 82 middle 12.5 800 #d8f3ec #7ea49d Attribute Benefit Characteristic spring 0 0 8 #a97d2c 2 middle 10.5 700 connect all three and the brand stops selling a product — it sells emotions and values ABC chain (${ABC_CASES[caseIdx].brand}) wait · step of 3 Chain status — : A B C · );

chapters.label: The bias lab
chapters.text: Principles of Marketing · Lecture 28 The bias lab Cognitive biases are systematic errors in judgment that run at an unconscious level — mental shortcuts that help consumers navigate complex choices, and the exact levers marketers build on. Conscious vs unconscious two very different kinds of bias Conscious biases Stereotypes developed through social conditioning, environmental influences, and how the people around us think. Unconscious biases Cognitive biases operating at a subconscious level — unintentional judgment errors that misinterpret information and shape consumer behavior. The Benetton controversy — conscious bias on display The lecture's example of conscious stereotyping: in the Benetton advertisement controversy, consumers stereotypically associated darker-skinned individuals with criminals and lighter-skinned individuals with authority figures — bias shaped by social conditioning, not by the ad's intent. Four biases, four live demos anchoring · bandwagon · scarcity · endowment — poke each one [ Cognitive biases are subconscious errors in thinking that lead to judgment errors in decisions. , They function as mental shortcuts (heuristics) — useful, but they often produce irrational purchases. , Marketers deliberately use them: anchoring (Save 16%), bandwagon (15,000 learning), scarcity (only 6 rooms left), personalization (your name on the cup). , Scarcity messaging nudges low-involvement purchases — and the stock often replenishes after 24 hours. , Biases are not always bad — but recognizing them makes consumers more deliberate . , ] /> const dims = ["Price", "Ratings", "Delivery"] as const; const [anchor, setAnchor] = useState<(typeof dims)[number] | null>(null); return ( Anchoring Attention anchors on one element — and everything else is excluded. In smartphone comparisons consumers anchor on price, ratings or delivery speed . Anchor the comparison on ${d} Clear the anchor mr-1 inline h-3.5 w-3.5 rounded-xl p-2.5 1px solid ${CREAM_BORDER} text-[.72rem] font-extrabold mt-1.5 text-[.62rem] font-bold uppercase tracking-wide mt-0.5 h-1.5 overflow-hidden rounded-full #e8e2d2 h-full rounded-full ${d === "Price" ? 60 + ph.length * 6 : d === "Ratings" ? 74 + ph.length * 2 : 48 + ph.length * 7}% #b9c6c1 Anchored on ${anchor} — the other information is excluded, and the decision moves to its next stage on this element alone. Pick an anchor — price, ratings or delivery — and watch the rest of the comparison fade. Zoom highlights "Save 16%" when switching from monthly to annual billing — anchoring you to the longer commitment. ); const [lens, setLens] = useState<"herd" | "excl">("herd"); const herd = lens === "herd"; return ( Bandwagon effect If others are doing it, it must be valuable — the more people use something, the more credible it appears. Course platforms show "15,000 people learning on edX today." Hotel A 1,157 reviews · 8.5 88% 84% credibility reads high Hotel B 281 reviews · 8.1 70% 88% fewer voices, less proof less crowding, more exclusivity View through the herd lens Herd lens View through the exclusivity lens Exclusivity lens Theory view: 1,157 reviews at 8.5 look more credible than 281 reviews at 8.1 — the herd validates.
